If you make a VM open while it runs confined, its launches keep it confined to its proxy, which now applies an open VM’s rules, until it next starts, and they warn you that the VM leaves its proxy’s confinement when it next starts. In a terminal, each of those launches first asks whether to restart the VM now, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too (restarting).

When it isn’t enforced

On every launch devvm checks on this machine that the VM still runs on the process devvm started confined, and that a direct connection from the VM to the internet fails. A VM that fails either check shows as unenforced, and devvm offers to restart it confined or stops it, as the self-check describes.

Learning the hosts a VM needs

Finding every host a project needs one block at a time takes a while, so a VM can learn them instead. It starts with the internet tier’s access, and its proxy logs each host it reaches, as it does on every tier. Once you’ve run the project’s installs, builds and tests, devvm network lock lets you choose which of those hosts the VM keeps, and puts it on the allowlist tier with them.

To make a new VM learn, choose learn in its tier list when you customize it, or give --network learn, such as devvm --network learn. To make an existing VM learn, run devvm network learn, which gives it the internet tier at once, as devvm network internet does, and starts its learning from now. Learning is for one VM at a time, so no default makes new VMs learn: devvm network -g, devvm setup and config.toml don’t take learn (choosing a tier).

Learning isn’t a tier of its own. While it lasts, the VM is on the internet tier, so it reaches every public host and only your denies apply, and links and groups treat it as an internet VM. That’s internet access for as long as the VM learns, and that includes the dependency installs you run to teach it, when packages’ install scripts run in the VM. So a compromised dependency that you install meanwhile can reach a host of its attacker’s choosing, and that host then shows up among the learned hosts. That’s why devvm network lock asks, starts with few hosts ticked, and leaves you to read the list before you confirm it. Your secrets stay on this machine as they do on every tier, and the VM still gets only placeholders.

Each launch of a learning VM says that it’s learning, since when, and how many hosts it has reached beyond its allowlist, and it names devvm network lock. Once the VM’s log holds more than 2 MiB, the launch leaves out the count, so it never reads the whole log each time. devvm ls and devvm network show its tier as internet (learning), and their --json adds learning_since, the time it started learning.

devvm network internet, none or open end the learning and give the VM that tier. devvm network allowlist refuses while the VM learns, because devvm network lock is how a learning VM goes to the allowlist tier, and devvm network lock --none does it without adding a host. A VM in a group can’t start learning or be locked, because a group’s VMs are all on one tier, so run devvm group leave first, and for the same reason a learning VM can’t join a group until you lock it.

Locking it

devvm network lock reads the hosts the VM reached since it started learning from its network log. It leaves out what the VM’s allowlist tier would allow already, judged by the proxy’s own rules: devvm’s built-in rules, its shared tools’ and layers’, your own rules for every VM and for this VM, and its secrets’ and logins’ hosts. It also leaves out what your rules deny, which no allow would reach, blocked requests, and internal and LAN addresses, which the internet tier never reaches. In a terminal it lists the rest, one row for each host and port, with how many connections each had and the first word of the User-Agent that the requests sent most. That User-Agent is the VM’s own claim, which any program in it can set to anything, so it’s a hint, not proof of which tool made the connection, and devvm shows it only when it’s at most 32 letters, digits and ._/+-. The hosts that only tools without proxy settings reached, which transparent mode sent to the proxy, come next, under a heading of their own, because background tools’ telemetry and update checks reach the proxy that way, and you may not want to keep them. Which way a connection came is the VM’s own doing, as its User-Agent is, so the heading is a hint about the tool, not proof of what it is. The risky hosts come last, under a heading of their own, so neither a long name nor a User-Agent can push off the row what makes them risky. A host name that doesn’t fit is cut from the left, so its domain shows, and a list longer than the terminal scrolls, with a line above and below that says how many more rows there are. In a terminal too short to show a few rows, devvm refuses rather than draw the list wrong:

Since 2026-11-08 09:03 the VM could reach any public host, so this list can hold a host that a compromised dependency reached. Only a host on port 443 of a package registry or vendor devvm knows starts ticked, so read the others before you tick them.
Choose the hosts devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c keeps. Use up and down to move, space to toggle, a to toggle them all and enter to confirm.
> [x] files.pythonhosted.org:443 2 connections, User-Agent: uv/0.9.2
 [x] static.crates.io:443 1 connection, User-Agent: cargo/1.91.0
 [ ] example.com:8443 1 connection
 [ ] uploads.github.com:443 1 connection, User-Agent: git/2.51.0
Reached only by tools without proxy settings, which the VM's names sent to its proxy:
 [ ] api.open-meteo.com:443 3 connections
Risky, each an easy way to send data out:
 [ ] 203.0.113.5:443 1 connection
 [ ] docs.google.com:443 1 connection, User-Agent: python-requests/2.32
 [ ] pastebin.com:443 1 connection, User-Agent: curl/8.5.0

A host starts ticked only when it’s on port 443 and belongs to a package registry or vendor on a short list that devvm keeps, each name checked so that nobody but its vendor can make a host or post a page under it: npm’s registry.npmjs.org, PyPI’s files.pythonhosted.org, crates.io, Go’s proxy.golang.org and sum.golang.org, NuGet’s api.nuget.org, the toolchains’ own release hosts such as nodejs.org and static.rust-lang.org, Docker Hub’s and GitHub’s container registries, and the agents’ APIs, api.anthropic.com and api.openai.com. A registry’s packages are its users’, but they only get there through the registry’s own upload, with a token. Nothing else makes a host start ticked: not a domain where anyone can get a subdomain or a page, such as github.io, googleapis.com, amazonaws.com or pypi.org, which takes uploads, not a host beside one your rules or your secrets name, and not one beside a host an earlier lock added. So files.pythonhosted.org:443 starts ticked, while files.pythonhosted.org:8080, docs.google.com and evil.github.io don’t. Every other host starts unticked, and so does every host when the list has more than 30, so read the list, or devvm network lock --json, before you tick them. A host that’s an easy way to send data out is risky, and it always starts unticked: an address rather than a host name, a name with a punycode (xn--) label, which can look like another name, a paste or file drop site such as pastebin.com, paste.ubuntu.com or gist.github.com, or a log that takes entries from anyone, such as rekor.sigstore.dev, file storage or file sharing such as transfer.sh, Dropbox, Google Docs, SharePoint or an S3 bucket, a mail server such as Gmail’s, a tunnel such as ngrok or trycloudflare.com, a service that records what it’s sent such as webhook.site or an OAST domain, free hosting such as vercel.app, workers.dev or cloudfront.net, and a chat service’s endpoint for bots such as Discord’s, Slack’s hooks or Telegram’s API. devvm’s own rules leave all of them out too. Tick one only when the project needs it.

Space ticks or unticks the row under the cursor, a ticks every row, the risky ones and those on other ports too, and again unticks them all, and Enter adds the ticked hosts to the VM’s own policy file. Each is an exact host and port, such as registry.example.com:443 or example.com:8443, with the port written even for 443, so it doesn’t allow port 80 too, and never a *. wildcard. Then devvm gives the VM the allowlist tier at once, as it does between confined tiers, so a running VM keeps running, and its learning ends. When the VM’s tier changed while the list was open, such as with devvm network internet in another terminal, devvm network lock changes nothing and says so. When the terminal doesn’t let devvm read single keys, or goes away while the list is open, or you press Ctrl+C, devvm network lock changes nothing, rather than lock with the hosts as they were ticked then. Later, devvm network allow, deny and rm change those rules as they change any other (changing rules).
devvm network lock list the hosts the VM learned, so you choose which it keeps, then give it the allowlist tier
--all keep every host it learned, the unticked ones too, without asking
--none keep none of them, without asking
--json list the hosts it learned, and change nothing

Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm network lock refuses and names --all and --none. When the VM reached no host beyond its allowlist, it locks at once without asking. A VM that isn’t learning has nothing to lock, so devvm network lock refuses and names devvm network learn. While the VM links to a target on a lower tier than allowlist, devvm network lock refuses as devvm network allowlist would (links between VMs).

The proxy keeps each VM’s log to its last 10 to 20 MiB (logs), so a VM that learns for a long time with a lot of traffic can lose the first hosts it reached. When the log no longer goes back to the time the VM started learning, devvm network lock warns you, and its --json sets partial. A host that’s missing then is blocked once the VM is locked, and devvm network log --blocked names the devvm network allow command that allows it.

devvm network lock –json

devvm network lock --json prints what the VM learned as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes, and changes nothing, so devvm refuses it with --all or --none. learning_since is when the VM started learning, partial is true when the log no longer goes back that far, and each of the hosts has the rule that devvm network lock adds for it, its host and port, the count of its connections, the last time the VM reached it, the User-Agent’s first word that reached it most as agent, when devvm shows one, tickable set to true for a host on port 443 of a registry or vendor on devvm’s list, which starts ticked unless it’s risky, for a risky host, its risk: address, lookalike, paste, storage, mail, tunnel, webhook, hosting or chat, and via set to dns for a host that only tools without proxy settings reached. The hosts come in the list’s order: the tickable ones first, then the others, then those that only tools without proxy settings reached, then the risky ones.

{
 "version": 1,
 "learning_since": "2026-11-07T10:00:00Z",
 "hosts": [
 {
 "rule": "files.pythonhosted.org:443",
 "host": "files.pythonhosted.org",
 "port": 443,
 "count": 48,
 "last": "2026-11-07T10:19:00Z",
 "agent": "uv/0.9.2",
 "tickable": true
 },
 {
 "rule": "registry.example.com:443",
 "host": "registry.example.com",
 "port": 443,
 "count": 12,
 "last": "2026-11-07T10:20:00Z",
 "agent": "npm/11.6.2"
 },
 {
 "rule": "pastebin.com:443",
 "host": "pastebin.com",
 "port": 443,
 "count": 3,
 "last": "2026-11-07T10:21:00Z",
 "agent": "curl/8.5.0",
 "risk": "paste"
 }
 ]
}

Allowlists

The VM’s proxy reads devvm’s built-in policies first and then your policy files, in order, as one list:

  • devvm’s own rules for every VM, which allow OS packages, mise’s version lists, the Sigstore and GitHub trust roots that mise checks a download’s attestations against, Node’s downloads for a project’s own node, and GitHub;
  • devvm’s rules for each shared tool in the VM’s image (node, claude and the others), which allow its registries, downloads and APIs;
  • devvm’s rules for each built-in layer in the VM’s image, so the docker layer allows Docker’s packages and the container registries Docker Hub and ghcr.io, and the nix layer allows Nix’s binary cache, channels and flake registry;
  • ~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.policy, for each of your own layers in the VM’s image;
  • ~/.config/devvm/policy, your own rules for every VM, which devvm network allow, deny and rm change with -g;
  • ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/policy, the rules for that VM only, in the VM’s own folder, which is named by the hash that the VM’s name ends with, which devvm network allow, deny and rm change;
  • the hosts of the VM’s secrets and logins, and the host its agents log in at, such as Codex’s and opencode’s auth.openai.com and Claude Code’s platform.claude.com and console.anthropic.com, on port 443, which devvm adds.

The first three are built in: they come with devvm, inside its binary, so you can’t edit them, and an upgrade of devvm is what changes them. To change what a VM reaches, add your own rules, and to keep a VM from a host that devvm’s rules allow, add a deny, which beats any allow. devvm leaves storage and paste sites out of its defaults on purpose, because they’re easy ways to send data out. Rules never come from the project folder, because the VM can write it. The proxy reads each of your files again when it changes, so an edit applies at once, from the next connection. How it works lists where each policy comes from.

Rules

A policy file holds one rule per line. # starts a comment, and matching a host ignores case.

Rule Matches
example.com that host only
*.example.com any subdomain, at any depth, not example.com itself
** any host, and any address, though an internal address still needs its own rule
10.0.0.5, 10.0.0.0/8, fd00::/8 addresses, IPv4 or IPv6 (also what lets a connection past the internal-address refusal)
RULE:22, [fd00::1]:22, 10.0.0.0/8:8080 only that port; without a port, 443 and 80
RULE:*, **:* any port
!RULE deny: a deny beats any allow
RULE METHODS PATH, such as api.github.com GET,HEAD /repos/ only those requests to a host name, by their methods, their path or both (rules by method and path)

A rule is plain ASCII, and a host’s part has no spaces in it, while a rule by method and path has its methods and its path after the host, each after a space. A port is a number from 1 to 65535, or * for any port. A host’s one trailing dot is dropped, so example.com. matches example.com. Brackets hold only an IPv6 address, and an address can’t follow *.. A line that holds anything else, such as example.com:x, a*.example.com or ! example.com with a space after the !, isn’t a rule.

When a line that isn’t a rule starts with !, it reads as a deny, but the proxy can’t tell what it would deny. So while the line is there, the proxy of every VM that reads the file denies every new connection apart from the VM’s links, whatever the other rules allow. Connections that are already open stay open. Each refusal names the file and the line, and it suggests no devvm network allow command, because no rule would help. Any other line that isn’t a rule is skipped, and the file’s other lines still apply. The proxy names each such line in its own log.

devvm warns about each line that isn’t a rule, with the file and the line’s number, and the warning for a broken deny says that the proxies deny everything until it’s fixed. It warns when you open a confined VM whose proxy reads the file, when devvm network allow, deny or rm changes the file, and in devvm doctor. devvm network also marks the line. Fix the line or remove it, and the change applies from the next connection.

The proxy never dials a denied address, even for an allowed name that resolves to it or to its NAT64 form. A missing file has no rules. A file that changed but can’t be read keeps its last rules, so a deny never lapses.

Changing rules

devvm network shows this folder’s VM’s allowlist after its tier. It prints each of the VM’s policies that holds more than comments, and then its rules without their comments. A built-in policy has its name after # devvm:, because it has no file you could edit, and one of your files has its path after #, followed by (denies only) on the internet and none tiers, where it shows only the file’s denies. An open VM has no policies, so devvm network prints its tier alone. A line that isn’t a rule is marked # not a rule, skipped, with its line number:

allowlist
# devvm: layers/base.policy
 ports.ubuntu.com
 github.com
# /Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy
 example.com
 example.com:x # not a rule, skipped (line 2)
devvm network allow RULE... add the rules to the VM’s own file
devvm network deny RULE... add them as denies, adding ! when it’s missing
devvm network rm RULE... remove the lines with these rules, a deny with its !, and warn about one that isn’t there
-g, --global with allow, deny or rm, change ~/.config/devvm/policy, for every VM, instead, which needs no VM
--method METHODS, --path PATH with allow, deny or rm, narrow each rule to those requests (rules by method and path)

A rule is what Rules lists, without spaces or a comment, and --method and --path add its methods and its path. devvm refuses anything else before it adds any rule, and it also refuses allow !RULE. A rule that’s already in the file, in any case, isn’t added again, and a rule by method and path is the same rule however its methods are written, while its path’s case is its own. Each change applies at once, from the next connection. For an open VM, devvm notes that no rule applies to it, and for an allow on the internet or none tier, that only denies apply there. When devvm network log --blocked or a blocked request in the VM suggests a devvm network allow command, its rule is one that devvm network allow takes.

If a VM was deleted outside devvm, devvm deletes what it kept for that VM when it makes a new VM for the same project folder, so the new VM never gets the old one’s rules.

Rules by method and path

A rule for a host name can also name the requests it covers, by their methods, their path or both. So a VM can read from an API without changing anything there, or reach a host without pushing to it. devvm network allow, deny and rm take --method and --path for this, and the file gets the rule as one line, such as api.github.com GET,HEAD /repos/:
devvm network allow api.example.com --method GET,HEAD let the VM only read from api.example.com, a host that no other rule allows
devvm network allow api.example.com --path /v1/ let it reach only the paths below /v1/ there
devvm network deny api.github.com --method POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE keep it from changing anything through GitHub’s API, which devvm’s rules allow
devvm network deny github.com --path '/*/*/git-receive-pack' keep it from pushing to GitHub over HTTPS
devvm network deny -g pastebin.com --method POST keep every VM from posting there

Allows add up and a deny beats any allow, as for every rule. An allow by method and path lets through only the requests it names, and the host’s other requests stay blocked unless another rule allows the whole host. So to narrow a host that a rule already allows whole, such as api.github.com, which devvm’s own rules allow, add a deny of what the VM mustn’t do. An allow by method and path for such a host narrows nothing, and devvm warns you so when you add one, naming the VMs where another rule allows the host whole, with -g each VM’s own rules counted, and the deny to add instead. Where a whole allow names port 443 alone, such as api.example.com:443, an allow by method and path still narrows the host’s plain HTTP on port 80, and the warning says that. A deny by method and path refuses only the requests it names, and the host’s other requests go on. You can narrow any host this way, devvm’s built-in ones, a secret’s and an agent’s included, for one VM or with -g for every VM. On the internet and none tiers your denies apply, by method and path too, while your allows apply only on the allowlist tier, as for every rule.

The methods are some of GET, HEAD, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, OPTIONS, TRACE and QUERY, in any case, joined by commas, and devvm writes them in capitals in that order. GET doesn’t include HEAD, so name both for reading. A deny refuses only the methods it names, so to keep a host read-only, name POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. A GraphQL API, such as GitHub’s at api.github.com/graphql, takes its reads as POST too, so such a deny refuses them as well, and the GitHub CLI, which reads through it, fails there.

Some servers take a request’s method from a header or a parameter instead of the request itself, so the proxy judges a request by every method it names. It reads the X-HTTP-Method-Override and X-HTTP-Method headers and every header with method-override in its name, in any case and with _ for -, as some servers read X_HTTP_METHOD_OVERRIDE, and the _method parameter of the query. While a rule by method covers a host, a request there whose header or parameter isn’t exactly one of those methods in capitals, such as DELETE, GET, delete or nothing at all, is refused, because servers could read it either way, and so is a request whose query has a ; in it, which some servers split the query at, or a query with an escape that doesn’t decode. Otherwise an allow needs the request’s own method and every one it names to be among its methods, so an allow of GET refuses a GET that says it’s a DELETE, and a deny refuses a request that names any of its methods. The proxy doesn’t read a request’s body, so a _method field in a form that a POST sends, which some frameworks take as the method, is judged as the POST it is: a deny of POST refuses it, and an allow of POST lets it through whatever the field says.

A path starts with /. In it, * matches any part of one segment, such as /repos/*/*/issues or /*/*.git/info/refs, and ** as a whole segment matches one segment or more. A path that ends with / matches everything below it, as /** there would, so /repos/ matches /repos/a and /repos/a/b but not /repos itself. A path without a / at its end also matches the request’s path with one, so /user matches /user/. The query never counts, so /search matches /search?q=x. A path has no . or .. part, no doubled slash, and no space, %, \, ;, ? or #.

Servers don’t all read a request’s path alike, so a rule’s path matches only a path that every server reads the same way: one with nothing percent-encoded, no \ or ;, no . or .. part and no doubled slash. An allow matches exactly, its method and its path in their own case, and no path in any other form. A deny matches broadly instead. It matches in any case and every path that isn’t in that plain form, a deny whose path ends with / also matches the path above it, a path’s last segment matches with what follows its first . cut off too, as frameworks that take a format from a suffix route /admin.json to /admin, and every segment matches with its trailing dots dropped, as some servers drop them, so a deny of /config.json refuses /config.json.. So a deny of /gists/ refuses /gists, /GISTS/1, /gists/, /gists.json, /%67ists/1, /x/../gists/1 and /gists;x/1 alike, and a deny of /admin refuses /admin.json and /admin. but not /administrator. So while a rule with a path covers a host, a request there whose path has an encoded character, such as a file name with a space, is refused unless a rule without a path allows it.

To see each request, the proxy decrypts the host’s HTTPS on port 443 with the VM’s own CA, as it does for a secret’s hosts, and it checks every request on the connection, each one on a kept-alive connection and on HTTP/2 alike, with the rules as they are then, so a change to them applies to a decrypted tunnel from its next request. A tunnel that was open to the host before a rule narrowed it isn’t decrypted, so it carries on unchecked until it closes. A tunnel to such a host on any other port is refused, because the proxy can’t see the requests in it, while plain HTTP on any port gets the same check for each request. A tool in the VM that doesn’t trust the VM’s CA fails there, and devvm network log gives the reason TLS with the VM failed, which is why devvm reminds you when you add such a rule that the host is now decrypted. A host that a whole allow covers, with no deny by method and path, stays a tunnel. A rule by method and path needs a host name or *.name, so devvm refuses --method and --path with an address or a CIDR, which have no name to decrypt by, and with **, which would decrypt every host. A WebSocket is checked by the request that opens it, and what it carries after that isn’t. A switch to any other protocol, such as Upgrade: h2c, and a CONNECT inside a decrypted tunnel are refused, because the proxy couldn’t check the requests that would follow.

A request that the rules block gets 403 from the proxy, with the reason, and never reaches the host. devvm network log shows it with its method and its path, and devvm-why lists it. For a request that no allow covers, the proxy suggests the devvm network allow command for the whole host, and for one that a deny refuses it suggests nothing, because no allow lifts a deny. A request that a rule by method and path let through shows that rule in devvm network log:

$ devvm network allow api.example.com --method GET --path /v1/
==> devvm added api.example.com GET /v1/ to devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c's rules.
The proxy now decrypts api.example.com's HTTPS on port 443 to check each request, so a tool that doesn't trust the VM's CA fails there, and a new tunnel to it on another port is refused. Tunnels to it that are open already carry on unchecked until they close.
https://devvm.dev/docs/safety/network/#rules-by-method-and-path

In the VM, a GET below /v1/ reaches the host, while a POST there gets the proxy’s answer:

$ curl -X POST https://api.example.com/v1/charges
devvm: api.example.com:443 is blocked (no rule allows this method and path). Allow it on the host with: devvm network allow api.example.com

And on this machine, devvm network log shows both:

2026-11-08T10:00:01Z allowed api.example.com:443 rule api.example.com GET /v1/, decrypted
2026-11-08T10:00:01Z allowed api.example.com:443 GET /v1/charges, rule api.example.com GET /v1/
2026-11-08T10:00:02Z BLOCKED api.example.com:443 POST /v1/charges: no rule allows this method and path

Learning stays by host: devvm network lock adds whole hosts, and you can narrow them afterwards with these flags (learning the hosts a VM needs). A line with a method that devvm doesn’t know, such as !api.github.com PSOT, isn’t a rule, so as a deny it makes the proxy deny everything until you fix it (rules). The shared Nix cache’s own downloads from cache.nixos.org meet these rules too, as GETs of the paths the VM asked the cache for (Nix).

A VM’s proxy is the devvm binary that started it, which is the one from before an upgrade until the VM’s next launch. A proxy from before rules by method and path reads such a rule as a line that isn’t a rule: it skips an allow by method and path, and a deny by method and path makes it deny the VM everything, until it starts again. Likewise, once one of a VM’s secrets goes in by method or by a path pattern, such a proxy puts none of the VM’s secrets in. So when you add or remove such a rule, or change such a secret, while a VM’s proxy runs from another devvm binary, or from one devvm can’t tell, devvm warns you and names the VM, and running devvm in the VM’s folder starts its proxy again.

devvm network –json

devvm network --json prints the VM’s tier and its allowlist as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. policy is open, internet, allowlist, none or unenforced, a learning VM also has learning_since, the time it started learning, and allowlist has each policy that holds more than comments, in the order the proxy reads them. Each has builtin, a built-in policy’s name, or file, the path of one of your files, then its rules and, in not_rules, each line that isn’t a rule, with its line number and its text. On the internet and none tiers, a file whose denies alone apply also has denies_only set to true, and its rules are its denies, as devvm network lists them under (denies only). Without denies_only, a file’s rules are all of its rules. transparent is the VM’s transparent mode, with on and from, as devvm network transparent --json has it. With -g, the object has only policy, which is the tier new VMs get, and source, which says where it came from: config.toml, settings.json for what devvm network -g or devvm setup saved, or built-in (where a default comes from). With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses a tier with it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "policy": "allowlist",
 "source": "config.toml"
}
{
 "version": 1,
 "policy": "allowlist",
 "allowlist": [
 {
 "builtin": "layers/base.policy",
 "rules": [
 "ports.ubuntu.com",
 "github.com"
 ],
 "not_rules": []
 },
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy",
 "rules": [
 "example.com"
 ],
 "not_rules": [
 {
 "line": 2,
 "text": "example.com:x"
 }
 ]
 }
 ],
 "transparent": {
 "on": true,
 "from": "default"
 }
}

On the none tier, a VM with Claude Code gets Claude Code’s built-in policy whole, and its own file shows only its denies:

{
 "version": 1,
 "policy": "none",
 "allowlist": [
 {
 "builtin": "shared-tools/claude.policy",
 "rules": [
 "api.anthropic.com",
 "claude.ai"
 ],
 "not_rules": []
 },
 {
 "file": "/Users/you/.local/share/devvm/vms/71a99b1076d92c/policy",
 "denies_only": true,
 "rules": [
 "!tracker.example.com"
 ],
 "not_rules": []
 }
 ]
}

Inside the VM

Every login in the VM has the proxy settings in its environment (HTTP_PROXY, HTTPS_PROXY and their lowercase forms, NO_PROXY for the VM itself, and NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY), and the CA variables that every VM has point the tools that don’t read the system’s store at the VM’s own CAs. devvm also points apt, sudo, ssh and Docker at the proxy (how), on every tier. On a confined tier, a direct connection to an address fails at once, even as root, and no DNS query leaves the VM. Names resolve in the proxy, and inside the VM every name resolves to one stand-in address, which leads to the proxy too, so a tool that skips the proxy settings still reaches the hosts the rules allow over HTTPS and HTTP (tools that ignore the proxy). Such a tool’s connection to another port of a name is refused at once, and nothing reaches the log for it (what to do).

A blocked request gets 403, and the response names the host, the reason and the rule that would allow it. The proxy also answers at http://devvm.proxy/:

  • /blocked lists the last 50 blocks.
  • /blocked/new?after=N gives the number of blocks so far, then those after the Nth, with each rule once, so a shell prompt can show what a command hit.
  • /ca.pem is the VM’s own CA certificate and the next one’s, never their keys.
  • /nix/ is the shared Nix cache, in a VM with the nix layer (below).
  • /transparent/ports lists the ports that transparent mode sends to the proxy, one a line.

A request for http://devvm.proxy/ that comes through transparent mode, without the proxy settings, reaches /blocked alone and gets 403 for the rest, because that way asks the tool for no password, so a container without the proxy settings can’t fetch the VM’s CA or the Nix cache.

In the VM, devvm-why prints what the proxy blocked lately, and a note before each prompt tells you when something new was blocked. When the proxy blocked nothing lately, devvm-why says so, and it adds that a connection refused, or a DNS error, for a host the tier allows means the tool skipped the proxy on a port or in a way devvm can’t send to it, so you turn on the tool’s own proxy setting or give it the address in $HTTPS_PROXY (a tool that skips the proxy fails). With transparent mode on, devvm-why then says which ports it sends to the proxy, lists the connections to other ports that the VM refused lately, by port and time, and lists the names that tools looked up lately. devvm also tells Claude Code and Codex, in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, why a request may fail and to run devvm-why, that a tool that ignores the proxy settings still reaches the proxy over HTTPS, HTTP and the ports the rules name, and that a connection refused on another port while devvm-why shows nothing blocked means the tool skipped the proxy.

Nix

In a VM with the nix layer, Nix’s daemon makes most of Nix’s downloads, and devvm also points it at the proxy, so its downloads go through the same allowlists. The layer’s allowlist has cache.nixos.org for Nix’s binary cache, and channels.nixos.org and releases.nixos.org for its channels and flake registry, and GitHub, where most flakes’ inputs come from, is in devvm’s rules for every VM.

Nix asks the proxy’s shared cache, http://devvm.proxy/nix, before cache.nixos.org, so every VM with the layer shares the packages that any of them downloaded (shared downloads). The proxy fetches what the cache doesn’t have from cache.nixos.org alone, and only while the VM’s tier and rules let it reach cache.nixos.org. It keeps a package only when cache.nixos.org’s signature on it checks, and the VM’s Nix checks that signature again. A VM can only make the proxy fetch from cache.nixos.org: the proxy refuses anything a VM sends to store, and every request that isn’t for one of Nix’s cache files. Each request shows in devvm network log as cache, with whether it was a hit, fetched, or why it wasn’t found. What one VM can learn of another through the cache is under Attack vectors. An open VM has its proxy too, so it shares the cache as well, and its proxy fetches from cache.nixos.org for it.

When a package isn’t in the binary cache, Nix builds it from source, and the build downloads its sources from their own hosts, such as ftpmirror.gnu.org. The proxy blocks those hosts until you allow them, so the build fails, and the error, devvm-why and devvm network log --blocked name the host and the devvm network allow command that allows it.

Behind a company proxy

When this machine reaches the internet only through a company proxy, the VM’s proxy sends the requests it allows through that proxy. devvm reads HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY, or their lowercase forms, from the shell you run it in. When that shell sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, devvm reads the [proxy] table of config.toml instead, so the proxy works from every shell, including an editor’s terminal that didn’t load your profile. The shell’s settings win whole: devvm never mixes them with config.toml’s, so a NO_PROXY alone in the shell still leaves config.toml’s proxy in effect, with its own no-proxy.

[proxy]
https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com"

devvm passes the settings to the VM’s proxy when the proxy starts, and when you run devvm again with different settings, devvm starts the VM’s proxy again with the new ones. So after you change them, run devvm again in the folder or devvm restart. When a VM’s proxy went through a company proxy the last time it started and devvm finds none this time, devvm warns you and names config.toml, because a VM’s proxy that a shell without the settings starts sends the VM’s requests directly.

The VM’s proxy still decides each request by the host name the VM asked for, against the same allowlists, and only then passes it on. It sends tunnels, which carry HTTPS and the requests it puts your secrets into, through HTTPS_PROXY’s proxy, and plain HTTP requests through HTTP_PROXY’s. It reaches the hosts that NO_PROXY names directly, and also localhost and loopback addresses. In NO_PROXY, example.com matches that host and its subdomains, .example.com matches only its subdomains, an address or a CIDR matches addresses, any entry can end in a port, and * matches every host. devvm network log adds through host:port to each request that went through the company proxy.

The company proxy needs an http:// address, such as http://user:password@proxy.example.com:8080 in HTTPS_PROXY, and a proxy without a port is on port 80. devvm doesn’t start a VM’s proxy while HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY or a [proxy] key names an https:// or socks5:// proxy, and it tells you which setting to change. The company proxy’s password stays on this machine. The VM never gets it, and devvm writes it into no log, no image and no process’s arguments.

config.toml never holds the password, because it’s a file you might copy to other machines or keep with your dotfiles, and devvm refuses a [proxy] URL that has one. Put only the user in the URL, as http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080, and save the password with devvm secret set proxy, which keeps it as it keeps the other secrets. devvm’s proxies look it up themselves when they start, so no file of devvm’s holds it in the clear. devvm doesn’t make a new VM, start a VM’s proxy, or build an image or the shared tools while config.toml’s proxy names a user and no password is saved, and it checks before anything starts. A VM’s proxy reads the password only when it starts, so after you change it, run devvm restart in each VM’s folder. No VM ever gets the proxy secret, and devvm secret use proxy refuses.

The company proxy sees the name and port of every host the VM reaches, and if it inspects TLS, the CA you add for it also lets it read the traffic. The company proxy also looks up each name itself, so the VM’s proxy can’t check every address a name leads to. It still refuses an address that’s this machine’s own or internal, unless a rule names it, and it refuses a name when this machine’s lookup gives an internal or denied address for it. A name that this machine can’t look up goes to the company proxy unchecked only when an allowlist names it, as example.com or *.example.com. When only ** allows a name that this machine can’t look up, the VM’s proxy refuses it, so ** never lets a VM send the company proxy a name of its own making. What a VM can still reach through the company proxy, such as hosts on your company’s network, is under Attack vectors.

Open VMs and builds

An open VM goes through its proxy as every VM does, and its proxy sends its requests through the company proxy, from the shell’s settings or config.toml’s, so the company proxy’s password stays on this machine for it too. The VM never gets the shell’s proxy settings, and Lima gets none to pass on to it. What an open VM reaches directly, past its proxy, such as the hosts its NO_PROXY names, doesn’t go through the company proxy.

Lima prints each proxy setting it gives a VM, password and all, as it starts the VM. devvm keeps the password out of its run log, and once the VM has started, it replaces the password with as many * in the log Lima keeps for the VM.

Builds never get your company proxy’s settings, and images never keep them. A build goes through the shell’s company proxy, or else config.toml’s, as a VM’s proxy does. When devvm builds an image, builds the shared tools or converts a --from container image on Lima behind a company proxy, the build goes through a proxy of devvm’s on this machine, made for that build alone, which goes through your company proxy. The build’s commands get only that proxy’s address, with a password devvm makes for the build, while they run, and devvm stops the proxy when the build ends. So the code a build runs, which includes a container image’s own, never sees your company proxy’s address or password. That proxy also runs on this machine, so a company proxy on localhost, such as one a VPN client runs, works for builds too.

A build’s proxy allows any host, as ** does. It sends a name that this machine can’t look up on to the company proxy, so builds work where only the company proxy looks up outside names.

devvm’s own downloads on this machine go through the company proxy too. They are devvm’s copy of mise and the versions it looks up for the shared tools, the list of Ubuntu’s cloud images, and a container registry’s answers for --from. With the shell’s settings, each of them uses the shell’s. With config.toml’s, devvm’s own requests send the password only to the company proxy. The mise it runs on this machine gets the proxy’s URL with the password in it, in its environment, because mise takes a proxy’s password nowhere else. devvm percent-encodes the password in that URL and mise decodes it before it sends it, so a password with characters such as @, :, /, #, % or a space works too. devvm never puts that URL in mise’s arguments or in a file. When a VM’s proxy refreshes a Codex or opencode login on this machine, the refresh goes through the same company proxy as the VM’s requests, with the password kept on this machine.

Tools that ignore the proxy

On every tier but open, devvm sends a tool that ignores the proxy settings to the VM’s proxy anyway, by the names it looks up. This is transparent mode, and it’s on unless you turn it off. In the VM, every name resolves to one stand-in address, 198.18.0.1, and a connection to that address on port 443, port 80 or a port that one of your allow rules names goes to the VM’s proxy. The proxy reads the host from the connection itself, from the TLS server name (SNI) on HTTPS and from each request’s Host on plain HTTP, and it judges that host as it judges a request through the proxy settings, against the same allowlist, with the same secrets and the same log. A blocked HTTPS host gets the proxy’s 403, over a certificate for that host from the VM’s own CA, so the tool shows the same message, with the devvm network allow command, that a request through the proxy settings would show. devvm network log and devvm-why mark each of these connections without proxy settings, and so does the note before the prompt. A tool such as workerd, which wrangler dev runs for Cloudflare’s adapters, makes its own lookups and connections, and transparent mode is what lets it reach your allowed hosts from a confined VM.

Transparent mode covers HTTPS and HTTP to a host by name on ports 443 and 80, and on up to 32 more ports that your allow rules name for hosts by name, such as api.example.com:8443, the lowest first. It never covers port 22 or 53, even when a rule names one, because SSH names no host in its first bytes and port 53 is the VM’s own names’. It leaves these to the tool’s own proxy settings:

  • Other ports. A connection to another port of a name is refused at once, and so is UDP to any port, QUIC included, so a client that tries HTTP/3 falls back to TCP. A client that uses HTTP/3 alone doesn’t connect.
  • Protocols that name no host in their first bytes, such as Postgres, MySQL, Redis, SSH and raw TCP, and those whose server speaks first, such as SMTP. The proxy refuses such a connection and logs why, even on a port a rule names.
  • Addresses. A URL with an address in it, such as https://1.2.3.4/, is a direct connection, which fails, and so does a tool that looks a name up itself and then gives the proxy the stand-in address, which the proxy refuses with a reason that says so.
  • IPv6. Names have no IPv6 address in the VM, so a client that uses IPv6 alone finds no address.
  • Names without a dot, and your network’s names. A name without a dot, such as db, resolves only when /etc/hosts has it, as the name of a link between VMs does. The VM’s resolver adds the search domain of this machine’s network to such a name, and transparent mode can’t tell db.corp.example.com made that way from one a tool names whole, so every name under that search domain gets no answer either, such as printer.lan or git.corp.example.com when your network’s search domain is corp.example.com. A tool that reaches such a host needs its proxy settings.
  • A DNS server of yours on the VM’s 127.0.0.1:53. Transparent mode sends the VM’s lookups there to its own names, so such a server, and a forward of port 53 to it, gets none. Put the server on another address or port, or turn transparent mode off for the VM.
  • Clients that don’t trust the VM’s CA, such as most Docker containers, and those that pin a certificate. For a blocked HTTPS host they show a certificate error instead of the 403, and the block is logged all the same.

With the docker layer, Docker’s containers get the same treatment as the VM’s own programs, on Docker’s default bridge and on the networks that docker network create and Compose make. A container without the proxy settings, whether its environment emptied them or a program made it through Docker’s API without them, reaches what the VM’s rules allow, as every program in the VM does. To give a container no network, run it with --network none, and a container on an --internal network reaches nothing either.

devvm network transparent shows a VM’s transparent mode, on or off, and where that comes from: the VM’s own setting, config.toml’s transparent-proxy, or devvm’s default, which is on. devvm network transparent off and devvm network transparent on give the folder’s VM its own setting, and transparent-proxy = false in config.toml turns it off for every VM that has none of its own. A change applies at the VM’s next launch, without a restart. With transparent mode off, names don’t resolve in a confined VM at all, so a tool that skips the proxy fails with a DNS error. Most tools, such as curl, get that error at once, on macOS and on a Linux host alike. On a Linux host, a few, such as workerd under wrangler dev, can wait about 40 seconds for each lookup before they fail. On the open tier there’s no transparent mode, and the VM resolves names with Lima’s DNS. A VM made from an image built before devvm had transparent mode lacks the programs it runs, so each launch says so, and devvm update makes the VM again from a newer image.

$ devvm network transparent
on # devvm: default
$ devvm network transparent off
==> devvm turns transparent mode off for devvm-web-0c3c7077e29f06 at its next launch, and it applies while the VM is on a confined tier.

devvm network transparent --json prints the same as JSON, with on and from, which is vm, config or default, and devvm network --json has it too, as transparent:

{
 "version": 1,
 "on": true,
 "from": "default"
}

On the open tier, a tool that ignores the proxy settings in the VM’s environment connects directly, past its proxy. Its connections still work, because an open VM reaches everything this machine can, but they don’t show in devvm network log, they don’t go through your company proxy, and a request of theirs that needs one of your secrets carries only its placeholder, so the secret’s host refuses it. On every other tier, a tool that transparent mode doesn’t cover needs the proxy’s address in its own settings. These common tools don’t read HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY, or read them only when told to:

  • Node’s fetch reads them only with NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1, from Node 24.0.0 and 22.21.0, or with --use-env-proxy, from Node 24.5.0 and 22.21.0. devvm sets NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY in every VM, so an older Node’s fetch is the one that connects directly.
  • Python’s aiohttp reads them only when a program makes its session with trust_env=True.
  • Go programs read them through Go’s default HTTP transport, but a program that makes its own transport without a proxy function connects directly.
  • Java reads none of them. It takes its proxy from the https.proxyHost and https.proxyPort system properties, such as -Dhttps.proxyHost=…, and http.proxyHost and http.proxyPort for plain HTTP.
  • The Docker daemon reads them only from its own environment as it starts, or from its daemon.json, never from your shell. devvm points the daemon at the proxy itself, as Inside the VM says.

Secrets

Secrets stay on this machine, whatever the VM’s tier. A VM gets a placeholder of its own for each one, and its proxy puts the real value into requests for that secret’s hosts. An open VM can send a request around its proxy, but then the request carries only the placeholder, which the secret’s host refuses (tools that ignore the proxy). The proxy puts each secret into one header:

Secret Hosts Header Used by
claude api.anthropic.com Authorization every VM whose image has claude
github api.github.com, github.com, codeload.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com Authorization VMs it’s bound to
your own the hosts you give it, for the paths and methods you give it Authorization, or the header you give it VMs it’s bound to

Agents’ logins work the same way. When a VM’s image has a coding agent and devvm’s agent store has a login or an API key for it, the VM gets placeholders for the login, and so do Claude Code’s MCP servers’ secrets (agents’ logins and settings). A Claude Code, Codex or opencode login that you make inside a VM goes to the store, and the VM gets placeholders for it too (Claude Code login). A VM saves a login only for an agent that its image has, and its proxy refuses a login for any other agent, so a VM without Codex can never replace the store’s Codex login. Because the store keeps one login for each agent, any VM with the agent can replace it, so a VM you don’t trust can log your other VMs in to an account of its choosing (logins made in a VM).

Saving and binding secrets

Command What it does
devvm secret set claude or github asks for the Claude Code token or the GitHub token without showing it, and saves it (--stdin reads a line instead)
devvm secret set proxy asks for the company proxy’s password, for the user that config.toml’s [proxy] names, and saves it (--stdin reads a line instead)
devvm secret set NAME --host HOST --env VARIABLE asks for a secret of your own, such as an API key, and saves it with the hosts it goes to and the variable that VMs find its placeholder in (--stdin reads a line instead)
devvm secret rm NAME deletes a saved secret, after asking
devvm secret lists the secrets, each with its variable, header and hosts, a secret of your own’s path and methods, whether it’s saved, and the VMs using it
devvm secret use NAME lets this folder’s VM use the secret, and reach its hosts on port 443
devvm secret unuse NAME stops this folder’s VM using it, though a VM whose image has claude always uses claude

devvm saves a secret in the macOS Keychain, or elsewhere in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/<name>, a file only you can read (details). No devvm command prints a saved secret, because each VM’s proxy reads the values it needs itself. devvm drops whitespace in a secret’s value, except inside the proxy password, which loses only the whitespace around it. It refuses a value with a quote, a backslash or a control character, a value that holds a VM’s placeholder, such as one copied from a VM’s GH_TOKEN, and a claude value that isn’t a setup token (sk-ant-oat01-…, from claude setup-token). A CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN in devvm’s environment wins over a saved one.

Saving, deleting, binding and unbinding apply at once to the proxies that are running. From its next launch, the VM gets the placeholder in CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN, GH_TOKEN or your own secret’s variable, and with github a git credential helper for https://github.com.

A secret’s hosts join the allowlist of each VM that uses it, on port 443 alone, whatever the VM’s tier, so a VM on the none tier reaches them too.

To put a secret in, the proxy shows the VM a certificate from the VM’s own CA, which every VM has, an open one’s included, and which no other VM trusts, so one VM’s proxy can’t make certificates that another VM accepts. Each CA lasts 30 days, and its key stays on this machine. Each launch installs the VM’s current CA and the next one, which starts a week before the current one ends, and the proxy switches to the next CA then on its own, without a launch. So a VM that you don’t open again keeps working for at least 30 days after its last launch with devvm in its folder. Connecting with ssh alone isn’t a launch. When a VM runs past its next CA’s end without a launch, its proxy refuses its HTTPS connections to secrets’ hosts, and devvm network log --blocked gives the reason devvm's CA has ended. The VM’s other requests keep working. Run devvm in the VM’s folder to install new CAs, which also starts the VM’s proxy again and ends the connections open through it (how). devvm rm deletes a VM’s CAs with the VM, and a VM keeps them when its tier changes.

devvm secret unuse and devvm secret rm take a secret away from a VM at once, because the VM only ever had its placeholder. Neither command revokes what a VM made with the secret (minting credentials with a secret), so rotate it if that matters. Use a fine-grained GitHub token, scoped to the repos your VMs need.

devvm secret –json

devvm secret --json prints the list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. Each of the secrets has its name, saved, which is true when it’s saved or, for claude, in devvm’s environment, and used_by, the names of the VMs using it. Then custom is true for a secret of your own, and hosts lists the hosts the proxy puts it in for, none for proxy. A secret that VMs get has its header and env, the variable that holds its placeholder, and prefix when its placeholder starts with one. A secret of yours also has its scheme, its path, its methods and basic_user when it has them. The JSON never holds a secret’s value.

{
 "version": 1,
 "secrets": [
 {
 "name": "claude",
 "saved": true,
 "used_by": [
 "devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c"
 ],
 "custom": false,
 "hosts": [
 "api.anthropic.com"
 ],
 "header": "Authorization",
 "env": "CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN",
 "prefix": "sk-ant-oat01-"
 },
 {
 "name": "github",
 "saved": false,
 "used_by": [],
 "custom": false,
 "hosts": [
 "api.github.com",
 "github.com",
 "codeload.github.com",
 "raw.githubusercontent.com"
 ],
 "header": "Authorization",
 "env": "GH_TOKEN"
 },
 {
 "name": "proxy",
 "saved": false,
 "used_by": [],
 "custom": false,
 "hosts": []
 },
 {
 "name": "stripe",
 "saved": true,
 "used_by": [
 "devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c"
 ],
 "custom": true,
 "hosts": [
 "api.stripe.com"
 ],
 "header": "Authorization",
 "env": "STRIPE_API_KEY",
 "prefix": "sk_"
 }
 ]
}

Your own secrets

Any other credential that a tool in a VM sends in a header, such as an API key for Stripe, OpenRouter or your company’s own service, can be a secret of your own. You give it a name, the hosts it goes to and the variable that VMs find its placeholder in, and devvm asks for the value without showing it:

$ devvm secret set stripe --host api.stripe.com --env STRIPE_API_KEY --prefix sk_
Paste the value of stripe, which VMs that use it send to api.stripe.com.
The VMs that use it can reach those hosts on port 443.
Token:
==> devvm saved the stripe secret in the Keychain.
$ devvm secret use stripe
==> devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c uses the stripe secret from its next launch, and its allowlist has api.stripe.com on port 443.

From its next launch, the VM has STRIPE_API_KEY set to its own placeholder, such as sk_devvm-proxy-managed-secret-stripe-…, and a tool there sends it as Authorization: Bearer $STRIPE_API_KEY. The proxy puts the real value in place of the placeholder only in requests to api.stripe.com on port 443, over TLS, and a request to any other host goes out with the placeholder alone. A program that loads a .env file gets the placeholder too, as long as the file doesn’t set STRIPE_API_KEY itself, because most dotenv libraries leave a variable that’s already set as it is. Keep the real key out of the project’s .env, which the VM can read.

A secret of yours goes only to the VMs you use it in with devvm secret use, and each one’s hosts then join that VM’s allowlist on port 443. devvm secret set takes these flags:

Flag What it gives the secret
--host HOST a host it goes to, such as api.stripe.com: repeat the flag, or join hosts with commas, for up to 16
--env VARIABLE the variable that VMs find its placeholder in, such as STRIPE_API_KEY
--header HEADER the header it goes in, such as X-Api-Key, when it isn’t Authorization
--prefix PREFIX what its placeholder starts with, such as sk_, for a client that checks how its key starts
--path PATH the path of the requests it goes in for, written as a rule’s path is, such as /api/ for everything below /api/, so a request to the host’s other paths carries the placeholder alone, or none for every path
--method METHODS the methods of the requests it goes in for, such as GET,HEAD, so a request with another method carries the placeholder alone, or none for every method
--scheme SCHEME a scheme of its own before it in Authorization, besides Bearer and Token, such as ApiKey, or none
--basic-user lets it go in as the username of Basic credentials, as Stripe and some other services take a key (--basic-user=false takes that away)

The proxy puts the value in only when exactly one of the header’s values holds the placeholder, in one of these shapes, so that the value lands where the server reads a credential:

  • the placeholder alone, such as X-Api-Key: PLACEHOLDER;
  • for Authorization, Bearer, Token or the secret’s own --scheme, in any case, then one space and the placeholder;
  • for Authorization, Basic credentials whose password is the placeholder, after a username of printable ASCII up to 64 characters, such as git’s x-access-token:PLACEHOLDER;
  • with --basic-user, Basic credentials whose username is the placeholder, before a password of printable ASCII up to 64 characters, such as PLACEHOLDER:.

The placeholder in any other shape stays as it is, and the proxy’s own log says why without the value. That includes bytes of the VM’s own around it, the placeholder twice, a Digest field, and the username of Basic credentials without --basic-user, because a server can show the VM those parts of a request it refuses, such as a username it doesn’t know. The same shapes apply to the github and claude secrets, which the GitHub CLI, git and Claude Code send as Bearer, token and git’s Basic password.

Without --path and --method, the value goes in for every path and every method. With them, the proxy judges each request as it judges an allow by method and path: by its method as written and each method it names in a method-override header or a _method parameter, and by its path only in a plain form (rules by method and path). So a key that may only read goes in for GET and HEAD alone:

$ devvm secret set reports --host api.example.com --env REPORTS_API_KEY --method GET,HEAD
Paste the value of reports, which VMs that use it send to api.example.com.
The VMs that use it can reach those hosts on port 443.
Token:
==> devvm saved the reports secret in the Keychain.

A POST from the VM to api.example.com then carries the placeholder, which the host refuses, while a GET gets the key. The proxy judges every request on a connection, so a kept-alive connection or an HTTP/2 one gets the key only in the requests that have those methods. The github and claude secrets go in for every method. To keep a VM from writing with your GitHub token, give it a deny instead, such as devvm network deny api.github.com --method POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE, which refuses those requests before they leave the proxy.

A name has lowercase letters, digits and dashes, and it can’t be claude, github or proxy, nor start with a coding agent’s name, such as codex-key. A host is a host name, such as api.example.com. devvm refuses a wildcard, such as *.example.com, because some domains let anyone own a name under them. It also refuses an address, any port but 443, and a name that’s only ever internal, such as localhost, printer.local or a Tailscale or nip.io name. The proxy refuses an internal address whatever name resolves to it anyway. The header can’t be Host, Cookie, Content-Length, Content-Type, Transfer-Encoding, Expect, Forwarded, Via, an X-Forwarded- or Proxy- header, or one that ends at the next hop, such as Connection, because the proxy drops or sets those itself. Nor can it be one that servers commonly log or send back, such as Origin, Referer, User-Agent, X-Request-Id or Traceparent. The variable can’t be one that devvm or the VM’s shell sets, such as PATH, GH_TOKEN, HTTPS_PROXY, NPM_CONFIG_PREFIX or any DEVVM_ variable, nor one that changes what a program runs or trusts, such as a GIT_ or PYTHON variable, NODE_OPTIONS, EDITOR or SSL_CERT_DIR, nor another secret’s. A prefix can’t hold devvm-proxy-managed, which every placeholder holds after its prefix. A value has printable ASCII alone and at most 3,800 characters, and devvm refuses a longer one before it touches the one saved.

To save a new value, such as after you rotate the key, run devvm secret set NAME without the other flags, and the secret keeps its hosts, header, variable, prefix, path, methods and scheme. To change one of those, give only its flag with the new value, and the rest stay as they are, so devvm secret set stripe --host api.stripe.com,files.stripe.com gives the secret a second host. --host gives the whole list of hosts each time. A host the secret loses goes from every VM at once. A host it gains reaches only the VMs you then run devvm secret use NAME in again, so a host you add never gets the value from a VM you didn’t give it to, and devvm names the VMs that keep the hosts they had. To take a prefix away, delete the secret and save it again. Running VMs keep the variable they launched with, so after you change --env or --prefix, a VM that uses the secret gets the new placeholder at its next launch.

devvm secret rm NAME deletes the secret with its definition after asking, and the question names the VMs that use it, which stop using it before it goes. It also deletes a value that a failed save left without its definition. Each VM records the secret it was bound to by an ID that the secret gets as it’s first saved, so a secret saved again later by the same name goes to none of those VMs until you use it there again. A VM still bound to an earlier secret of the name gets nothing of the new one, its launch says so, and devvm secret unuse NAME takes the name away whether a secret has it or not.

devvm keeps your secrets’ hosts, headers, variables, prefixes, paths, methods and schemes in ~/.local/share/devvm/custom-secrets.json, without their values, and checks each entry again whenever it reads the file. When it can’t read the file, or an entry breaks the rules above, such as after an edit by hand, devvm secret and the launch of each VM that uses one of your secrets fail and name the file. Fix the entry, or delete the file and save your secrets again with devvm secret set (details).

The proxy passes the replies from a secret’s hosts to the VM as they are, so a host that sends the request’s headers back, such as an echo or debug endpoint, shows the VM the real value. Give a secret only hosts that you trust with it, and a key scoped to what the VMs need. A secret’s hosts are also open to the VMs that use it for requests without the placeholder, on every tier, the none tier included. So on a host where anyone can make an account, such as a storage or payments service, code in the VM can send data to an account of its own there.

Logs

devvm network log shows the proxy’s decisions for this folder’s VM, oldest first, one line each. A line has the time, allowed, BLOCKED or cache, and the host and port. An allowed line then has the rule that allowed it (, decrypted for an intercepted tunnel), or the request (GET /user), with the rule by method and path that let it through when one did, and the secrets put in (, token: github). A blocked line has why it was blocked, after the request when the proxy saw one, and a cache line, a request to the shared Nix cache, has the request and what came of it. A line ends , without proxy settings when transparent mode sent the connection to the proxy:

2026-10-09T10:00:00Z BLOCKED example.com:443 not on the allowlist
2026-10-09T10:00:05Z allowed github.com:443 rule github.com
2026-10-09T10:00:06Z allowed api.github.com:443 GET /user, token: github
2026-10-09T10:00:07Z BLOCKED api.github.com:443 POST /gists: denied by !api.github.com POST,PUT,PATCH,DELETE
2026-10-09T10:00:08Z cache cache.nixos.org:443 GET /nix/yv1zf3y6all4j99aad30cb8i55dw9zmp.narinfo: hit
2026-10-09T10:00:09Z allowed api.open-meteo.com:443 rule **, without proxy settings
-n N, --lines N the last N (default 50)
--follow then each new one as it happens, until Ctrl+C
--blocked the blocks instead, one row per host and port, by when last blocked: LAST, COUNT, HOST and ALLOW WITH, the devvm network allow command that allows it

ALLOW WITH is - for a request that the proxy refuses whatever the allowlist says, such as a GitHub call that makes a credential, and for a host that isn’t a host name or an address. An open VM’s log holds what went through its proxy and its links’ connections, but not what the VM reached directly, and devvm network log says so. The proxy keeps each VM’s log to its last 10 to 20 MiB by starting a new file once the current one reaches 10 MiB and keeping one older file, which devvm network log reads too. devvm rm deletes the VM’s logs, and How it works describes the files.

devvm network log –json

devvm network log --json prints the last N events as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes, and devvm refuses it with --follow. Each of the events has what the proxy logged, without the VM’s name. That’s the time, the event, the host and the port, and, when the event has them, the request’s method and path, the rule that allowed it, the reason it was blocked or what came of a cache request, the request’s User-Agent header as agent, the secrets put in, refused for a request refused whatever the allowlist says, the company proxy it went through as upstream, the VM that a link’s connection went to as target, and via set to dns for a connection that transparent mode sent to the proxy. The event is tunnel for an allowed connection, intercept for an allowed tunnel that the proxy decrypted, forward for an allowed request, blocked, or nix-cache for a request to the shared Nix cache. A link’s connection is link when devvm carried it, and link_refused, link_target_stopped or link_limit when devvm refused it, with the link’s name as its host. A log with nothing in it gives "events": [].

{
 "version": 1,
 "events": [
 {
 "time": "2026-10-09T10:00:00Z",
 "event": "blocked",
 "host": "example.com",
 "port": 443,
 "method": "CONNECT",
 "reason": "not on the allowlist"
 },
 {
 "time": "2026-10-09T10:00:06Z",
 "event": "forward",
 "host": "api.github.com",
 "port": 443,
 "method": "GET",
 "path": "/user",
 "secrets": [
 "github"
 ]
 }
 ]
}

With --blocked, each of the blocked has the last time it was blocked, the count, the host and the port, and allow, the rule that devvm network allow takes to allow it. A block that ALLOW WITH shows as - has no allow.

{
 "version": 1,
 "blocked": [
 {
 "last": "2026-10-09T10:01:00Z",
 "count": 2,
 "host": "example.com",
 "port": 443,
 "allow": "example.com"
 }
 ]
}

Links between VMs

A link between VMs lets a program in one VM, the client, reach a port that another VM, the target, publishes. devvm carries a link’s connections over ssh through this machine, so they use neither VM’s network, and a confined VM reaches only what its tier allows and the links you added to it. A client’s proxy is a second way into its links: it carries a request for one of the client’s own links, by the link’s name and port, to the same link on this machine, and passes it on as it is, without looking into it or putting a secret into it. It reaches no other socket on this machine and no other VM’s links. The allowlist’s rules don’t apply to links, so devvm network deny doesn’t stop one, and devvm link rm does.

A link joins the two VMs’ trust. Code in the client can often run code in the target through the target’s service, such as Postgres’s COPY … TO PROGRAM, and it then has whatever the target has: its network, the secrets it may use and its project folder. So devvm keeps two rules:

  • A client links only to a target on its own tier or a stricter one. An allowlist client links to allowlist and none targets, but not to internet or open ones, because a link to a target on a lower tier would let the client reach more through the target, around its own proxy. devvm checks this when you add a link, at each launch of the client and on every connection, and for a client on a confined tier, on every connection the target’s tier must be in force as it runs, so devvm refuses the connection while the target shows as unenforced, and it warns you of such a target when you add the link, when you publish a port in its folder that the client links to, and when the client starts. While such a link exists, devvm refuses to give the target a tier lower than the client’s, such as devvm network open, and it refuses to give the client a tier higher than a target’s, such as devvm network allowlist for a client that links to an open target. An open client may link to any target, and it then has the target’s secrets and project folder within reach as well as its own network.
  • The target publishes. A link reaches only a port that the target’s folder publishes with devvm link publish, and only on the target’s own loopback. Publishing offers the port to any of your VMs, and each link is still added in the client’s folder, so a VM reaches another’s service only when you’ve run a command in both folders.

The first rule keeps a client’s tier whole, but it doesn’t keep the target’s data in the target. A client on a confined tier can read whatever the target’s service gives it and send that out through the hosts its own tier reaches. Link two VMs only when you’d trust each with what the other has.

A group links each of its VMs to the ports that the others publish, once you’ve run devvm group join in each VM’s folder. Its VMs are all on one tier, so every link it makes keeps the first rule, and devvm refuses to change a VM’s tier with devvm network while it’s in a group. A group joins the trust of all its VMs, so put VMs in one only when you’d trust each with what the others have.

Not covered

The tiers leave some things open, such as what an allowed host accepts beyond what rules by method and path narrow, whatever your secrets allow, such as pushes and API calls, and what a company CA that you add can read. Attack vectors lists them under Narrowed, not closed and Left to you. What transparent mode leaves to a tool’s own proxy settings, such as other ports, databases’ protocols, addresses and HTTP/3 alone, is under tools that ignore the proxy.

item.title: Overview
item.description:
This page explains what devvm does, step by step, when it makes, opens, changes, stops and deletes a VM, and how it keeps each VM’s state. Everyday commands and Managing VMs cover the same commands from your side, and Settings and files lists your settings.

A new VM

When you run devvm in a folder that has no VM, devvm makes one in these steps:

flowchart TD
subgraph before["until the first shell opens"]
check["checks everything first:<br>image, size, ports,<br>network tier, SSH agent,<br>features, devcontainer.json"] --> tools["checks the shared tools<br>for newer versions, if due"]
tools --> build["builds the image,<br>if it isn't built"]
build --> state["writes the VM's state,<br>with its network choice"]
state --> make["makes the VM<br>from its image"]
make --> lock["locks .git,<br>unless --clone"]
lock --> start["starts its proxy,<br>then the VM"]
start --> self["the self-check"]
self --> setup["sets the VM up, then the clone<br>and devcontainer.json's commands"]
end
setup --> shell["opens the shell"]
before -. "interrupted" .-> undo["deletes the VM and what<br>devvm made for it,<br>and unlocks .git"]
  1. devvm checks everything the new VM needs before it builds anything, because a build can take minutes. That covers the folder, its toolchains, agents and layers, which it shows in a list in a terminal when you give none of --tools, --agents and --layers (what a new VM gets), the size, the ports, the network tier (choosing a tier), the SSH agent, the backend’s features and what the folder’s devcontainer.json says. Last, when the VM gets an agent and devvm saved an export of agents’ history for this folder before, devvm offers the newest one, asking in a terminal with no as the default (history_import_ask) and naming devvm history import without one (history_import_later). Before any of it, devvm takes the folder’s creation lock, which it holds until it has recorded that it made the VM in step 5.
  2. When the VM gets shared tools and the daily check is due, devvm checks for newer versions of them.
  3. devvm builds the image if it isn’t built yet (building), then the VM’s shared tools that the share lacks.
  4. devvm writes the VM’s state, with the network choice in it, before it makes the VM. If a later step fails, the VM never starts without its network choice. devvm also clears what an earlier VM of this folder that was deleted some other way left behind: it stops that VM’s proxy and link session and deletes the VM’s folder in its data folder, with its own rules, its run files and its logs.
  5. devvm makes the VM from its image. The VM mounts only the project folder, read-write, and the shared tools and its agents’ settings folders from devvm’s agent store, read-only. With --clone, devvm doesn’t mount the folder, and the VM gets its own clone of the repo instead (working on a clone).
  6. Unless the VM is a --clone VM, devvm locks the folder’s .git hooks and config (.git protection). It warns when the repo’s origin is an SSH remote and the VM has no SSH agent (ssh_remote_hint), and on Linux hosts it names the set-id files in the folder, including those an earlier VM of this folder made. When the VM forwards your SSH agent, devvm checks that the agent has keys.
  7. devvm starts the VM’s proxy, then the VM, confined to the proxy on every tier but open.
  8. The self-check runs, before the setup and the shell. Then, when you said yes to the export devvm offered, devvm warns when the tier that its .folder file records is less strict than the VM’s, or when it records none (history_import_less_strict, history_import_tier_unknown), and streams it into the VM, whose own tar checks its paths and unpacks it as the VM’s user (importing history), and a failed import only warns.
  9. devvm sets the VM up (the VM’s setup) and makes it reachable by name over SSH. It makes a --clone VM’s clone, or a workspace clone’s repos, all in one command in the VM, then pushes each repo’s branches and copies the folder’s own files, and then runs the commands of the folder’s devcontainer.json.
  10. devvm opens a shell in the VM in its own place, so devvm ends when the shell does. Without a terminal, the shell reads its commands from devvm’s input.

Until the first shell opens, nothing of yours is in the VM yet. If you interrupt devvm before then, it deletes the VM, stops its proxy, deletes its pinned host keys and its folder, with its state, its own rules and its run files, takes the locks off .git, and for a --clone VM removes the repo’s remote for it.

Adding to a VM

When devvm tools add, or devvm tools in a terminal, adds shared tools to an existing VM (adding to a VM), the tools it builds join the VM’s state and are mounted as devvm then launches the VM, and nothing is installed on the VM’s disk. A new agent’s config folders are mounted as the launch matches the VM’s agent folder mounts, which restarts a running VM after asking. devvm tools shows an existing VM’s layers but can’t change them, and --tools, --agents and --layers change nothing on an existing VM, because a layer goes onto the VM’s disk, which only making the VM again changes.

Making a VM again

devvm layer add LAYER... makes the folder’s VM again from a new image, its own layers with the new ones on top, and keeps devvm’s settings for it and its home folder (adding layers to a VM). devvm layer rm LAYER... makes it again from an image of its other layers, in their order (taking layers out of a VM). devvm update first moves the VM to the newest shared tools, the step devvm tools update takes (Tools.update), which needs no remake because the tools are mounted. Then it makes the VM again from the image it has, when that image or one below it has a new key, so the VM gets the image’s new build (outdated VMs), and when the folder’s devcontainer.json isn’t the one the VM was made from, as reading the devcontainer.json again describes. An outdated VM without --force or a terminal is refused before the tools step, so a refusal changes nothing. The remake is one path in the VM’s lifecycle, which takes the image to make the VM from, so each command only works out that image and its own refusals: devvm layer add names the layers the VM has already, devvm layer rm names those it lacks (lacks_layers) and refuses a name that’s no layer’s, though it takes out one of the user’s whose script is gone, and devvm update says the VM is current (vm_current) when it had the newest tools and nothing in its chain changed, or names what changed (vm_changed) before it asks.

Before anything changes, devvm refuses a name that isn’t a layer, a VM made for another folder, one whose creation didn’t finish and, except for devvm clone, a --clone VM, and it checks that the VM’s backend has every feature the VM needs with the new image (Require) and that the disk has room for a VM. Then it asks (remake_confirm, or remake_confirm_clean_home with --clean-home), and a parent folder’s VM only in a terminal (remake_parent_vm_ask). The remake then goes in this order:

  1. devvm builds the new image, as for a new VM.
  2. It exports the agents’ history as devvm rm does, unless --no-export, and saves the VM’s home folder, unless --clean-home. The VM runs tar --one-file-system --ignore-failed-read in its home as its user, and devvm reads that stream on this machine and writes only what it keeps to home.tar.gz in the VM’s folder (the home folder’s copy). A failure in either keeps the VM as it was (export_failed_kept, remake_home_failed), but an export over 2 GiB only warns (history_too_large), and the remake goes on without one.
  3. devvm records the remake in the VM’s state (remake), stops the VM, its proxy and its link session, and has the backend rename the VM’s machine to its aside name, devvm-<hash>-old, which is no project VM’s name, so nothing else takes it for one. On Lima that’s limactl rename, which keeps the old disk whole.
  4. devvm makes the new machine by the VM’s name from the new image, with what the state records: its project folder, its agents’ folders, the tools share, its SSH agent, its size, its ports and its ssh port. It records that the new machine was made, and it keeps in the remake’s section what the VM had of its base’s from, its shared tools, its ports and its devcontainer section (remake.was), so an undo can give them back. It clears which of its devcontainer.json’s commands ran, so those that run once run again. Then it starts the VM as every start does (an existing VM, steps 4 to 8), which pins its new host keys.
  5. devvm puts the saved home folder in, with tar --skip-old-files as the VM’s user, so what the new image has stays the image’s. The new machine is the VM from then on, so devvm records the new image and chain, and that the new machine is done.
  6. devvm deletes the old machine and ends the remake, which removes the section, then deletes home.tar.gz and opens the VM as an existing VM, setting it up first. The proxy reads the VM’s layers from its image, so the new layers’ allowlists apply from then, and those of layers taken out no longer do, as what the proxy started with has changed (the proxy). The VM’s id, its alias and every other field stay as they were (a VM made again).

Until the new machine has the home folder in step 5, a failure or an interrupt runs the remake’s cleanup (remake_undone).
