the structure test’s owners, the coding agents internal/agents, whose Defs hold every fact devvm keeps of each agent, so no copy of an agent’s list or paths goes stale when one is added. A string literal that is an agent’s name or a login file’s kind, whole, or that holds an agent’s folder below the home folder, fails, and code of one agent’s own names the agent by its constant there (adding a coding agent) internal/stubtest, whose stubs are named after the commands they stand in for, and tests
the structure test’s owners, the toolchains internal/image, whose SharedTools holds every fact devvm keeps of each toolchain: its members, the files that call for it, its installer, its guest environment, its PATH folders and its version files. A string literal that is a toolchain’s name or a member’s, whole, fails, so code elsewhere asks the table, and a new toolchain is an entry there (adding a toolchain) internal/stubtest, and tests
the structure test’s owners, image names internal/image, whose Name is an image’s name and splits it into its layers (Layers, Parent, Has), whose NameOf joins layers into one, and whose ParseName reads the name the user gives, which build.Names’ Parse checks against the layers there are. devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm read their names there once, and the rest of devvm passes the image.Name on tests
the structure test’s owners, state.ReadHash and project.Parents the finder in internal/vm/finder.go, whose target finds the VM every command acts on: the folder’s own, the nearest parent folder’s under --here and --parent (resolveFolder), or one named (devvm rm VM). It finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder (finder.state, by the path’s hash first, then recorded), offers to move a VM whose folder moved there (moveHere in internal/vm/move.go, the match here.movedFrom), and names a new VM by the first of the folder’s names whose VM folder is free (newName, project.Nth). Its need says what the command needs of the VM, and need.check is the one place that refuses one that isn’t there, one made for an earlier folder at its path, one whose remake didn’t finish and one whose creation didn’t, the last with refuseUnfinished, which every start (starter.bringUp in internal/vm/start.go) makes too. It reads the folder devvm runs in only then, so the commands that act on no folder’s VM run in a folder that’s gone. The VM it finds is a target (internal/vm/target.go). It holds what the VM’s backend told the finder, which each start and stop of the VM then updates, and it runs what a command does with that VM: exec, shell, stop, running, ownSSH and the name of its ssh config entry internal/state, and tests
the structure test’s owners, hostsafety.Walk the start in internal/vm/start.go, whose starter.walk walks a VM’s project folder once for each check of the folder on the host, for the git repos nested in it, which .git protection goes by (gitprotect.Protector.Nested), and on Linux hosts its set-id files, so a check never walks the folder twice. It walks when a VM is made and when a check finds it stopped, at a launch or at devvm stop (starter.hostChecks), and at devvm git-protect on a stopped VM, never at a launch into a running VM internal/hostsafety, and tests
the structure test’s owners, state.ReadAll the inventory in internal/vm/inventory.go, which reads every VM’s state (ReadStates), and with ReadInventory the backends’ lists too, each within its wait, for every listing of VMs: devvm ls, devvm space, devvm images and devvm gc, the ssh config, devvm gc --orphans, the links, devvm secret’s list, finding a VM by its name and the mounts that devvm’s SSH agent checks a key against. Its one failure policy is that a backend that can’t list fails a listing (Inventory.Err) only when some VM’s state names it, and that a state that can’t be read is a row of its own, which the readers leave out and ToolsInUse and Mounts fail on. state.VMNames, which fails on such a state, stays for the readers below internal/vm: netpolicy, ports and sshconfig.ChooseAlias internal/state, and tests
the structure test’s owners, paths.Dirs.AgentSettings and paths.Dirs.AgentLogins devvm’s agent store: agentStore in internal/vm/agents.go for the agents’ settings, which the mounts, the setup’s copies, a remake’s home and devvm agent import take, and secrets.LoginFile in internal/secrets/secrets.go for their logins, which the setup’s copies and the proxy read, so nothing reads an agent’s files from the home folder but vm.AgentImport internal/paths, and tests
the structure test’s owners, paths in devvm’s folders internal/paths, whose Dirs and VM name every file and folder devvm keeps, so the layout, its golden listing in testdata/script/layout.txtar and a VM’s teardown miss none. A filepath.Join onto a Data or Config field fails, and so does an os.MkdirTemp or os.CreateTemp there whose name is a literal; a name from paths, such as paths.ToolsBuildPrefix, passes tests

forbidigo matches only the function a call names, so the checks that look at a call’s arguments are in the structure test. It finds a host command in an exec.Command or exec.CommandContext call that names it, as a literal or as a constant, whatever name the file imports os/exec under. It finds a DEVVM_ variable in a call to any function or field named Getenv or LookupEnv, in any case, so t.Getenv and a getenv parameter count as well as os.Getenv, and it finds HOME the same way. The settings envSettings lists are the ones users set, DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK, DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK, DEVVM_LIMA_HOME, DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE and DEVVM_FROM; names mode, DEVVM_MESSAGES, which any build has; and the variables devvm sets for its own processes, DEVVM_GUESTFWD for devvm _qemu and DEVVM_DAEMON_STATUS for each background process internal/daemon starts.

The structure test also finds a copy of an owner’s code by its text, in literals. A string literal outside tests that holds '\'', the escaped quote a shell quoter writes, belongs in internal/shell, and one that holds [0-9a-f]{14}, the hash at the end of a project VM’s name, belongs in internal/vmname. A quote written as a rune, such as '\'' in Go, isn’t a string literal, so it doesn’t count. One that holds a coding agent’s folder below the home folder, such as .codex/ or .pi/agent, belongs in internal/agents, and so does one that is an agent’s name or a login file’s kind, whole, such as "opencode" (names), so code of one agent’s own names it by its constant there, such as agents.Opencode, and a longer text that mentions an agent, such as a command’s example, doesn’t count. A literal that is a toolchain’s name or one of its members’, whole, such as "dotnet" or "pnpm", belongs in internal/image in the same way, so code elsewhere finds a toolchain’s facts in its image.SharedTools entry. In the same way, separators finds a copy of a parser by what it splits on: a call to any function of package strings with + as an argument, as a literal or as a constant, splits or joins an image’s layers, so it belongs in internal/image. A call with another argument that holds a +, such as strings.ContainsAny(arg, "+,"), doesn’t count.

The shared tools have one owner too, the table image.SharedTools in internal/image/tool.go, whose agents’ entries it makes from the coding agents’ registry, agents.Defs (adding a coding agent). Each entry, an image.ToolDef, holds a tool’s name, its kind (a toolchain or an agent), its members (the tools in the lock that its name stands for, such as pnpm and bun for node), the files in a project folder that call for it, and its installer, which is mise for every tool but rust, which rustup installs, and dotnet, which assets/shared-tools/build.sh unpacks from Microsoft’s SDK archive. A toolchain’s entry also holds the environment that every VM’s shells get for it, such as NPM_CONFIG_PREFIX and .NET’s telemetry switch (Env), the folders of the VM’s home that go on every VM’s PATH, where its global installs go (PathDirs), and the members whose version files mise reads in a project (VersionFiles). mise locks dotnet’s version without a download, because its own installer runs Microsoft’s install script, which checks nothing, so devvm adds each platform’s archive and its SHA-512 from Microsoft’s release metadata to the lock (withSDKDownloads in internal/tools/dotnet.go), and Share.Build passes them to build.sh (image.OwnDownload), which checks the archive with devvm-fetch. image.Toolchains, image.Agents, image.GroupTools, the files that make devvm choose a toolchain for a new VM, the lock’s check for downloads (image.NoDownload) and the devcontainer.json features that devvm maps to a toolchain all come from it. So do the files that every launch’s setup writes for the toolchains: /etc/devvm/toolchains.sh, with every toolchain’s environment and PATH folders (image.GuestEnv and image.GuestPath), which base’s /etc/profile.d/devvm-tools.sh reads in every shell, as it reads the agents’ /etc/devvm/agents.sh, and the VM’s mise setting that names the tools whose version files it reads (image.VersionFileTools). The image builds read none of them, so a toolchain’s environment changes no image. The structure test fails on a string literal outside internal/image that is a toolchain’s name or a member’s, whole, so code elsewhere asks the table, through image.Def, an entry’s Installer or its other fields, rather than naming a toolchain. Adding a toolchain and adding a coding agent list the files a new shared tool needs, and the agreement tests fail until the table and those files match.

The scripts that devvm’s builds run with bash have one owner for the machine they run on, assets/prelude.sh, whose $devvm_arch, $devvm_libc and devvm_sha give each script its architecture, its C library and its pinned checksum for each download (the scripts’ prelude). A script reads them rather than run uname -m or look for apk itself, and checks that the prelude came first with : "${devvm_arch:?}" for each variable it reads, which also tells shellcheck that the variable is set. Go reads each of those scripts through image.OwnScript, which puts the prelude before it, so a recipe, a tool image’s key and the conversion’s copy of oci/build.sh all hold the two together. TestPreludeUsers in internal/image fails when a script that doesn’t get the prelude, such as assets/oci/bootify.sh or assets/guest/’s, uses it, or when a script reads a variable without that check. testdata/script/prelude.txtar checks which pin devvm_sha picks from each script’s pins on arm64 and amd64, with glibc and with musl. A CLI test or a Go test that sources one of these scripts sources assets/prelude.sh first.

internal/paths also owns how a path on the host is resolved and compared with a folder, in resolve.go, whose comment says which resolver each question takes. paths.Physical resolves every symlink as far as the path exists, for where a folder or file really is, such as a project folder against devvm’s own folders or an SSH key against the folders VMs mount. paths.PhysicalParent resolves only the folder’s symlinks and keeps the last element as named, for a path that may itself be a symlink devvm mustn’t follow, such as a key’s recorded path or a Seatbelt rule. filepath.EvalSymlinks itself, which fails when the path doesn’t exist, is for a path that must exist, such as the folder devvm runs in. Then paths.Within tells whether a path is a folder or inside it, and paths.Below whether it’s inside it only. Both compare names, so both paths are resolved the same way first.

A VM’s state, vm.json, has one owner too, internal/state, which reads and writes the whole file and knows only its core fields. Every other package that keeps something of a VM’s owns one section of it, with its own type, its name (Section), and an Of that reads it through state.Section: internal/netpolicy owns net, internal/gitprotect git, internal/ports ports, internal/sshagent agent, internal/tools tools, internal/secrets secrets, and internal/vm size, clone, devcontainer, desktop and links (internal/vm/state.go). A section’s type keeps what the user asked for at its top level and what devvm made under made. A change goes through state.VM.Update, which takes the VM’s lock, reads the file again, runs the change and writes the file once: the change sets its section with state.SetSection and works out a list’s new value from the file as it is then, never from what the command read earlier, so a change another devvm made meanwhile is kept. A change that fails writes nothing. Update holds one VM’s lock, so a change takes no other lock inside it, and a change to several VMs updates each in turn. state.VM.Claim is Update that also holds the claims lock, for what no two VMs may have (ports.Allocator chooses every VM’s host port through it), and state.VM.Create writes a new VM’s whole state once, its ssh alias chosen under the claims lock. A build VM has no state, so ports.Allocator.Build chooses its ssh port through state.Claims, which holds the claims lock alone. A VM’s alias is one vmname.IsAlias accepts, or devvm doesn’t use it. internal/vm’s checkState reads every section of the folder’s VM’s state as the VM is found, so a section that can’t be read stops the command instead of reading as empty. A new section adds its check there.

Agreement tests

When two places must agree but can’t be one, a test checks that they agree. TestEveryPartHasAPolicy checks that every image part has its policy, TestSharedToolsPolicies that the policies in assets/shared-tools/ are one for each shared tool in image.SharedTools, TestConfigTools that assets/shared-tools/mise.toml lists each shared tool’s members and nothing else, TestBuiltinPolicies that every policy devvm ships parses, TestEveryMessageIsUsed that every message has a caller, TestDocLinks that every doc link is a message and a heading, TestPreludeUsers that only the scripts that get the prelude use it, TestDefsComplete that every coding agent has its [tool_alias] line and its row in the docs’ Supported agents table, TestProvidersComplete that every provider in agents.Providers has its row in the docs’ table of the API keys the proxy puts in, TestToolchainsComplete that every toolchain has files that call for it and its row and section on the toolchains page, which names those files and its PATH folders, TestFormatsCoverLogins that every agent’s login file has its format in internal/agentlogin, and TestReferenceIsCurrent that the CLI reference matches the commands. A new pair of places that must agree gets such a test.

The consolidation pass

A review of a body of work, and the review before a release, look across the code for copies:

  • two parsers of one format
  • a path built outside internal/paths
  • a list of files kept beside the folder that holds them
  • a value encoded in a string
  • two messages that say one thing
  • a comment that says to keep two places in sync
  • a test that copies a constant

Each copy gets one of three outcomes: extend the owner, make one owner, or leave it. Leave it when the only shared helper would be the wrong one, because a copy costs less than the wrong helper, and wait for a third copy before making one. The pass is part of those reviews, not a step every change runs.

Changing the state layout

State files describes the layout, and the design note says why it’s built that way. Every path in it comes from internal/paths. paths.Dirs names the shared folders and files, and Dirs.VM(name) gives a VM’s paths.VM, whose methods name each file in the VM’s folder: Dirs.VMDir(hash), vms/<hash>/, for a project VM, and run/builds/<name>/ for a build VM. A new file of a VM’s gets a method on paths.VM, so it lands in the VM’s folder, and vmFolders.teardown in internal/vm/teardown.go deletes it with the folder, with no list of files to update. A new socket goes in Dirs.Run(), named by a hash, and TestSocketsFit checks the longest path against paths.SocketMax. A new record that only devvm writes is JSON, read with encoding/json, which ignores fields it doesn’t know, and written whole with state.WriteFile. A new default goes in internal/settings, which reads config.toml strictly and saves settings.json, and a new lock is an OS file lock (platform.LockFile and its kin) on a file that paths names.

The data folder and the config folder each hold a version file with their layout version, state.Layout in internal/state/layout.go. Before each command that reads them, state.CheckLayout takes version.lock in the data folder and compares both files with state.Layout. A folder without the file gets this devvm’s version, the same version goes on, and a newer one stops the command with layout_newer, because a newer devvm changed the folders. An older one runs the migrations from that version to this one, in order, and then writes state.Layout into both files. skipsLayout in internal/cli/root.go lists the commands that skip the check: help, completion, the version and devvm’s own hidden commands.

testdata/script/layout.txtar makes two VMs on the allowlist tier, a forwarded port, a link and a secret, lists every file and folder under the data and config folders, and compares the lists with the ones at the end of the script, one for macOS and one for Linux. A change to the layout, such as a new file, a renamed folder or a file that moves, changes a listing, so the test fails until you update it. When it does, decide whether the change needs a new layout version:

  1. A change that an older devvm would read wrongly, or a file that moves, raises state.Layout by one.
  2. It adds a state.Migration at the end of migrations(), which changes the folders from the version before to the new one. A migration takes paths.Dirs, and a run that it fails stops before the versions change, so the next run tries it again. TestMigrations checks that there’s one migration for each version before this one, and TestCheckLayout runs fake ones.
  3. It updates the listings in layout.txtar.

A new file that an older devvm doesn’t need to know about, or a field added to a JSON file, which an older devvm ignores, keeps the version and changes only the listings.

Released state

Someone who upgrades devvm keeps their VMs, defaults, agent store and secrets as the release they came from left them. Until 1.0, an upgrade from every release since 0.1.0 has to work. Each final release that changed what devvm writes on disk has a frozen copy of the state it left, called its fixture, and the tests run today’s devvm on every fixture, so a change that breaks an older release’s state fails the gate.

What a fixture holds

A release’s fixture is the folder testdata/v<release>/. Its darwin/ folder holds the state that the release left on a Mac, and its linux/ folder the state it left on Linux. For 0.1.0, that’s four VMs’ states, its defaults, its agent store and logins, the stubs’ record of the VMs, and what its --json printed for them, and the folder’s README.md lists what each VM has. The release made these files itself. Its generate.sh checks out the release’s tag in a temporary folder and runs generate.txtar with that version’s own CLI test harness, then copies what the run left, with each file’s mode in modes, because git doesn’t keep modes.

A fixture is frozen. It’s generated once, from the release’s own binary, and never edited or generated again, so never run its generate.sh from a newer devvm and never change its files. A release whose state is the same as the one before it adds no fixture, and neither does a release candidate, such as 0.1.1-rc.1, because only a final release that changes the state gets one.

The tests on every fixture

The unit tests read every fixture’s files with today’s readers. stateFixtures in internal/vm/fixture_test.go lists each release’s expectations: its VMs, the version of their vm.json, its layout version, its clones of one repo, and functions that check its VMs, its defaults and its agent store. 0.1.0’s entry is v010Fixture in fixture_v010_test.go. TestFixtureVMStates, TestFixtureVMsRead, TestFixtureSettings, TestFixtureAgentStore and TestFixtureClonesReadAsOneRepo run once for each release and system, and they check that each field the release wrote reads and writes back unchanged. TestStateFixturesListed fails when a folder in testdata has no entry, or an entry has no folder. Two packages keep a table of their own for what only they read. In internal/proxy, fixtureBinaries records the SHA-256 of the binary that made each release’s state, which its proxy configs name, and TestFixtureBindings and TestFixtureProxyConfig read every release’s bindings files and proxy configs. In internal/secrets, storeFixtures names a secret that each release’s store on Linux keeps as a file, which TestFixtureStoreGet reads through a VM’s binding. TestV010Rules is a copy of 0.1.0’s own tests of the proxy’s rules, kept apart from today’s.

The CLI tests run today’s commands on each fixture. A release’s scripts are in testdata/script/, named fixture_v and the release’s version without its dots, such as fixture_v010.txtar, fixture_v010_clone.txtar and fixture_v010_network.txtar for 0.1.0. Each one puts the state into a sandbox with fixture v<release>, which moves it to the sandbox’s folder: the folder’s path, each VM’s name hash, its folder’s and .git’s identities and its backend’s place become what they are there, and nothing else changes. The script then runs today’s devvm on it. Each --json must have everything the release’s had (json_superset), the read-only commands must change no file, and a launch must start each VM as it is, without a Lima edit. The scripts stay separate for each release, because their checks name that release’s VMs and what each one has, and TestFixtureScripts in internal/cli fails when a fixture has no script or a script names a fixture that isn’t there.

Changing what devvm does with state

A change that reads or writes state, such as a new command, a new section in vm.json or a new field in a record, runs its new commands on every fixture in the same commit, and reading the files isn’t enough. Add the steps to each release’s scripts, as fixture_v010_network.txtar runs rules by method and path on 0.1.0’s app VM and fixture_v010_clone.txtar runs devvm clone add on its web VM. When a fixture’s test fails, today’s devvm breaks the state that the release’s users have. Fix devvm, or add a migration, but never change the fixture.

A change in what devvm does with existing state gets an entry marked Breaking in CHANGELOG.md, in the section for the release it goes out in. When the user has to do something about it, such as run a command, devvm also tells them once, at the first launch after the upgrade.

Freezing a release’s state

At release time, after the tag exists, a final release that changed the state format gets its fixture. A release candidate gets none, even when it changed the state, and its final release’s fixture holds that state:

  1. Copy the newest fixture’s generate.sh, generate.txtar and README.md into testdata/v<release>/. Set the tag, the version and the script’s name in generate.sh, and add the VMs and commands to generate.txtar that make the state the release added.
  2. Run generate.sh on a Mac and on Linux, which writes darwin/ and linux/. 0.1.0’s were made on an arm64 Mac and on x86_64 Fedora.
  3. Add the release’s entries in stateFixtures, fixtureBinaries and storeFixtures, and its scripts, made from the newest release’s scripts with checks of its own VMs.
  4. Commit the folder as the run left it. The older fixtures stay as they are.

The support window

An upgrade from every release since 0.1.0 works until 1.0. When a release leaves the window, its fixture and the code that only its state needs, such as a reader of a field that only that release wrote, go together, in one commit that says which release left and why. The commit deletes testdata/v<release>/, its scripts and its entries in the tables above.

item.title: Backends, toolchains and agents
item.description:
How a backend plugs in

devvm runs every VM on Lima, but the rest of devvm reaches Lima only through the backend.Backend interface in internal/backend, so another backend is an addition rather than a change to the callers. A backend lives in a package of its own under internal/backend, and it does four things:

  • It implements backend.Backend and returns its errors instead of ending the run: a msg.M, or backend.Logged(m) once a logged command failed, so the command shows the run log’s end before the message. Backend is the backend’s Name and Caps and four roles, each an interface of its own that every backend implements in full:

    • backend.Host is what the backend needs of this machine and where it keeps its VMs there. Problems lists what the host lacks for it, and backend.Check(ctx, b) returns the first of them, so a backend doesn’t write a check of its own. NameMax is the longest VM name it takes, Location is where its VMs live when that can change between runs (backend.LocationOf), and DiskDirs and Floors are the folders its disks are in and the free space it wants there (backend.Space). A backend whose VMs can’t move returns "" from Location, and one whose disks aren’t on this machine returns no DiskDirs.
    • backend.Images builds images and the shared tools’ images and keeps the images. BuildImage runs the spec’s Recipe (image.Recipe, which internal/build puts together and image.Input hashes) as it is, each image.Step with its arguments and as root when it says so. Origin is the backend’s own steps that base starts with, such as the Ubuntu image Lima pinned on this machine, a --from image’s conversion, base’s disk size (backend.BaseDiskGiB) and base.yaml. Base’s size is backend.BaseCPUs, backend.BaseMemoryGiB and backend.BaseDiskGiB, never read from a backend’s files. internal/build puts them first in base’s recipe, as its Origin, so base’s key hashes them, and BuildImage is given them back and runs those rather than reading its own files again. PinOrigin pins what base starts from on this machine, which internal/build asks for before it keys a build (backend.PinFirst): on Lima, that’s the newest Ubuntu cloud image (state.UbuntuPin, found by ubuntu.Finder). A base build’s ImageSpec.Packages sends its packages into the VM’s backend.PackagesDir before the steps and takes them out after, which internal/build/packages.go records or replays and checks, and a step that exits backend.ExitUnreachable fails as build_sources_unreachable.
    • backend.Machines makes, starts, stops, renames and deletes VMs, lists them, and runs commands and shells in them. A stopped VM changes only at Start, which first checks with backend.Validate that it can apply the VM’s backend.Want, such as a disk no smaller than the VM’s own, and then applies what the Want asks where it differs from the VM. Start leaves a running VM as it is, and the callers, not the backend, warn that a change waits for the VM’s next start. On Lima, Start owns the config’s env:, propagateProxyEnv, dns and hostResolver, and a project VM’s size, agent mounts and forwardAgent, which it compares with the VM’s before its one edit (what devvm sets on a VM). Ports are never the backend’s: vmssh.Forwards forwards them over the backend’s SSH. Running says how a VM runs now, in one backend.Run: the ID of its current start, whether it’s confined to its proxy, and its lifeline, the file that the VM’s proxy and port forwarder follow. The backend runs no port forwarder of its own, and SSH says how ssh, links and devvm’s forwarder (vmssh.Forwards) reach a running VM’s sshd, a target that vmssh.FromTarget checks. All three get it through vmssh.Checked, which checks the review lets the backend’s ssh through, checks the target, and adds the VM’s host keys for its current start, reading the record (vmssh.ReadKeys) or pinning the keys first (vmssh.PinKeys). A VM whose ssh isn’t usable fails with a *vmssh.UnusableError and one without host keys with vmssh.ErrNoHostKeys, which the ssh config skips on.
    • backend.Housekeeping is what devvm space and devvm gc ask: Usage, Strays, and DevvmCache and DeleteCache for its own caches. A backend that can’t tell returns none.

    backend.Forgetter is the one role a backend may leave out, for the files it keeps for a VM besides the VM. Lima keeps none. Lima’s type, lima.Lima, holds the backend’s fields, Name, Caps and the helpers its roles share, and it embeds one type for each role, host, images, machines and housekeeping, each over the Lima it’s part of. backendtest.Fake is split the same way. So no type has more methods than the structure test allows, and a new method goes on the type of its role.

  • It declares Caps, saying for each of backend.Features whether it has the feature natively, emulates it, or lacks it (features). It lists every feature by hand, None included, and Registry.Register refuses Caps that leave one out or rate a feature better than the one Feature.BuiltOn says it’s built on (Caps.Check). The callers, not the backend, decide what a VM needs, and they check it with the registry’s Review.Require(b, vm, spec.Features()...) before they act. A feature the backend lacks fails in one line that names the VM and what to do, and devvm never falls back to something weaker. An emulation stays refused until its review passes: a design note in the design notes, a threat check with the security-audit skill, and end-to-end checks that prove its guarantee.

  • It’s registered in registry.New (internal/backend/registry), the only place besides internal/cli that imports a backend. The registry hands the backend out behind its guard, which checks every CreateVM, Start, BuildImage and BuildTools call before the backend sees it. The guard refuses a spec that needs a feature Review.Require would refuse, using the specs’ own Features, and a build spec whose ImageSpec.Validate or ToolsSpec.Validate fails, such as one with a network that isn’t a build’s or a key that isn’t one. So a caller that forgets Require still can’t reach a backend with a feature it lacks, and the backend doesn’t check those specs itself. The guard has every role’s methods, its own in place of the backend’s for those calls, so a guarded backend handed on as a backend.Images or a backend.Machines is still guarded. The guard’s type has only backend.Backend’s methods, so code that looks for an optional role, such as backend.Forgetter, uses backend.As instead of a type assertion, and the structure test fails on a type assertion to a backend package’s type anywhere but the guard.

  • It names its images by key, and an image’s key hashes the backend’s name, so two backends never share an image.

  • It passes the conformance suite, backendtest.Conformance(t, factory), which checks the contract that backend.Backend’s documentation gives. The backend’s tests call it with a factory that returns a new backendtest.Subject for each check, and each check runs as a subtest. The subject is the backend, holding one image, whose key is Image, and no VMs. Dir is a folder of the check’s own for the folders its VMs mount, Boots says whether its VMs start, and Restart starts a running VM again outside Start, as a command of the user’s own would. The suite checks every role’s answers and the empty answers each role allows, that a VM is made, renamed and deleted as its spec says, and that a missing VM is backend.ErrNotFound. It also checks that Running gives a stopped VM its lifeline with an empty ID, that every start gets another ID, that a VM is Confined only while it runs on a start Start made with NetProxy, and that the registry’s guard still refuses what the backend lacks when the backend is used as backend.Images or backend.Machines alone. When Boots is false, the checks that need a running VM are skipped with the reason, and when Restart is nil, so is the one that needs it. backendtest.Fake runs the suite in internal/backend/backendtest, and TestConformance in internal/backend/lima runs it on Lima twice: on the limactl stub, whose VMs start, and on real Lima’s dummy instances, which can’t boot, so the checks that need a running VM are left to the end-to-end tests. The real Lima run skips when limactl isn’t on PATH. TestConformanceFinds checks the suite itself: each of a set of fakes that breaks the contract in one method fails the check meant to catch it.

The registry’s For chooses a VM’s backend: a VM that exists gets the one its state records in backend=, and a new VM gets backend.Default, which is lima. Tests set the registry’s NewVMs to give new VMs a fake backend (backendtest.Fake). The command line has no way to choose a backend, so a second backend would also add one, following the cli skill, together with its column in the tables that list VMs, images and caches. --json output already names each VM’s, image’s and shared tool’s backend.

A new backend gets a design note and a threat check with the security-audit skill before any of its emulations is marked reviewed, and that check covers what Lima gets from its VMs’ design. A VM started outside devvm must not forward an agent devvm didn’t choose, a VM whose root can change its own network must not count as confined, a secret the proxy needs goes in a private file and never in a command’s arguments, and a socket on this machine goes in a private folder.

Adding a toolchain

Each toolchain is one image.ToolDef entry in image.SharedTools, in internal/image/tool.go, and the rest of devvm reads every list of the toolchains and every fact of one from there: its members in the lock, the files in a project folder that call for it, its installer, the environment that every VM’s shells get, the folders of the VM’s home that go on every VM’s PATH, and the members whose version files mise reads. --tools, devvm tools, the picker, shell completion, the new VM’s summary and the devcontainer.json features that devvm maps list the toolchains from the table too, and every launch writes the environment, the PATH folders and the version files into the VM, so a new toolchain changes no image. A new toolchain that mise installs from the lock’s checked downloads, as it installs node, python and go, needs these files and nothing else:

  • internal/image/tool.go: its entry, with its Env, PathDirs and VersionFiles when it has them.
  • assets/shared-tools/mise.toml: a line in [tools] for each member, with its hold, and a line in [tool_alias] for each member that isn’t one of mise’s own (core:), naming the backend it comes from.
  • assets/shared-tools/<name>.policy: the hosts its allowlist allows, such as its package registry and the downloads of the versions a project asks for.
  • testdata/mise.lock and tests/e2e-mise.lock: each member’s lock entry, which scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools writes into the second.
  • docs/content/docs/using/toolchains.md: its row in the table, in the registry’s order, its section, with what it brings, the files that call for it, its version files, its global installs and its allowlist, and its row in the glibc table of Which bases they run on.
  • tests/e2e/tools_test.go: its checks, such as a project’s VM that its files call for, a global install and a version file’s own version.

Then the golden files in internal/vm/testdata/golden take its environment, its PATH folders and its version files with UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/vm -run Golden, and a reviewer reads their diff. TestToolchainsComplete, TestToolchainGuest, TestSharedToolsPolicies and TestConfigTools fail until those files match the table, and the structure test fails on a string literal elsewhere that is its name or a member’s.

A toolchain that needs more than mise’s install gets code of its own, which the table can’t hold. A step in each VM, such as rust’s rustup in ~/.cargo, go’s telemetry switch or dotnet’s /etc/dotnet/install_location, is a block of assets/guest/sync.sh that reads the toolchain’s version from the VM’s tool list. An install that mise can’t check, such as rust’s, which rustup checks against its own signed manifest, or dotnet’s, whose SDK archive devvm adds to the lock with its SHA-512, is an Installer of its own, with its branch in assets/shared-tools/build.sh and its handling of the lock in internal/tools.

Adding a coding agent

Each coding agent is one agents.Def in internal/agents/agents.go, and the rest of devvm reads every list of the agents and every fact of one from there: its shared tool (image.SharedTools makes its entry, glibc-only or not), its settings folders and files with each file’s format, the folder that devvm agent import copies from, its login files and their kinds, its history and what an export leaves out of it, the environment that every VM’s shells get, which turns off its self-update and telemetry, the secret every VM with it uses, how devvm agent login logs it in (its own login, a ChatGPT login or API keys) and whether config.toml’s [pass-keys] takes it. The commands’ help, --agents, the picker and shell completion list the agents from the registry too. A new agent that works like one devvm has needs these files and nothing else:

  • internal/agents/agents.go: its Def and its name’s constant.
  • assets/shared-tools/mise.toml: its line in [tool_alias], the backend it comes from, and in [tools], its version.
  • assets/shared-tools/<name>.policy: the hosts its allowlist allows.
  • testdata/mise.lock and tests/e2e-mise.lock: its lock entry, which scripts/bump.sh e2e-tools writes into the second.
  • docs/content/docs/using/coding-agents.md: its row in the Supported agents table, in the registry’s order, and a section on its login when it has one.
  • README.md, whose short list of the agents stays in step with the table.
  • When it keeps a login file: a format for each of its kinds in internal/agentlogin, a type with the format interface’s methods in a file of its own (and keyFormat or chatGPTFormat when its Def says it saves API keys or holds a ChatGPT login), added to formats in format.go, with its fixture in goldenLogins (internal/agentlogin/golden_test.go) and its golden file, and its format’s section in internals/network.md.

Then mise run cli-docs writes the CLI pages whose help lists the agents, and the golden files in internal/vm/testdata/golden take its paths with UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/vm -run Golden. TestDefsComplete, TestFormatsCoverLogins, TestSharedToolsPolicies and TestConfigTools fail until those files match the registry, and the structure test fails on any string literal elsewhere that is the agent’s name or holds its folder, so code of the agent’s own, such as a settings filter or a login of its own, names it by its constant in internal/agents. The network section of the e2e tests drives every agent, so the new one gets its checks there.

Adding a provider

The model providers whose API keys the VM’s proxy puts in for the agents with a key for each provider, opencode and pi, are one table, agents.Providers in internal/agents/agents.go. Each agents.Provider holds the provider’s ID, which is its entry’s name in both agents’ auth.json, its name as people know it, the hosts the agents send its key to, its Path when the agents send the key below one path of those hosts alone, such as OpenRouter’s /api/, the Headers they send it in, most often one but two for OpenRouter, whose Anthropic models take the key in x-api-key, and its Prefix, which starts the key’s placeholder when an agent checks how the provider’s keys start: pi takes an OpenAI key that doesn’t start with sk- for a Sign in with ChatGPT login, so OpenAI’s is sk-. The opencode and pi formats’ bindings, agentlogin.KeyProviders, which devvm agent login --provider takes and its help lists, and the allowlist lines of each binding’s hosts all come from it. A new provider is its entry there, in the order of its ID, and its row in the table in using/coding-agents.md’s API keys the proxy puts in, which TestProvidersComplete checks against the registry. Read the hosts, the paths, the headers and any check of how a key starts in both agents’ own source first, and in the SDK that each one sends its requests with, because a header that differs from the agents’, or one that an agent uses for some models alone, leaves the key’s placeholder in the request, and a host that the agents never send the key to would get the key anyway. The proxy puts a provider’s key in only when the header’s value is the placeholder alone, or Bearer and the placeholder in Authorization, so check that both agents send the key that way too. A Path starts and ends with /, is clean, and goes into each binding as its Path, below which pathWithin takes a request’s path, so set one only when every request of both agents with the key goes below it. Then mise run cli-docs writes the CLI page whose help lists the providers, and UPDATE_GOLDEN=1 go test ./internal/agentlogin -run Golden writes the golden files that list them.

item.title: Port forwarding
item.description:
This page explains how devvm’s forwarder forwards a VM’s ports to this machine, which ports it never takes, and how it runs. Ports and size covers choosing a VM’s ports with --ports and devvm ports.

devvm forwards a VM’s ports with its own forwarder, never with Lima’s own forwards. Lima explains why, and what devvm sets on Lima instead.

What it forwards

Ports lists which ports the forwarder forwards, for --ports all, the default, and for a list such as --ports 5173,8000-8010, and how soon. A listed port also carries a server on the VM’s loopback (127.0.0.1 or ::1) to this machine. You can list port 22, which forwards the VM’s sshd to port 22 on this machine, while ssh by name keeps using the VM’s own ssh port.

The forwarder never forwards a server on an address in 127.77.0.0/16, on any VM, because that’s where a VM listens for its links to other VMs, so a link never appears on this machine’s localhost. A server of the VM’s own on 127.0.0.1 with the same port is forwarded as usual. It also never forwards a server on 127.0.77.1, where the desktop’s local proxy listens, because the local proxy adds the VM’s password to what it sends to the VM’s proxy, and on this machine’s localhost other users and programs could use it.

What it never takes

The forwarder never takes a port that a program on this machine has on any address. That program keeps the port and its localhost connections, and the forward waits until the VM’s server stops and starts again.

The forwarder also never takes a port that devvm records for a VM, even while that port is free. Those are the ssh, proxy and desktop ports that devvm chooses for VMs, the VM’s own ssh port, and the ports other VMs list. devvm chooses and records every VM’s ssh port, whatever its tier, so no forwarder takes it in the seconds before Lima binds it (the threat check).

When a start, or a change of a running VM’s ports, finds that a program on this machine has a listed port, devvm doesn’t forward that port and warns you (ports_taken). The VM starts or runs on all the same, and the next start or change that finds the port free forwards it again. Ports says what happens to a program that binds a port on all addresses after the forwarder has forwarded it.

How it reaches the VM

The forwarder reaches the VM over the VM’s ssh, with a key and a host key that devvm pins, and it asks for no forwarding into this machine. Only a link session asks a VM for a remote forward, on a connection of its own. Every connection starts on this machine, and the VM opens none to it. The VM sees each forwarded connection only as one to its own loopback, and on a confined tier the VM still reaches only its proxy.

A connection to a forwarded port, such as 5173, takes this path:

flowchart TD
browser["your browser, on this machine,<br>where every connection starts"] -- "localhost:5173" --> fwd["devvm's forwarder,<br>on this machine"]
fwd -- "ssh, with a key and<br>a host key devvm pins" --> sshd["the VM's sshd"]
sshd -- "127.0.0.1:5173,<br>its own loopback" --> server["your server, in the VM"]

The forwarder is devvm’s own, the same on every backend. The backend only says how the forwarder reaches a running VM’s sshd, which is a user, a key and a port on this machine’s loopback, and which file the forwarder follows to know the VM still runs, as Lima’s Ports section describes.

Its process and files

The forwarder runs as a hidden devvm command, devvm _ports, one process for each VM. devvm starts it after each start of the VM, once the backend says the VM runs, and again with the new ports when you change a running VM’s ports. devvm stop, devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans stop it, and a VM that stops some other way ends it, because the forwarder exits once the backend’s process for the VM is gone. Which ports a VM forwards is in the VM’s state, which devvm reads each time it starts the forwarder, so devvm ports changes the state and never the backend’s config, and the backend never hears of them. The forwarder’s log is ports.log in the VM’s logs folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/logs/, and its ports.pid, ports.status and ports.lock are in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/, beside the VM’s host keys for its current start, known_hosts, which the forwarder checks the VM against, as devvm’s ssh config does (ssh into VMs). Its control socket is ~/.local/share/devvm/run/port-<hash>.ctl, named by a hash of the VM’s name, outside the VM’s folder, because a unix socket’s path has fewer than 104 characters.

devvm reads every list of ports the same way, whether it comes from --ports, devvm ports or the VM’s state. Each entry is a port from 1 to 65535 or a range of them, such as 8000-8010. When the VM’s state holds a list that devvm can’t read this way, such as a file edited by hand, the VM doesn’t start and devvm names the value it couldn’t read with port_invalid, so a bad entry never becomes a port the VM didn’t ask for.

When it can’t forward

When a forwarder doesn’t start, devvm warns you and names its log (ports_forward_failed), and the VM runs on without forwarded ports.

Links between VMs

A link between VMs carries a client VM’s connections to a port that a target VM publishes. Like the forwarder, it goes over ssh, every connection starts on this machine, and it uses neither VM’s network, so no backend’s confinement changes and a confined VM still reaches nothing past its proxy over its own network. The design note has the rules, the threat check and what the prototype showed.

The addresses

Each target that a client links to gets an address of its own in 127.77.0.0/16 in that client, starting at 127.77.0.1. devvm chooses it when the client’s first link to that target is made and keeps it for every port of that target, so two targets can share a port. The client’s /etc/hosts holds a block between # devvm links begin and # devvm links end, with a line 127.77.x.y NAME NAME.devvm.internal for each target. The VM’s setup replaces the block whole at each launch, and again when links change on a running client. The setup writes the file in place, never renaming over it, and only when the block changed.

A link listens at its target’s address on the target’s own port, never on the client’s 127.0.0.1 or ::1. At each start, the setup sets net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start to 0 where it’s 1024, which is on Lima’s Alpine VMs, so a link to a port below 1024 listens on that port too. Lima’s Ubuntu and Debian VMs already have 0.

The addresses are internal to devvm. devvm link and its JSON never show them, and the forwarder never forwards them (above).

The link session

For each running client with links, devvm runs a hidden command, devvm _links VM, as one detached process on this machine. Its pid is in links.pid in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/, and its log is links.log in the VM’s logs folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/logs/. It keeps an ssh connection of its own to the client, never the forwarder’s, which starts with no forwards and asks for each link as a remote forward from 127.77.x.y:PORT in the client to a unix socket on this machine. That’s the only remote forward devvm asks a VM for. It reads the client’s links again every second and adds or cancels one forward at a time as they change, and a cancel leaves the connections that are open. A link whose address and port a program in the client already holds fails alone, with link_port_taken in the session’s log, which the next launch shows. Each line that the session’s ssh processes print starts with ssh: in its log, so no line of theirs reads as one of the session’s own, and devvm link add and the launch read only the session’s own lines.

The process ends once the client no longer runs the start it was made for, or has no links left, and devvm stop stops it with the client, which ends its connections and removes its sockets.

Every VM’s sshd allows remote forwards on 127.77.0.0/16 alone, with AllowTcpForwarding all, GatewayPorts clientspecified and PermitListen 127.77.*:*, written once into every image, so links never change or reload sshd. sshd matches the address a request names against that rule as text, so a remote forward on localhost, 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0 or ::1 is refused. Root in the client can change sshd, so those settings protect only an honest VM. What keeps the VM from choosing where its connections go on this machine is the host’s ssh client, which accepts a forwarded channel only for a forward it asked for and connects it only to that link’s socket.

Each connection

A program in the client that connects to db:5432 takes this path:

flowchart TD
app["your program, in the client"] -- "db:5432, which /etc/hosts<br>names as 127.77.0.1" --> csshd["the client's sshd"]
csshd -- "the link session's ssh,<br>which this machine opened" --> links["devvm _links,<br>on this machine"]
links -- "ssh, with the target's key<br>and pinned host key" --> tsshd["the target's sshd"]
tsshd -- "127.0.0.1:5432,<br>its own loopback" --> server["the server, in the target"]
  1. The client’s sshd carries the connection over the link session to this machine, where ssh connects it to the link’s unix socket. The socket is mode 600, in ~/.local/share/devvm/run (mode 700), and named by a hash of the client, the address and the port, because a socket’s path has fewer than 104 characters.
  2. devvm _links checks the link again. The link must still exist, the target must be the VM it was made for, by its ID, the port must be published, the tier rule must hold, and the target must be running, as its backend says. For a client on a confined tier, the target’s tier must also be enforced as the target runs, as devvm ls shows it, because a target that got a confined tier while it ran stays outside its proxy until its next start, and one whose self-check failed may reach the internet directly. devvm never starts the target for a connection. The link session asks the target’s backend whether the target is running and how its ssh reaches it, and the connections to that target share that answer for one second, so a burst of connections asks the backend once and devvm notices a target that stops within a second. For a client on a confined tier, the check of the target’s tier asks the backend for each connection, so it notices at once that the target stopped, and devvm logs the connection as refused because the target isn’t running, not because its tier isn’t in force. An answer that a connection closing cut short isn’t shared, so the other connections ask again. devvm makes every other check again for each connection, including the check of the target’s tier as it runs.
  3. It carries the connection over one ssh connection that it keeps to each target, with the target’s key and pinned host key, and the target’s sshd connects to 127.0.0.1:PORT in the target. That connection to a target ends when the target stops, and the next one reads the target’s host keys again, because a VM whose Lima config changed gets new ones when it boots.

An HTTP client that uses the VM’s proxy settings sends db:5432 to the VM’s proxy instead, and the proxy connects to the same link socket on this machine (links through the proxy). Steps 2 and 3 are the same for it, so the link’s checks, its cap and its events hold for both ways in.

At most 256 of a client’s connections are carried at once, and the next one is refused. A link’s socket holds at most 128 connections waiting to be accepted on macOS, and devvm _links accepts nothing while it starts a process, so it accepts a burst of connections whole before it starts any of their ssh processes: it hands them on once 5 ms pass with nothing more to accept, once the first has waited 50 ms, or once 257 wait. Each one it accepted is carried, or refused when 256 are carried already. The ssh connection to a target takes in two file descriptors for each connection it carries, more than macOS’s default limit of 256 open files allows, so devvm _links and the port forwarder give the ssh processes they start the higher limit that devvm runs with. Each connection carried or refused is written to the client’s event log, which devvm network log shows, so every VM gets an event log for its links’ connections, whatever its tier.

When links change

devvm link add and devvm link rm record the change in the client’s state on this machine, never in a VM. On a running client they send its setup again, which rewrites /etc/hosts, and they start devvm _links if it isn’t running. devvm _links reads the links again every second and writes the list that the client’s proxy reads, so the proxy reaches a new link as soon as its forward is in place. A stopped client gets the change when it next starts. Links change nothing else in the VM: no link name is in its NO_PROXY (the VM’s setup), so no daemon restarts, and on Lima no link changes the VM’s Lima config or its ssh host keys.

devvm rm of a target removes every link to it from every client’s state and updates the running clients, and devvm gc --orphans removes links to VMs whose state is gone and the sockets that a killed link session left.

Groups

A group is recorded in each of its VMs’ own state, with the name the others reach it by, so a VM made again in a folder, which gets new state, is in none. The links a group makes are links in each VM’s state like the ones devvm link add makes, marked as the group’s, so the link session, the proxy’s list and every check of a connection treat them alike. devvm works out each VM’s group links again from its own links and the other VMs’ published ports whenever one of them joins or leaves, publishes or unpublishes a port, or adds or removes a link of its own, and it records and applies only the VMs whose links changed, as above. The design note has the rules and the threat check.

item.title: Ports and size
item.description:
This page covers the ports a VM forwards to this machine and the CPUs, memory and disk it gets. You choose both when devvm makes a VM, and you can change both later with devvm ports and devvm size. Port forwarding explains how devvm’s forwarder works.

Size and ports

A new VM gets its image’s size unless you set one with --cpus, --memory and --disk, as in devvm --cpus 6. For base that’s 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk. On a machine with fewer than 4 CPUs, base gets as many CPUs as the machine has, and when 8 GiB would leave the machine less than 2 GiB of its own, base gets half of the machine’s memory, which is 4 GiB on an 8 GiB machine. When devvm builds base on such a machine, it says how many CPUs and how much memory base gets, and devvm size -g sets the size that new VMs get instead.

  • --cpus takes a whole number. --memory and --disk take a size in GiB, written 16, 16G or 16GiB, and decimals are allowed.
  • What the flags leave unset comes from the [size] table of config.toml when it sets it, else from what devvm size -g and devvm setup saved (choosing new VMs’ size).
  • devvm refuses more CPUs than this machine has, and a disk smaller than the image’s, because disks can’t shrink. It refuses them before it builds anything.
  • devvm also refuses more memory than a VM can have, because a VM that asks for all of this machine’s memory doesn’t start. A VM can have this machine’s memory less 2 GiB, counted in whole GiB, so 6 GiB on an 8 GiB machine. On a machine with 4 GiB or less, it can have half, so 2 GiB on a 4 GiB machine. When you ask for more, devvm says how much memory this machine has and the most you can give a VM, so you can run the command again with that.

A new VM forwards every TCP port from 1024 up that it listens on, unless --ports says otherwise, as in devvm --ports 5173.

  • --ports takes all, none, or ports and ranges such as 5173,8000-8010.
  • Without --ports, the default comes from ports in config.toml when it sets it, else from what devvm ports -g saved, and without either, a new VM forwards every port.
  • When you customize a new VM without --ports, devvm asks whether it forwards every port, none or the ports you type, starting from the default, and saves the answer for that VM alone (what a new VM gets).

devvm refuses a default that isn’t a valid value, as it refuses a bad flag, and for one in config.toml it names the file and the line (when devvm can’t read it).

Ports

A VM forwards the TCP ports it listens on to the same port on this machine’s localhost, so a server on :5173 in the VM is at localhost:5173 here. To change which ports a VM forwards:

devvm ports # what this folder's VM forwards: all, none or a list
devvm ports 5173,8000-8010 # only these ports and ranges
devvm ports add 5432 # one more
devvm ports rm 5173 # one fewer, as listed; the last leaves none
devvm ports none # nothing; devvm ports all forwards every port again
devvm ports -g none # what new VMs forward (default: all)
  • A change applies at once. A stopped VM forwards the new ports from its next start. On a running VM, devvm starts its forwarder again with the new ports while the VM runs on, so a server on an added port reaches this machine within a few seconds. The connections that were open through the old forwarder close, so a client that was connected through it has to connect again.
  • add and rm take ports and ranges, not all or none. devvm refuses rm on a VM that forwards every port, because there’s no list to remove from. -g also works with add and rm.
  • devvm ports -g shows what new VMs forward, followed by where it came from after a #, and devvm ports -g --json adds it as source. When config.toml sets ports, devvm ports -g refuses to change it and names the file, so edit config.toml instead (where a default comes from).
  • devvm forwards ports on every network tier, and it forwards no ports from builds.

When a VM forwards every port, devvm forwards each TCP port from 1024 up that a server in the VM listens on, whether on the VM’s loopback or on all its addresses. When a VM lists its ports, devvm forwards those ports alone, however many there are, ports below 1024 included. A port reaches this machine within a few seconds of the server starting, only on localhost (127.0.0.1 and ::1), and the forward goes away when the server stops. At most 256 ports are forwarded at once. Your browser sends the cookies of every app you use on localhost to a forwarded port as well, so the server in the VM gets them (your browser).

A VM never takes a port that a program on this machine already has, a port that another VM lists, or a port that devvm uses for its VMs’ ssh and proxies. When a port you listed is taken by a program on this machine as the VM starts, or as you change its ports, devvm warns you and the VM runs on without that port. The next start or change that finds the port free forwards it. A program that starts on a port after the VM’s forward does can still bind it on all addresses, as most servers do, and then that program’s localhost connections reach the VM.

If the forwarder can’t start, devvm warns you and names its log, and the VM runs on without forwarded ports.

UDP isn’t forwarded, on any backend. Run the UDP client in the VM instead, or tunnel it over a forwarded TCP port with socat, installed on both sides. For a UDP server on port 8125 in the VM, with TCP port 9125 forwarded:

socat TCP-LISTEN:9125,fork,reuseaddr UDP:127.0.0.1:8125 # in the VM
socat UDP-LISTEN:8125,fork TCP:127.0.0.1:9125 # on this machine

TCP is a stream, so datagrams can arrive merged or split. This suits low-rate request and response traffic, such as DNS, statsd or syslog, but not high-rate or latency-sensitive traffic, such as games, QUIC or WebRTC media.

Size

To see or change a VM’s size:

devvm size # what this folder's VM has: cpus=4 memory=8GiB disk=100GiB
devvm size --cpus 6 --memory 16 # change it; what isn't given stays
devvm size --disk 200 # a bigger disk; never a smaller one
devvm size -g --memory 16 # the size new VMs get (default: the image's)
devvm size -g # cpus=, memory= and disk= lines, empty for the image's, each with its source
  • The flags take the same values as for a new VM and have the same limits, so devvm refuses more CPUs than this machine has and more memory than a VM can have (size and ports). devvm size -g checks a default size in the same way when you set it. A VM that already has more memory keeps it and still starts, because devvm checks a size only when you set one.
  • devvm size -g ends each line with where its value came from, after a #: the path of config.toml, devvm: settings.json for what devvm size -g or devvm setup saved, or devvm: default for the image’s. When config.toml sets cpus, memory or disk, devvm size -g refuses to change that one and names the file, so edit config.toml instead (where a default comes from).
  • A stopped VM gets its new size when it next starts, such as with devvm, and until then devvm size shows what the VM has now and says what changes. For a running VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart it now, which stops anything running in it, and if you answer yes, devvm restarts it as devvm restart does. Otherwise, and without a terminal or with --no-input, the VM keeps its size until it next starts, for example with devvm restart. When devvm opens the running VM while its new size still waits, it asks once more in a terminal, with no as the default unless an agent’s new folders wait too, and a yes restarts the VM with its new size before the shell opens (restarting).
  • Disks grow but never shrink, so devvm refuses a disk smaller than the VM’s.

Choosing new VMs’ size

devvm asks for the CPUs and memory that new VMs get on your first run, before it asks which features base gets, and again whenever you run devvm setup:

devvm setup # asks its questions, the size among them
devvm size -g --cpus 6 --memory 16 # only the size, without asking

Before the two questions, devvm says how many CPUs and how much memory this machine has. Each question shows in brackets the value new VMs get now. That’s what config.toml sets or devvm size -g saved, or else base’s own size fitted to this machine: 4 CPUs and 8 GiB, or less on a machine that doesn’t have room for them (size and ports). Confirm to keep the value, or enter another one. devvm checks what you type as it checks --cpus and --memory, and when this machine can’t give it, devvm says why and asks again.

devvm doesn’t ask for a value that config.toml sets, and says so. It saves only the values you type, where devvm size -g saves them, and keeps a saved disk size as it is. When you keep both values, devvm saves nothing, so new VMs go on getting the image’s size. Either way, devvm prints the size new VMs get. A new size changes only the VMs made after it, and nothing is rebuilt, so existing VMs keep their size until you change it with devvm size.

The first run asks only in a terminal, and only when no size is set and you didn’t give --cpus or --memory. It asks once, because that run also chooses base’s features, and devvm asks only before they’re chosen. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm asks nothing, and new VMs get the image’s size. devvm setup asks only in a terminal, without --no-input, and only when you give it no flags (devvm setup). To set the size without asking, use devvm size -g --cpus N --memory GiB, which takes the same values and has the same limits.

Disk use

A VM’s disk size is how far the disk can grow, not how much space it takes. A project VM starts as a copy of its image’s disk that shares the image’s blocks, so a new VM takes almost nothing until it writes (clones and overlays):

  • macOS: the copy is an APFS clone. du counts the shared blocks as the clone’s own, so it overcounts.
  • Linux: the copy is a qcow2 overlay of the image’s disk, which holds only the VM’s changes, about 12 MB for a new VM instead of 2 GB.

Free space

Before devvm builds an image or makes a VM, it checks the free space on the disk that will hold it, and it refuses to start the step when there’s less free than the step needs:

Step macOS Linux
building base 8 GiB 8 GiB
building any other image 2 GiB 8 GiB
building shared tool images 3 GiB, and 0.5 GiB for each tool 9 GiB, and 0.5 GiB for each tool
making a VM 2 GiB 2 GiB

devvm rounds each number up to whole GiB, so building one shared tool with Lima on macOS needs 4 GiB, and building all ten needs 8 GiB. Each build checks again before it starts, so the first VM on a Mac, which builds base, needs 8 GiB free.

The numbers leave a margin over what each step took when devvm’s tests measured the free space before, during and after it. Most of a step’s space is only needed while it runs. On Lima on macOS, base took about 1 GiB with Ubuntu’s cloud image already downloaded, and downloading the image takes up to another 0.9 GiB. base’s features add up to 2.5 GiB. A build of all ten shared tools took 6 GiB at its peak and kept 1.5 GiB of images. On macOS, an image built on another and a new VM take only what they write. On Linux hosts, an image and the VM that builds shared tools start as a full copy of their parent’s disk, but a new VM’s disk holds only its own changes. A VM then grows as you work in it, and its disk never shrinks.

devvm checks the disk that holds the images and VMs, which is the disk of devvm’s Lima home. Shared tool images come out into devvm’s data folder, so a tools build also checks that folder’s disk, which needs 0.5 GiB and 0.25 GiB for each tool, rounded up: 1 GiB for one tool and 3 GiB for all ten. When devvm’s data folder is on a small temporary disk, such as a tmpfs /tmp on Linux, devvm checks that disk.

devvm doctor also warns when that disk has less free space than building base needs, but the warning doesn’t make doctor fail. When devvm refuses, see Not enough free space for how to make room.

As JSON

devvm size --json and devvm ports --json print what the commands show as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. With -g, they print the same fields for new VMs. With --json they only show, so devvm refuses --cpus, --memory, --disk or a list of ports with it.

devvm size --json has cpus, memory_gib and disk_gib, and leaves out what isn’t set. For -g, that’s what new VMs take from the image. When the VM’s size changes at its next start, pending has the cpus, memory_gib and disk_gib that change.

{
 "version": 1,
 "cpus": 4,
 "memory_gib": 8,
 "disk_gib": 100,
 "pending": {
 "memory_gib": 16
 }
}

With -g, devvm size --json also has sources, which says where each of cpus, memory and disk came from: config.toml, settings.json for what devvm saved, or built-in for the image’s (where a default comes from).

{
 "version": 1,
 "cpus": 6,
 "memory_gib": 16,
 "sources": {
 "cpus": "settings.json",
 "disk": "built-in",
 "memory": "config.toml"
 }
}

devvm ports --json has ports, which is all, none or a list of ports and ranges, written as devvm ports takes it. With -g, it also has source, which is config.toml, settings.json or built-in.

{
 "version": 1,
 "ports": "5173,8000-8010"
}

item.title: The desktop
item.description:
This page explains how devvm desktop serves a VM’s desktop on this machine, how it checks a viewer’s password and keeps the clipboard out of the VM, and why devvm uses VNC and never forwards X11. A VM’s desktop covers adding the desktop and opening it.

In the VM

The built-in desktop layer installs Xfce, TigerVNC’s Xvnc, socat for the local proxy and a command of devvm’s, devvm-desktop, into the desktop image, which only the VMs with the layer are made from (the desktop layer). Its packages come from the distribution’s archive as it is when the layer builds, and it downloads nothing else. When you run devvm desktop, devvm first checks that the VM has devvm-desktop, and refuses a VM without it (desktop_no_layer). Then it runs devvm-desktop start off, or start on with --clipboard, as the VM’s user.

devvm-desktop starts Xvnc on display :1 unless it’s running. Xvnc listens on the socket /run/devvm-desktop/vnc.sock alone, in a folder of the VM’s user’s own (mode 700), the socket itself mode 600. It listens on no TCP port (-rfbport -1), and takes no X11 connections over TCP (-nolisten tcp), so devvm’s port forwarder never sees it, even on a VM that forwards every port. It asks for no password of its own (-SecurityTypes None), because devvm checks the viewer’s password on this machine first. The clipboard settings (AcceptCutText, SendCutText, SetPrimary, SendPrimary) are on or off as asked, and on a desktop that runs already, devvm-desktop changes them in place with vncconfig. Then it starts an Xfce session on the display, in a D-Bus session of its own, with the session’s proxy settings pointed at the VM’s local proxy. Nothing starts the desktop at boot, so a VM whose desktop you never open runs none. Its log is ~/.cache/devvm-desktop.log in the VM.

The local proxy

Every request from the VM to its proxy carries the VM’s password in Proxy-Authorization, and the VM’s proxy settings carry it in their URL, http://devvm:KEY@192.168.5.2:PORT. Command-line tools take the password from that URL, but Chrome, Chromium and Firefox ignore it and ask for the proxy’s username and password instead, on every site. So the desktop’s programs use a local proxy in the VM, devvm-local-proxy, which needs no password and adds the VM’s.

The VM’s setup writes devvm-local-proxy into /usr/local/bin at each launch, mode 700 and the VM’s user’s, with the VM’s proxy address and password in it, and installs it whole, so a connection that’s already running keeps the copy it started with. The VM already holds the same password in its environment. devvm-desktop runs devvm-local-proxy start before it starts Xvnc, which starts socat unless it’s running. socat listens on 127.0.77.1:3128 alone, which is on the VM’s loopback, takes connections only from 127.0.0.0/8, carries at most 256 at once, and runs devvm-local-proxy on each connection itself. Its log is ~/.cache/devvm-local-proxy.log. The address comes from devvm (proxy.LocalProxyAddr and proxy.LocalProxyPort), which the setup gets as DEVVM_LOCAL_PROXY, and devvm-desktop sets http_proxy, https_proxy, HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY to http://127.0.77.1:3128 for the Xfce session. On Xfce, Chrome and Chromium read those variables for their proxy, and Firefox reads them first when its proxy setting is the system’s, which is its default.

For each connection, devvm-local-proxy reads the request line and the headers, waiting at most 30 seconds for each line and taking at most 100 headers. It takes only what a proxy is sent:

  • a CONNECT to a host and port, which becomes a tunnel;
  • a request for an absolute http:// or https:// URL, such as GET http://example.com/.

Anything else gets 400, and nothing of it reaches the VM’s proxy. That includes a request in origin form, such as GET /, which is what a web page sends when it reaches the local proxy as a server, so a page in the browser can’t use it. The local proxy drops the client’s own Proxy-Authorization and Proxy-Connection headers and adds the VM’s password. For a request that isn’t a CONNECT, it drops Connection and Keep-Alive and asks for Connection: close, because the password goes with each request’s head and the local proxy reads only the first, so each connection carries one request. Then it connects to the VM’s proxy, and to nothing else, sends the head and carries the rest both ways with socat. The VM’s proxy decides as it does for any request: a host the tier allows is reached, and one it doesn’t allow gets the proxy’s 403 with its reason.

devvm’s port forwarder never forwards a server on 127.0.77.1, on any port, because a forward would put a proxy that adds the VM’s password on this machine’s localhost, where other users and programs could reach it.

On this machine

devvm desktop listens on 127.0.0.1 alone, on the VM’s port. That’s the port its state records in its ports section (host.desktop) while no program on this machine has it, and otherwise a new one that no program and no VM has, which devvm chooses and records in its place under the claims lock, as it does every port it chooses for a VM. New ports come from 20000 up to just below the range this machine gives outgoing connections, which starts at 32768 on Linux by default and 49152 on macOS, because Linux refuses a listener on a port that a live outgoing connection holds. devvm reads that range from the system, and when it can’t, or the range leaves fewer than 1000 ports above 20000, it picks from 20000 to 32767. The port is among those devvm records for VMs, with their ssh and proxy ports, so no VM’s port forwarder takes it and no new VM gets it for its ssh or its proxy. devvm listens without address reuse, so a program that has the port on any address keeps it. The listener stays open until you press Ctrl+C, or until the VM no longer runs, which devvm checks every 5 seconds (desktop_vm_stopped). Nothing else listens for the desktop on this machine, at any other time.

Each connection to the port goes through devvm’s relay, which runs in devvm desktop:

  1. The relay speaks VNC’s protocol (RFB 3.8, and 3.7 and 3.3 for older viewers) as a server, and offers VNC’s own authentication alone. It sends a random challenge and checks the viewer’s answer against the VM’s password, with one check at a time, so a wrong answer holds every other viewer’s check for a second. A viewer whose answer is wrong is refused and never reaches the VM.
  2. Only then does the relay connect to the VM: an ssh channel to the VM’s socket (ssh -W /run/devvm-desktop/vnc.sock), through devvm’s ssh config’s entry for the VM, with its pinned host key. The channel opens no session, and it carries no agent and no forwarding either way (IdentityAgent=none, ForwardAgent=no, ForwardX11=no, ClearAllForwardings=yes). The relay does the viewer’s side of the VM’s handshake, asking for no authentication, and tells the viewer it’s in.
  3. From then on it carries the viewer’s messages to the VM and the VM’s to the viewer. Without --clipboard, it reads each of the viewer’s messages and drops its clipboard ones (ClientCutText, extended clipboard ones included). It ends a connection that sends a message it doesn’t know, so nothing it can’t read reaches the VM.

At most 8 viewers connect at once. The VM’s password is 8 characters of lowercase letters and digits without 0, o, 1, l and i, about 40 bits, because VNC’s authentication uses 8 characters at most. devvm makes it the first time and keeps it in the VM’s state, in its desktop section (made.password), in a file that only you can read. It never goes into the VM, and devvm prints it only with the address, never into the run log.

What the VM can and can’t change

Root in the VM can change its desktop, or run another server on the socket in its place. The relay doesn’t depend on the VM’s server for its guarantees:

  • The password: the relay checks it on this machine before it opens the channel, so a VM’s server that asks for none still gets no viewer without it.
  • The address: the relay listens on this machine’s loopback, so no server in the VM reaches other machines through it. A server root starts on a TCP port of the VM’s is an ordinary server of the VM’s, which the VM’s ports forward to this machine’s loopback, or don’t, as for any other.
  • This machine’s clipboard: without --clipboard, the relay drops it, whatever the VM’s server accepts.
  • No way out: every connection starts on this machine, and the VM opens none to it through the relay. The channel is a local forward that devvm’s ssh asks for, which the VM’s sshd connects to the VM’s own socket. On a confined tier, the VM’s own connections still reach only its proxy.

The relay can’t stop a VM’s server from sending its clipboard to the viewer, because that would mean reading every screen update the server sends. So the VM’s clipboard stays off this machine only while its server is as devvm set it up, or while the viewer doesn’t take it, which Screen Sharing’s Use Shared Clipboard setting decides.

Why not X11

ssh’s X11 forwarding gives programs in the VM a connection to this machine’s display, and an X11 program on a display can read the keys typed into other windows on it, read their contents and send them input. So devvm turns X11 forwarding off on both sides of the VM’s ssh. Its ssh config’s entries set ForwardX11 no, and the VM’s sshd has X11Forwarding no (ssh into VMs). With VNC, the VM’s programs draw on a display of the VM’s own, and this machine only shows a picture of it, so nothing in the VM reaches this machine’s windows.

item.title: Managing VMs
item.description:
This page covers a VM from the time devvm makes it until you delete it: opening, restarting and stopping it, deleting it, listing your VMs, and what devvm does when you run a command in a subfolder or when the project folder is made again, moved, deleted or on a disk that isn’t connected. Overview has each step devvm takes for a new VM and an existing one.

Opening a VM

devvm makes a new VM from its image of base and the layers you chose, building the image first if it isn’t built yet, then starts the VM and opens a shell in it in devvm’s place, so devvm ends when the shell does. The VM mounts only the project folder, read-write, and the shared tools and its agents’ config folders, read-only, or with --clone it gets its own clone of the repo instead of the folder. devvm also locks the .git hooks and config of the folder and of the repos nested in it against changes from the VM. On macOS it locks them with a file flag, and on Linux it makes them read-only in the VM where the kernel lets it and only watches them where it doesn’t (.git protection). For a VM that exists, devvm starts it if it’s stopped and opens it as it is.

A VM is running or stopped from the time devvm makes it until you delete it.

flowchart TD
none(["no VM"]) -- "devvm" --> running(["running"])
running -- "devvm restart,<br>devvm update" --> running
running -- "devvm stop" --> stopped(["stopped"])
stopped -- "devvm,<br>devvm restart,<br>devvm update" --> running
running -- "devvm rm" --> deleted(["deleted"])
stopped -- "devvm rm" --> deleted
outdated@{ shape: braces, label: "When its image changes, a VM<br>is outdated, and it keeps<br>its image until devvm update." }
running ~~~ outdated

Restarting and stopping

devvm restart stops this folder’s VM, then starts it and opens a shell in it as devvm does. Some changes apply only when a VM starts, such as a new size for a running VM, a change into or out of the open tier, a change to its SSH agent forwarding, or the config folders of an agent that devvm tools add added, and a restart applies them.

When you make one of these changes to a running VM with devvm size, devvm network into or out of open or devvm ssh-agent, or change its .git protection on macOS with devvm git-protect, which waits for the VM to stop, devvm asks in a terminal whether to restart the VM now, because anything running in it stops.
