If you answer yes, devvm restarts it as devvm restart does and opens a shell in it. If you answer no, devvm keeps the change and says that devvm restart applies it, and it does the same without asking when there’s no terminal or you pass --no-input.

When devvm opens a running VM that still has changes waiting for its next start, it names them, such as its size and its agent folder mounts, and asks in a terminal once whether to restart the VM now. It names each change on a line of its own, and when more than two wait, it names the first and says how many more there are. When the VM’s agent folder mounts are among the changes, the default answer is yes ([Y/n]), because an agent you just added needs its folders. Otherwise the default is no ([y/N]), because the VM is already running and you may only want its shell. If you answer yes, devvm stops the VM, starts it with the changes and opens a shell in it. If you answer no, or there’s no terminal, or you pass --no-input, devvm warns about each change and opens a shell in the running VM.

devvm stop stops this folder’s VM and its proxy (stopping a VM). Once the VM is stopped, devvm locks its .git again and checks it, as a launch that finds the VM stopped does, and it takes the VM’s entry out of devvm’s ssh config. devvm, devvm restart, and the commands that need the VM running, such as devvm host, start it again.

Deleting a VM

devvm rm deletes this folder’s VM together with what devvm keeps for it. That’s the VM’s state, its own allowlist, its network log, its .git locks or, for a --clone VM, the repo’s devvm remote, and its ssh config entry (deleting a VM). It asks first in a terminal, and --force deletes without asking, which devvm rm needs when there’s no terminal.

When the VM has an agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history, unless you give --no-export, and when the export fails, devvm keeps the VM (history). For a --clone VM, devvm offers to fetch the branches this repo hasn’t fetched, and it deletes the VM’s uncommitted changes only after you confirm. --no-clone-check skips that check and warns you that the clone’s unfetched commits and uncommitted changes go with the VM (deleting the VM).

devvm deletes the VM made for an earlier folder at this path only after you confirm (a folder made again). In a folder without a VM of its own, devvm rm acts on the VM of the nearest folder with one that this folder is inside, and it names that VM and deletes it only after you confirm (a subfolder). devvm asks these questions only in a terminal, and --force never answers them. To delete a VM whose folder you deleted or moved, give its name, as in devvm rm devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c (a VM whose folder is gone).

Listing VMs

devvm ls prints a table of the project VMs, sorted by name, with a header first. Images and build VMs aren’t in it.

Column
NAME the VM’s name, devvm-<folder>-<hash>
STATUS its state as its backend reports it, such as Running or Stopped
IMAGE its image, base and its layers, with a base from a container image as base (from node:24) (details)
TOOLS its shared tools, joined with commas, such as node,claude, or - for none
GIT its .git protection, on or off, or clone for a --clone VM
NET its network tier, open, internet, allowlist or none, or unenforced (the self-check), and internet (learning) while it learns the hosts it needs
LINKS how many links it has to ports of your other VMs, or - for none
FOLDER its project folder, with (gone) after it when nothing is at that path, which devvm rm VM deals with (a VM whose folder is gone), or (not connected) when the folder was on a disk that isn’t connected (details)

A value the VM’s state doesn’t have shows as -, so a VM whose creation didn’t finish shows only its name and status.

devvm ls –json

devvm ls --json prints the same list as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. vms has a VM’s columns as fields, sorted by name. image is the image alone, tools is the list of its shared tools, [] for none, and from is the container image its base started from, which is left out for a base from Ubuntu’s cloud image. A value the VM’s state doesn’t have is "". folder is the folder alone, and folder_state is there when something is at its path, gone when nothing is, and not_connected when the folder was on a disk that isn’t connected. links is how many links the VM has, 0 for none. net is the tier alone, and a VM that’s learning the hosts it needs also has learning_since, the time it started learning.

{
 "version": 1,
 "vms": [
 {
 "name": "devvm-website-71a99b1076d92c",
 "status": "Running",
 "image": "base",
 "tools": ["node", "claude"],
 "from": "node:24",
 "git": "on",
 "net": "internet",
 "learning_since": "2026-11-07T10:00:00Z",
 "backend": "lima",
 "folder": "/Users/you/code/website",
 "folder_state": "there",
 "links": 0
 }
 ]
}

A subfolder

A VM mounts its whole project folder, so the folders inside it are in the VM at the same paths. When the folder you run a command in has no VM of its own, devvm looks for one in the folders it’s inside, starting with the nearest. It stops before your home folder and the filesystem root, so it never uses a VM made for either. It stops at the nearest folder that has a VM, and when that VM was made for an earlier folder at its path (a folder made again), or its backend has lost it, the folder you’re in has no VM, so devvm never reaches past it to a VM further out. Using a parent folder’s VM mounts nothing new, because the subfolder is already inside the folder that VM mounts.

When you run devvm in such a subfolder, such as ~/some-project/src, devvm opens the parent folder’s VM there, with the shell at the subfolder’s path, and first prints a line that names the VM and the folder it was made for. It does the same with or without a terminal, and it asks nothing. --tools, --agents and --layers change nothing on the parent folder’s VM, as on any VM that exists, and devvm warns that they don’t (adding and removing tools). devvm --here makes a new VM for the subfolder instead, and so does devvm --clone, which makes the subfolder’s own clone VM. Once the subfolder has its own VM, devvm opens that one. In a parent folder’s --clone VM, the shell opens in the subfolder when the clone has it (subfolders).

The other commands that act on this folder’s VM, such as devvm stop, restart, tools, size, ports, host and code, use the parent folder’s VM in the same way, without asking. Each one first prints a line that names the VM and the folder it was made for. devvm rm is the exception, because it never deletes a parent folder’s VM unasked. In a terminal, it names the VM and its folder and asks before deleting it, with no as the default, and --force never answers that question. Without a terminal, it refuses and tells you to run devvm rm in the parent folder instead. The commands that give the VM more access ask in the same way, because the parent folder’s project may not expect them. They are devvm secret use, devvm ssh-agent on and devvm ssh-agent devvm, devvm network with a lower tier, such as devvm network open, devvm network allow, devvm network rm when it removes a deny, and devvm git-protect off. In a terminal, each one names the VM and its folder and asks before it changes the VM, with no as the default. Without a terminal, it refuses and tells you to run it in the parent folder, or in a terminal to confirm. The commands that take access away, such as devvm secret unuse and devvm network deny, ask nothing. devvm host gives the subfolder as the folder to open in the VM, and devvm code opens the subfolder. devvm adopt acts only on the VM made for this folder’s own path, never on a parent folder’s.

A subfolder that is a git repo of its own is treated as a separate project, and so is a subfolder inside such a repo, when the repo is below the folder with the VM. That covers a nested repo, a submodule and a worktree, which each have a .git folder or file of their own. When you run devvm there, devvm makes a new VM for the subfolder, with or without a terminal, and asks nothing. The other commands don’t use the parent folder’s VM there, and they say this folder has no VM, as in any folder without one.

Every command that acts on this folder’s VM, devvm included, takes --here and --parent, and each finds the VM in the same way. --here uses only this folder’s own VM, so devvm --here makes one when the folder has none, and the other commands say this folder has no VM. --parent uses the VM of the nearest folder with one that this folder is inside, even across a git repo of its own and even when this folder has a VM of its own, so devvm --parent in a repo of its own opens the project’s VM there. When no folder that this folder is inside has a VM, a command given --parent fails and changes nothing. You can’t give the two together, or either of them with -g, and devvm --clone doesn’t take --parent, because a clone VM is always the folder’s own. devvm rm VM takes neither, because it deletes the VM you name, and neither does devvm adopt, because it acts only on this folder’s own path. With --parent, devvm rm and the commands that give the VM more access still ask before they change the parent folder’s VM.

A nested project replaced

A project with a VM of its own inside a folder with another VM, such as a nested repo, is in both VMs, because the parent folder’s VM mounts everything inside its folder. Code in the parent folder’s VM can change the nested project’s files, though not the hooks and config of its .git while the parent folder’s VM protects it, as .git protection does for the repos nested in a VM’s folder. It can also move the nested project folder aside and put a link in its place, or another folder. On Linux, if devvm then started the nested project’s VM, the VM would mount whatever the link points to, such as your home folder. On macOS the VM mounts the project folder itself, wherever it was moved, and never what a link at its path points to. On both, devvm checks the nested project folder just before it starts the VM and again once the VM runs. If the folder is now a link, sits below a link, or is another folder, devvm doesn’t start the VM, or it stops the VM again, and it tells you which. Find what replaced the folder, move the project folder back to its path, and run the command again. Replacing the folder while the VM runs never shows the VM what the link points to. On Linux the VM keeps the folder it mounted when it started, and on macOS the VM gets “Operation not permitted” for its project folder, as it does when the folder was moved aside while the VM started and put back later, so run devvm restart once the folder is back. To keep a nested project out of the parent folder’s VM altogether, move it out of the parent folder.

Each time devvm makes or opens the nested project’s VM, it warns once and names the VM of the nearest parent folder that mounts the project. It warns whether that VM runs or not, because the VM can write to the folder whenever it runs. A --clone VM mounts nothing, so devvm doesn’t warn when you open one, and a parent folder’s --clone VM never counts. The other commands, devvm restart included, don’t warn.

A folder made again

A VM belongs to the folder it was made for, which devvm knows by its path and by the folder itself (one VM per folder). When that folder was deleted and a new one made at the same path, every command that opens, stops or changes the VM refuses it, such as devvm, devvm stop, devvm restart and devvm tools. Two commands deal with it, and each acts only after you confirm in a terminal:

  • devvm rm deletes the VM and never exports its history, because its folder is gone. The VM may hold that project’s work, so --force never answers this question.
  • devvm adopt gives the VM to this folder, with its files, secrets and allowlist. Its .git protection starts again, as if .git had just appeared. devvm adopt --force gives it without asking, which devvm adopt needs when there’s no terminal.

A moved or renamed folder

When you move or rename a project folder on the same disk, as with mv ~/code/app ~/work/app, the folder keeps its VM once you say so. The first time you run a command on this folder’s VM at the folder’s new path, such as devvm or devvm stop, devvm finds the VM made for the folder at its old path, names the VM and that path, and asks whether to move the VM here, with no as the default. When you answer yes, the VM belongs to the folder at its new path, with its home folder, secrets, allowlist, links and settings, and devvm finds it there from then on without asking. When you answer no, the folder has no VM, so devvm makes a new one, and the old VM stays with the old path, where devvm rm VM deletes it (a VM whose folder is gone). Without a terminal, devvm refuses and tells you to run devvm adopt in a terminal, or devvm adopt --force, which moves the VM without asking.

The VM mounts the folder at its new path from its next start. When the VM is running as you move it, it still mounts the old path, so devvm stops it before it moves it, and devvm then starts it with the folder at its new path. If a VM runs with its folder at another path all the same, devvm asks whether to restart it as it opens the VM, with yes as the default, and when you answer no, it warns that the VM mounts the folder at its new path only when it next starts. The folder’s .git moves with it, locks and all, so its .git protection goes on as before. Links to the VM and its group go by the VM’s name, so they stay, and a link whose TARGET is the folder’s path finds the VM at its new path. The folder’s path in the VM changes with it.

Claude Code’s history follows the folder. Claude Code keeps a folder’s sessions and its settings for that folder, such as whether you trust it and the MCP servers you added there, by the folder’s path. At the VM’s next start, devvm moves them in the VM from the old path to the new one, so claude --continue and claude --resume offer the sessions from before the move. When Claude Code already has sessions at the new path, the old path’s sessions join them, and a session the new path already has stays as it is. Settings that Claude Code already keeps for the new path stay as they are, and the old path’s stay under the old path. devvm moves only what Claude Code keeps for the project folder itself, so sessions you started in one of its subfolders stay under that subfolder’s old path.

Codex records each session’s folder in the session, and codex resume and codex resume --last look only at the current folder’s sessions, so they miss the ones from the old path. codex resume --all lists the sessions of every folder, the old path’s included, and codex resume with a session’s ID resumes that session wherever it started. opencode keeps the sessions of a git repo by the repo’s first commit, so they follow the folder without any change. In a folder that isn’t a git repo, opencode keeps sessions by the folder’s path, so they stay under the old path.

devvm offers the move only when the folder at the new path is the folder the VM was made for, which devvm knows by its device, inode and birth time (one VM per folder), and when nothing is at the old path any more, or only a symlink to the new path. It never offers a VM to a copy of the folder, which is another folder, or to a folder on a file system that may give a new folder the inode number of a deleted one. That leaves folders whose file system records a birth time: on macOS, folders on APFS and HFS+, and on Linux, folders on ext4, XFS, Btrfs, tmpfs, ZFS, F2FS and bcachefs. Folders on network shares, FUSE file systems and USB drives formatted with FAT or exFAT never get the offer. devvm also offers no VM for a folder that another user owns, or a --clone VM, which keeps its own clone of the repo at the old path inside the VM. When more than one VM was made for the folder at paths it had before, devvm moves none of them and names them, so you can choose one with devvm adopt VM. devvm refuses to move a VM to a folder that it wouldn’t make a new VM for, such as your home folder (project folders devvm refuses). A new folder at the old path gets a new VM of its own, with another name.

Moving a folder to another disk copies it, so the folder at the new path is another folder, which devvm never offers the VM to on its own. To give the copy the VM, delete the folder at the old path or disconnect its disk, then run devvm adopt VM in the copy, with the VM’s name as devvm ls lists it. devvm names the VM and its old path and asks first, with no as the default, and --force moves it without asking, which devvm adopt VM needs when there’s no terminal. The VM’s .git protection starts again, as if .git had just appeared, because the copy’s .git is another folder too. devvm refuses a VM whose folder is still there, a --clone VM, and a folder that has a VM of its own, which you delete first with devvm rm.

A VM whose folder is gone

When you delete or move a project folder, its VM stays, because the VM may hold work that’s nowhere else and devvm never deletes a VM on its own. A folder you moved gets its VM back at its new path once you say so (a moved or renamed folder), and until then the VM’s folder counts as gone. devvm ls writes (gone) after the folder of each VM whose folder is gone (listing VMs), and devvm space names each one with its folder. A folder on a disk that isn’t connected isn’t gone, and a folder on a disk that isn’t connected covers it. A folder that was deleted and made again at the same path isn’t gone, and devvm handles it as a folder made again. A VM whose folder is gone explains how devvm tells.

devvm rm VM deletes a VM whose folder is gone, and you can run it in any folder. VM is the VM’s name, as devvm ls lists it, or the alias that ssh reaches it by. In a terminal, devvm names the VM and its folder and asks before deleting it, with no as the default. --force deletes it without asking, which devvm rm VM needs when there’s no terminal. Like devvm rm, it deletes what devvm keeps for the VM, and when the VM has an agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history unless you give --no-export (history).

The export reads the history from the running VM. Starting a stopped VM would make its folder again, because Lima makes a missing folder that a VM mounts, so for a stopped VM with an agent devvm refuses and tells you to run devvm rm VM --no-export. If you moved the folder and want the history, run devvm history export or devvm rm in the folder at its new path, which moves the VM there first (a moved or renamed folder). A --clone VM mounts no project folder, so devvm starts it to export the history. Its clone’s work can’t be fetched into a repo that’s gone, though, so devvm refuses to delete it unless you give --no-clone-check, which deletes the VM and that work with it.

devvm rm VM refuses a VM whose folder is still there, including a VM made for an earlier folder at that path, and tells you to run devvm rm in that folder. Given this folder’s own VM, it does what devvm rm does. It also refuses a name that isn’t one of your VMs, and a VM that its backend no longer has, for which devvm gc --orphans deletes what devvm keeps (leftovers of a VM deleted outside devvm). When the VM’s state names this folder but the folder has a VM of its own, which only a state changed by hand can do, devvm refuses it as a VM whose folder is still there, so devvm rm VM never deletes the folder’s own VM in its place.

A folder on a disk that isn’t connected

When a project folder is on an external disk, a USB stick or a network share that isn’t connected, nothing is at its path, but the folder may still hold the project’s work, and so may the VM. devvm tells this apart from a deleted folder by the disk: it finds the nearest folder above the path that’s still there, and when that folder is on another disk than the project folder was, the project folder isn’t connected. devvm ls writes (not connected) after such a folder, and devvm space names each such VM with its folder. To use the VM again, connect the disk.

devvm rm VM refuses such a VM when there’s no terminal, even with --force, and tells you to connect the disk, or to run devvm rm VM in a terminal to delete the VM anyway. In a terminal, devvm names the VM and its folder and asks before deleting it, with no as the default, and --force never answers that question. Otherwise it deletes the VM as it deletes one whose folder is gone. A folder that you moved to another disk and then deleted counts as not connected too, so devvm asks in that case as well.

item.title: Network tiers
item.description:
This page explains how devvm confines a VM to its proxy on each tier, what the proxy does with each connection, and how your secrets get into the VM’s requests without the VM holding them. Network tiers covers choosing a tier, the allowlists and their rules, the secrets and the logs as you use them.

Starting a VM on its tier

A VM’s state records its tier in its net section, as "tier": open, internet, allowlist or none (network tiers). A section without a tier reads as allowlist, and one with a tier devvm doesn’t know can’t be read, so devvm refuses the VM rather than take it as open. The tier decides the VM’s confinement (confinementFor): on every tier but open, the VM starts confined to its proxy (backend.NetProxy); an open VM starts on its backend’s own network (backend.NetDirect) with its proxy’s port and password in its confinement, so its guest’s proxy settings name the proxy all the same (Confinement.GuestProxy). A running VM keeps the confinement it started with until its next start.

When devvm starts a VM on a confined tier, it takes these steps in order:

  1. It readies the VM’s own CA and the next one (the VM’s CA), and on macOS it keeps them out of Time Machine.
  2. It writes the VM’s secrets as the VM’s proxy sees them.
  3. It starts the VM’s proxy on a free port on the host’s loopback, and waits for the proxy to say it’s listening.
  4. It starts the VM confined, with the VM’s proxy settings pointing at the proxy.
  5. It runs the self-check before the VM’s setup and before its shell.
  6. It sets the VM up, as the VM’s setup describes. The setup puts the VM’s CA and the next one in the VM, points the tools that don’t read the environment at the proxy, and writes the VM’s placeholders and its agents’ logins and settings with your keys taken out.

An open VM’s start takes the same steps, but it starts the VM unconfined and runs the open self-check. Its proxy has the VM’s CAs and its secrets as any VM’s does, and applies no rules. Its setup installs both CAs in the VM, points the same tools at the proxy, and writes the same placeholders and copies of the agents’ logins and settings, so an open VM holds no real secret either. The VM reaches its proxy directly, through the HTTPS_PROXY that names it (Lima), and a request that goes around the proxy carries only the placeholder.

VMs that can’t be confined

A VM whose backend can’t confine it to its proxy (egress-proxy) can only be open: devvm refuses to make it on any other tier, unasked, in one line that names the backend and --network open (net_tier_backend), and the registry’s check refuses devvm network with a confined tier.

The proxy

One proxy runs for each VM. It runs on the host as devvm _proxy, a hidden command, and listens on a loopback port. The VM reaches nothing else over its network, so every connection the VM makes goes through its proxy. The one other way out of the VM is the links you add to it, which this machine carries over ssh to the ports your other VMs publish, so they don’t use the VM’s network. The proxy is a second entrance to those links, for the VM’s HTTP clients (links through the proxy).

Other programs on the host can also reach that port, so the port alone doesn’t identify the VM. Every request must carry the VM’s password in Proxy-Authorization, with the user devvm, or it gets 407. Each VM has its own random password in its proxy settings. The proxy reads the password from its config, a file only you can read, never from its arguments, which other users can see, and it refuses to start without one (devvm _proxy). The VM’s settings also get the password through files (Lima).

For each connection, the proxy does the following:

  • It sends a request for one of the VM’s own links to that link before any rule, and passes its bytes on as they are (links through the proxy).
  • It checks CONNECT host:port and absolute-form requests (GET http://host/…) against the VM’s policy files, and then tunnels or forwards the allowed ones untouched.
  • It takes only host names, made of letters, digits, -, _ and ., and addresses. It lowercases a name and drops one trailing dot, and the name that’s left may have no empty label, so evil.test.., evil..test and .evil.test get 400 too, because a company proxy that drops trailing dots would otherwise reach a host that a deny of evil.test never matched. It lowercases ASCII alone: a name with any other character keeps it, and gets 400, because Unicode’s case folding turns some letters into ASCII ones, such as the Kelvin sign into k, so the host it judged wouldn’t be the one the VM named. Anything else gets 400 before the policy or the log sees it.
  • It refuses devvm.proxy, its own domain, and any name under it, in a CONNECT and as a host, with 403, before the links, the policy or a company proxy see the name, on every tier. Only a request in absolute form for http://devvm.proxy/ itself reaches its endpoints, and CONNECT transparent.devvm.proxy:PORT is transparent mode’s. It refuses the stand-in address, 198.18.0.1, with a reason that says the tool resolved the name itself.
  • It resolves names itself and dials the addresses it checked. It refuses the host’s own addresses and internal ones unless a rule names the address. Internal addresses are loopback, private, link-local, multicast, unspecified, CGNAT 100.64.0.0/10 and the other ranges that aren’t the public internet, and a NAT64 address 64:ff9b::a.b.c.d counts as its IPv4 address.
  • It requires a TLS ClientHello in a tunnel to name the CONNECT host in its SNI, in ASCII, letters’ case aside. The proxy doesn’t see the Host inside the encrypted traffic, so a CDN that routes by it can reach other sites it serves.
  • For a host with a bound secret, it replaces the placeholder in one header with the real value, as how the proxy puts them in describes.
  • For a host whose rules narrow it to some methods or paths, it decrypts the host’s HTTPS and checks each request, as requests by method and path describes. Everything else passes unread.
  • It carries at most 1024 CONNECT tunnels at once for the VM, as described below.
  • It logs every decision (log files).

A CONNECT tunnel meets the proxy’s checks in this order:

flowchart TD
conn["CONNECT host:port from the VM"] --> pw["the VM's password?<br>no: 407"]
pw --> name["a host name or an address?<br>no: 400"]
name --> room["fewer than 1024 tunnels open?<br>no: 503"]
room --> reserved{{"transparent.devvm.proxy?"}}
reserved -- "yes" --> named0["the host in its first bytes:<br>TLS's SNI, or each HTTP Host<br>none: closed"]
named0 --> link
reserved -- "no" --> own["devvm.proxy or under it,<br>or 198.18.0.1?<br>yes: 403"]
own --> link{{"one of the VM's links?"}}
link -- "yes" --> linked["the link's socket,<br>tunneled untouched<br>(transparent: refused)"]
link -- "no" --> allow["on the allowlist, and not denied?<br>no: 403<br>(transparent TLS: 403 over the VM's CA)"]
allow --> floor["public and not this machine's,<br>or an address a rule names?<br>no: 403"]
floor --> narrowed["rules by method and path<br>judge its requests:<br>on port 443?<br>no: 403"]
narrowed --> bound{{"a bound host, on port 443,<br>or its requests judged?"}}
bound -- "no" --> sni["its TLS SNI names<br>the CONNECT host?<br>no: closed"]
sni -- "yes, or not TLS" --> tunnel["tunneled untouched"]
bound -- "yes" --> intercept["intercepted, with<br>the VM's CA"]
intercept --> named["each request names<br>the host?<br>no: 421"]
named --> rules["each request allowed by<br>the rules, by method and path?<br>no: 403"]
rules --> swap["the placeholder swapped<br>for the real value"]

A tunnel that the proxy doesn’t intercept carries the bytes both ways as they are. When the VM finishes sending, the proxy closes its side of the connection to the far end, so the far end sees the end of what the VM sent and can still answer. The tunnel ends when the far end’s bytes end, or when the proxy can’t pass them on because the VM’s connection has gone, and then the proxy closes both connections. In a tunnel to a host the policy allows, the far end’s bytes reach the VM at once, so a protocol whose server speaks first, such as SMTP, gets its greeting before the VM sends anything. The VM’s bytes wait until the proxy has checked them: when the first one starts a TLS record, the proxy reads the whole ClientHello and checks its SNI before any of it reaches the far end, and any other first byte passes at once. The VM may wait as long as it likes before its first byte, as on any open tunnel, but once a ClientHello starts, it must arrive whole, in one record of at most 16 KiB and 256 bytes, within 10 seconds, or the proxy closes the tunnel and logs why. The proxy reads no record past that length, so a VM can’t make it hold 64 KiB for each of its tunnels, nor hold a slot by sending its ClientHello a byte at a time.

The proxy carries at most 1024 CONNECT tunnels for the VM at once, counting tunnels to links and intercepted ones too, from the request until the tunnel ends. That’s four times the 256 connections a browser such as Chrome keeps open at most, and many times what a package manager opens, such as npm’s 15 sockets or uv’s 50 downloads, so several installs and builds at once fit. Each tunnel holds two of the proxy’s file descriptors, so the limit keeps a VM that opens tunnels without end from taking them all. A CONNECT past the limit gets 503, which a client may retry, and the reason 1024 tunnels open already, logged as a refused block, so neither the VM’s prompt nor devvm network log suggests an allow rule. The proxy’s own log, proxy.log, says when the VM reaches the limit, once until a tunnel ends. Plain HTTP requests in absolute form and idle kept-alive connections don’t count toward the limit (attack vectors).

Links through the proxy

A VM’s NO_PROXY names only the VM itself, so an HTTP client that uses the VM’s proxy settings sends a request for a link, such as http://db:5432/, to the proxy. A running VM can’t take a new environment, so the proxy carries those requests itself, and a link added while the VM runs works for every HTTP client at once.

devvm _links writes every link the VM has, carried or not, to a list, links.json in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/, mode 600 in a folder of mode 700, whenever they change or the file is gone. Each entry has the link’s names (NAME and NAME.devvm.internal), its address and port in the VM, its target, and its socket on this machine. The list stays when devvm _links ends, and devvm removes it with the VM, so a link that isn’t carried, which has no socket, is refused rather than asked of the rules. devvm puts the list’s path in the proxy’s config as links, and its run folder, where the links’ sockets are, as link_sockets. The proxy checks the list for every request and reads it again when it has changed, as it does the policy files. A list it can’t read has no links, which its log says once. The list must be a regular file, not a symbolic link, that only you can write, and at most 1 MiB.

The proxy checks a request’s host against the list after the VM’s password and before any rule, as it does for devvm.proxy. It lowercases the host and drops one trailing dot, and then a host and port match only an entry that names them exactly, so DB.:5432 matches db:5432, while db..:5432, db.devvm:5432 and 127.77.0.1:5432 don’t. The request names a host and a port, never a socket. An entry counts only when its socket is the one that devvm _links names for this VM’s link at that address and port, in the run folder of devvm’s data folder, so the proxy never connects to another VM’s link or to any other socket, whatever the list holds. Its address must also be in 127.77.0.0/16. Any other name under devvm.internal is refused with 403 and logged as a refused block, whatever the rules allow, so the rules, the host’s resolver and a company proxy never see one. A host and port on no entry are otherwise the policy’s, as before.

For a match, the proxy connects to the link’s socket, which is the same socket that the link’s remote forward reaches, so devvm _links checks the connection as it checks every other (each connection), and the 256-connection cap counts both. A CONNECT is tunneled as it is, with no SNI check and no interception, and an absolute-form request, such as GET http://db:5432/, goes to the socket in origin form, without Proxy-Authorization or Proxy-Connection, over a new connection for each request, which ends when the client gives up the request. A kept-alive connection to the proxy that asks for a link and then for another host has each request handled on its own. HTTPS in absolute form gets 400, because CONNECT carries it. The proxy puts no secret into a link’s connection, even when a secret’s hosts would match the link’s name, and its rules don’t apply, so devvm network deny db doesn’t stop the link db.

The proxy logs nothing for a link’s connection that it passes on, because devvm _links logs it as link, once. When the socket doesn’t answer, because the link was removed since the proxy read the list or devvm _links isn’t running, the proxy answers 502 and logs link_refused with the reason not carried. A socket whose backlog is full refuses a connection, so the proxy tries again for under a second.

Through a company proxy

When devvm starts a VM’s proxy, it reads HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY from its own environment, each in capitals first and then in lowercase, as Go’s clients do. When its environment sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, it reads config.toml’s [proxy] table instead, its https, http and no-proxy, and never a mix of the two. It writes them into the proxy’s config, proxy.json in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/, as upstream, so a password in the environment’s URL is in a file only you can read and in no process’s arguments. devvm checks the settings first: a proxy URL is http://user:password@host:port, or host:port alone, and a proxy without a port is on port 80. devvm refuses an https:// or socks5:// proxy (upstream_proxy_scheme) and a setting it can’t read (upstream_proxy_invalid), so a VM doesn’t start until you change it.

A config.toml URL never holds a password (proxy_password_in_config, as it’s read), because people copy that file between machines and keep it with their dotfiles. When its URL names a user, upstream gets "secret": "proxy", and the proxy looks the proxy secret up as it starts, through the same lookup as the secrets it puts in, the Keychain or ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/proxy, and uses it as the password of each URL that names a user and none of its own. So proxy.json never holds that password. A proxy whose lookup fails doesn’t start, and devvm checks that the secret is saved before it makes a new VM, starts a VM’s proxy, or builds an image or the shared tools (proxy_password_missing). Each of these checks is settings.CompanyProxy.Upstream.

devvm’s own requests on this machine go through the same company proxy. They are the download of its own mise, the list of Ubuntu’s cloud images, and the registries --from asks for digests. When the environment sets the proxy, their clients use Go’s own environment proxy. When config.toml sets it, settings.CompanyProxy.Route is their transport’s proxy. At the first request, it looks the proxy secret up and puts it in each URL that names a user and none of its own. It routes each request as a VM’s proxy does: HTTPS_PROXY’s for HTTPS, HTTP_PROXY’s for plain HTTP, and directly for NO_PROXY’s hosts, localhost and loopback addresses. Go sends the user and password only to the company proxy, in Proxy-Authorization. A missing password fails the request without a retry. The mise that devvm runs on this machine inherits devvm’s environment, so it uses the environment’s proxy as it is. With config.toml’s proxy, devvm adds HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY to mise’s environment, in capitals and in lowercase, with the password in each URL that names a user. mise takes a proxy’s password only in its URL, so its environment is the one place it can go. It’s never in mise’s arguments or in a file.

A VM’s proxy refreshes Codex’s and opencode’s OAuth logins through the company proxy it sends the VM’s requests through, its upstream, whether that came from the environment or from config.toml. As it starts, it makes that upstream’s route for its own requests, with the proxy secret it looked up as the password, as proxy.Upstream.WithPassword and proxy.Upstream.Route do for devvm’s own requests. It gives the route to each lookup in the lookup’s context (proxy.WithRoute), and agentlogin sets it as the refresh’s transport proxy (proxy.RouteOf). A VM’s proxy without an upstream sends the refresh directly, as it does the VM’s requests.

An open VM’s proxy goes through the company proxy as a confined VM’s does. Its guest gets no proxy settings of devvm’s environment: Lima’s propagateProxyEnv is off for every VM whose guest names devvm’s proxy, so neither the shell’s nor config.toml’s password reaches the guest.

devvm warns (upstream_proxy_gone) when the config the VM’s proxy last started with has an upstream and the one it starts it with now has none, as happens when a shell without the settings starts it.

The proxy decides each request as it does without a company proxy, by the host name the VM asked for, and only then picks the way out:

  • A host that NO_PROXY names, localhost, a name under .localhost and a loopback or unspecified address go directly, through the checks above.
  • A tunnel, and the connection the proxy makes to a bound host to put a secret in, go through HTTPS_PROXY’s proxy. The proxy sends CONNECT host:port with the name the VM asked for, and Proxy-Authorization: Basic from the URL’s user and password, and it reads the answer. Anything but 200 refuses the VM’s request, naming the company proxy by its host and port. Over that tunnel, the proxy’s TLS connection to a bound host checks the server’s certificate against the system’s roots and the CAs in your CA folder, as it does directly.
  • A plain HTTP request goes to HTTP_PROXY’s proxy in absolute form, with its Proxy-Authorization in place of the VM’s. The company proxy’s address in the request has no password, so no error the proxy logs holds one.
  • Without HTTPS_PROXY or HTTP_PROXY, those requests go directly.

NO_PROXY is a comma-separated list, which the proxy reads as Go’s clients read it. In it, * matches every host, and an address or a CIDR matches addresses. A name matches itself and its subdomains, while a name with a leading . or *. matches only its subdomains. Any entry can end in a port, which limits it to that port.

The company proxy resolves the names it’s sent, so the proxy can’t hold it to the addresses it checked, and the floor changes for those requests. An address in the VM’s request is checked as before, and a host whose last label is all digits or starts with 0x, such as 127.1, gets 400, because a company proxy may read it as an address. For a name, the proxy asks this machine’s resolver, for at most three seconds, and refuses the request when any answer is internal or denied, unless a rule names the address. A name this machine can’t resolve, which is common behind a company proxy, goes to the company proxy unchecked when a rule names it, as itself or under *.domain. When only ** allows it, the proxy refuses it with 403, and the event log says that this machine can’t resolve it and only ** allows it. The proxy reads at most 64 KiB of the company proxy’s answer to CONNECT. The design note explains what that leaves open, which Attack vectors lists, and how builds reach the company proxy through a proxy of their own.

The event log’s upstream field names the company proxy, by host and port, for each tunnel and request that went through it, and devvm network log adds through host:port to the line. The proxy’s own log names both company proxies by host and port when it starts. Neither holds the user or the password.

How long a proxy runs

The proxy exits when the VM’s Lima hostagent does, which it learns from the hostagent’s pid file, the VM’s lifeline (lifeline in its config). The proxy starts before the VM, so it waits for the lifeline to name a process that runs. What the file held when the proxy started is an earlier start’s, and the proxy waits past it, but when a new start writes the file and its process is already gone, the proxy exits. Once it follows a start, it runs while the file holds what it held then and that process runs, so a VM started again gets a new proxy. If the hostagent never appears, the proxy exits 15 minutes after it started, and devvm stop stops it at once.

A VM that starts again gets a new proxy on the same port. A running VM also gets a new proxy when the config devvm would start it with differs from the one it started with, which devvm tells by the SHA-256 of each (proxy.Config.Sum). The config holds everything that, changed, starts the proxy again: the VM’s list of policies, the VM’s CA and the next one, by the SHA-256 of each certificate, so a CA that was replaced counts, the SHA-256 of devvm’s binary, so a proxy from another devvm binary counts, the CAs in your CA folder, the company proxy settings in devvm’s environment and the shared Nix cache’s cap. A config that’s gone, or that the proxy wouldn’t read, counts as one that differs. To start a new proxy, devvm stops the old one with SIGTERM, and with SIGKILL when it’s still running two seconds later. The old proxy counts as stopped only once its process is gone, not once its arguments can no longer be read, because an ending process loses its memory before its files, and for that moment its port still looks taken by another program, which would fail the launch with proxy_port_taken. SIGKILL goes only to a process whose arguments devvm can still read as the proxy’s, so a proxy still ending gets none, and neither does another process given its pid since, even one whose arguments devvm can’t read. If it still runs two seconds after that, devvm stops with proxy_stop_failed and starts nothing, because the old proxy would go on with its old settings.

devvm counts a proxy as started only once the proxy says it’s listening on the VM’s port and is still running, because a program that took the port first would otherwise get the VM’s traffic. The proxy says so in a status file of its own in the VM’s run folder (vms/<hash>/run/proxy.status), which devvm names to it when it starts it and removes before each start. The file holds the proxy’s pid and the address it listens on, so a status that an earlier proxy left, or that another program wrote, never counts. While devvm waits, the proxy counts as running as long as its pid file still names it, it hasn’t ended, and its arguments are the VM’s proxy’s, _proxy -config with the VM’s proxy.json, or still devvm’s own, or can’t be read yet. On Linux, a process that has just started shows devvm’s own arguments for a moment, then none, because the kernel lets devvm go on as the new program begins to replace devvm’s copy, and shows the program’s arguments only once it has loaded. If the proxy doesn’t start, devvm stops and names the proxy’s log (proxy_start_failed). When a stopped VM’s port was taken by another program, devvm chooses a new free port. A running VM’s backend holds the port it started with, so when a running VM’s proxy is gone and another program took its port, devvm can’t start the proxy again (proxy_port_taken). devvm then stops the VM (net_proxy_down_stopped), and it does the same when the proxy fails to start for any other reason, because a confined VM never runs on without its proxy. The next devvm starts both. An interrupt during the start of a confined VM stops the VM and its proxy too (interrupted_start, a cleanup that starter.start registers around the backend’s Start), because a backend can leave the VM running while its start still waits for it: Lima’s hostagent keeps running the VM after limactl start ends, and devvm records the confined start only once limactl start returns. Without the stop, the VM would run with no record of its confined start, so devvm ls would show it as unenforced and its next launch would offer to restart it.

Policy files

On the allowlist tier, a VM’s proxy reads these policies, in this order, as one list. Allowlists describes what they allow and the rules they hold. The other tiers read fewer, as netpolicy.Policies lists them for each:

  • internet: one built-in policy, network/internet.policy, which holds **:*, every host and address on any port, then secrets.policy, then your files below, whose denies alone apply. The proxy’s config lists those files in deny_policies, and the proxy drops their allows as it reads them, keeping their denies and a broken deny. ** lifts no floor, so internal addresses and this machine’s stay refused.
  • none: the built-in policies of the VM’s agents, each agent’s shared-tools/<agent>.policy, such as shared-tools/claude.policy, and no other built-in one, then secrets.policy, then your files as denies alone. The VM’s links come before every rule, as on every tier.
  • open: no policy at all. The proxy’s config has "open": true, which allows every host and address on every port, internal ones and this machine’s included, and a config with open and any policy is refused. The floor doesn’t apply, and a name that the host can’t resolve goes to the company proxy unjudged, as it does for a build.
Policy Read for
layers/base.policy (built in) every VM
shared-tools/<name>.policy (built in) each shared tool in the VM’s image
layers/<name>.policy (built in) each built-in layer in the VM’s image
~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.policy each of your layers in the VM’s image
~/.config/devvm/policy every VM
~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/policy that VM only
~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/secrets.policy every VM, which devvm writes with the hosts of the VM’s secrets and logins and of its agents’ token endpoints

The built-in policies are paths in devvm’s own files, assets/ in the repo, which are built into the binary, and no copy of them is ever on disk. netpolicy.Policies lists both kinds for a VM: the built-in ones go in the proxy’s config as names in builtin_policies, and your files as paths in policies. The proxy reads the built-in ones from the binary once, as it starts, ahead of your files in the list, and never again, so only an upgrade of devvm changes them, and an upgrade starts every VM’s proxy again because the binary changed. A built-in policy that’s missing, or that holds a line that isn’t a rule, is a bug in devvm, so the proxy refuses to start rather than run with fewer rules than devvm meant, and devvm stops the VM as for any proxy that doesn’t start. A missing file of yours, on the other hand, has no rules. devvm network reads the built-in policies from the binary too, and it labels each with its name (# devvm: layers/base.policy, and "builtin" with --json) where it shows your files’ paths. Both lists are in the config that a proxy started with, so a change to either starts the proxy again.

The proxy, devvm network and devvm doctor read every policy with one parser, proxy.ParsePolicy, which returns each line that holds more than a comment, with its number and whether it’s a rule. A line is a rule only when proxy.ValidRule takes it, which is exactly what devvm network allow and deny take. Each time the proxy reads a file, it logs each line that isn’t a rule, with its file, number and text, quoted, to its own log, proxy.log in the VM’s logs/ folder. It skips such a line, unless the line starts with ! (proxy.BrokenDeny). A broken deny fails closed: while any of the VM’s policy files has one, the proxy’s policy denies every name and every address, and each request gets 403 and a refused block whose reason names the file and the line, so neither the VM’s prompt nor devvm network log suggests an allow rule. The VM’s links and the proxy’s own answers at devvm.proxy come before the rules, so they still work, and tunnels already open stay open, as they do for any new deny. Fixing the line lifts it at the proxy’s next read of the file, which is the next connection. The proxy reads a file again when its mtime, size or inode changes, or when it comes back after it was missing, whatever its mtime. It also reads a file again at every connection while its mtime is less than 2 seconds old, because some filesystems keep mtimes only to the second or two, so a second write within that time could leave the stamp as it was. A change of a file’s mode or owner alone, with chmod or chown, changes none of the three, so the proxy doesn’t see it until the file’s next write. The same goes for the bindings file and the links list, so one that you make readable or writable by others after the proxy read it keeps its last contents until it changes, and the proxy refuses it then. A file the proxy refused is read again at the next connection, so fixing its mode works at once. An error other than a missing file keeps its last rules and its broken deny, which the proxy’s log says once. The proxy, devvm network and devvm doctor read a policy file only when it’s a regular file, through a symbolic link if it’s one, of at most 1 MiB (proxy.ReadPolicy, through internal/safefile). They open it without blocking and check the file they opened, so a FIFO or a link to /dev/zero in a policy file’s place can’t hang them, and each refuses it with a named error, safefile.ErrNotRegular or safefile.ErrTooLong. A leading byte-order mark isn’t part of the first line. netpolicy.PolicyWarnings warns about each line that isn’t a rule, with policy_broken_deny for a broken deny and policy_not_rule for the others. netpolicy.Proxy.Prepare uses it for the VM’s policy files at each launch of a confined VM, devvm network allow, deny and rm for the file they change, and devvm doctor for the files you edit: ~/.config/devvm/policy, your layers’ and each VM’s own. devvm network also marks the line, and --json lists it in not_rules. A unit test parses every policy file that devvm ships and fails on any line that isn’t a rule.

Each change that devvm network allow, deny or rm makes rewrites the file whole, through a link if the file is one, so a proxy never reads half of it.

Requests by method and path

A rule for a host name or *.name can have its methods and then its path after it, each after spaces or tabs, such as api.github.com GET,HEAD /repos/ (rules by method and path). proxy.ParsePolicy reads such a line as one rule, whose text is its canonical form: the host as before, the methods in capitals in proxy.Methods’ order, and the path as written, joined by one space. That’s what devvm network allow, deny and rm write from --method and --path (proxy.NarrowRule), and what they compare a line by, so HEAD,get and GET,HEAD are the same rule. A method outside proxy.Methods, CONNECT among them, an address, a CIDR or ** with methods or a path, and a path that isn’t a pattern (proxy.PathOK) aren’t rules, so a typo in a deny is a broken deny, which denies everything, rather than a deny of nothing.

The proxy judges a host in two steps. For the connection, CONNECT host:port or an absolute-form request, a deny that narrows doesn’t refuse the host, and an allow that narrows allows it, so a host that only rules by method and path allow is reached. Its requests are then judged one by one (policy.judge) when a rule that narrows covers the host and either it’s a deny or no rule allows the whole host (policy.byRequest). Both come from one read of the policy files (policy.rulesFor, a hostRules), so a file that changes between the two can’t give the connection one rule’s verdict and another’s way through. Such a host’s CONNECT on a port the proxy intercepts, :443, is intercepted with the VM’s CA, as a bound host’s is, and on any other port, or without a CA, it’s refused with 403, logged as a refused block, because the proxy can’t see the requests in it. An absolute-form request, plain HTTP on any port or https://, is judged before it’s forwarded.

Inside an intercepted tunnel, the proxy’s own HTTP server reads each request, HTTP/1.1 kept alive or HTTP/2, and calls one handler for each, which checks that the request names the host (421 otherwise), then judges it with the rules as they are then (server.judgeRequest), then forwards it. So every request on a connection is judged, not just the first, and a rule added or removed applies from the tunnel’s next request. A WebSocket is judged by its upgrade request, after which the proxy passes its bytes as they are, so for a host that rules narrow, an Upgrade to any other protocol, such as h2c, whose requests would pass the same way, is refused, and so is a CONNECT inside the tunnel. A refused request gets 403, and the event log gets a blocked event with its method and path. A deny’s refusal is marked refused, so neither the VM’s prompt nor devvm network log --blocked suggests an allow, and a request that no allow covers suggests the allow of the whole host. An allowed request’s forward event names the rule that allowed it, as its rule.

policy.judge takes the rules that cover the host and port in order. A whole deny refuses, then a CONNECT and an upgrade to a protocol other than WebSocket are refused when a rule narrows the host, and so is, when a rule narrows it by method, a method that the request names besides its own that isn’t exactly one of proxy.Methods (hostRules.unjudgeable), then each deny that narrows refuses what it matches, and then the first allow that matches lets the request through. One matcher judges both rules and secrets’ bindings (proxy.match):

  • A path in plain form (plainPath): the path as the proxy forwards it starts with /, has nothing percent-encoded, no \ or ;, and is clean, with no . or .. segment and no doubled slash. The query is no part of it. These are the forms that servers read apart, by decoding an encoded slash or dot, reading \ as /, dropping ; and what follows it, or not cleaning the path, so a request in any of them could reach a path that the proxy didn’t judge.
  • A pattern (proxy.PathOK, matchPath): its segments are split at /, * matches any run of characters within one, and ** as a whole segment matches one segment or more. A pattern’s last / stands for /**, so /api/ is /api/**, which is a binding’s path below which the value goes in. A path’s one trailing / may be there or not. Matching is a table over the pattern’s and the path’s segments, linear in the path for each of the pattern’s at most 32 segments, so a VM’s long path can’t make it slow.
  • The methods a request names (overrides): besides its own, each value of a header that some servers take the method from, X-HTTP-Method or any with method-override in its name, read in any case and with _ for - (overrideLike), as Rack’s and CGI’s servers turn - into _, and each _method parameter of the query, in any case of its name. A value that isn’t exactly one of proxy.Methods, trimmed, is odd: a list such as DELETE, GET, which servers read apart, lower case or nothing. The proxy reads no body, so a form’s _method field is the POST’s.
  • An allow, and a binding, match strictly (match.allows): the request’s method, and every method it names besides, as written, must be among the rule’s methods, with none odd, and its path must be plain and match the pattern in its own case. A request the matcher can’t judge alike for every server is never allowed by a rule with a path.
  • A deny matches broadly (match.denies): the method, or any method the request names besides, every word of a list among them, in any case, or any odd one; and the path in any case, any path that isn’t plain, the path above a pattern that ends with / or /**, the path with its last segment cut at its first ., which frameworks that take a format from a suffix (Rails, Spring) route to the same handler, and the path with each segment’s trailing dots dropped, as servers that drop a trailing dot read it (trimDots).
  • A query servers read apart (overrides): while a rule narrows the host by method, a query with a ;, which some servers split pairs at and Go’s url.ParseQuery skips the pair around, or with an escape that doesn’t decode, which ParseQuery drops, is odd, so a _method hidden in it can’t pass.

Judging a request costs the policy files’ stat, which every connection already has, and a scan of the host’s rules. Decrypting the tunnel costs a TLS handshake with a certificate from the VM’s CA, which the proxy keeps for the 1024 hosts it used most recently, and another to the host, so the proxy decrypts only the hosts whose rules need it: a host that a whole allow covers, with no deny that narrows, stays a tunnel that the proxy doesn’t read.

The VM’s setup

On every launch, the VM’s setup does the following:

  • It installs the VM’s own CA and the next one into the VM’s trust store, as devvm-proxy.crt and devvm-proxy-next.crt, so the proxy’s certificates for hosts with a bound secret verify, in this VM only. It never gets their keys.
  • It points the programs that ignore the proxy variables at the proxy. Those are apt, sudo (which keeps the variables), every ssh connection, Docker’s daemon and containers with the docker layer, and Nix’s daemon with the nix layer. Under systemd, each daemon gets a drop-in, devvm-proxy.conf, that holds the VM’s own proxy address and nothing else, and without systemd, Docker’s settings in /etc/conf.d/docker get a block instead, and Nix’s daemon gets /etc/conf.d/nix-daemon. Every VM has a proxy, an open one’s included, so every VM gets them, and the setup restarts a daemon whose settings changed. An ssh connection gets a ProxyCommand that tunnels through the proxy, and the proxy checks its host and port against the allowlist.
  • It writes devvm-local-proxy, a proxy on the VM’s loopback that adds the VM’s password to each request, for browsers, which ask for a proxy’s password rather than take it from the proxy variables. The desktop layer starts it and points the desktop’s session at it (the local proxy).
  • With the nix layer, it points Nix at the shared Nix cache first: /etc/nix/devvm-cache.conf, which /etc/nix/nix.conf includes with !include, sets substituters = http://devvm.proxy/nix https://cache.nixos.org. Every VM gets that file, an open one’s included, and the setup restarts Nix’s daemon when the file changed.
  • It sets NO_PROXY and no_proxy to the VM itself, localhost,127.0.0.1,::1, in the daemons’ settings above and in Docker’s client settings (~/.docker/config.json), as the VM’s backend does in the environment it sets at each start. The VM’s links aren’t in it, because HTTP clients reach them through the proxy, so a change of links changes no daemon’s settings and restarts nothing.
  • It puts the VM’s placeholders in ~/.config/devvm/env, which login shells read, as CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN and GH_TOKEN. When github is bound, it also sets up git’s credential helper for GitHub over HTTPS.
  • It adds devvm-why, the note before each prompt, and the notes for Claude Code and Codex (inside the VM). devvm-why prints the proxy’s /blocked, and when that list is empty, the proxy’s answer adds that a connection refused, or a DNS error, for an allowed host comes from a tool that skipped the proxy where devvm can’t send it there, with a link to troubleshooting. With transparent mode, devvm-why then prints devvm-transparent status as root, through sudo -n. The notes, a block between <!-- devvm-proxy --> markers in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md and ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, say to run devvm-why after a connection error or a 403 from the proxy, that a tool that ignores the proxy settings still reaches the proxy by name over HTTPS, HTTP and the ports the rules name, and that a refused connection on another port, or a DNS error, while devvm-why shows nothing blocked means the tool skipped the proxy and needs its own proxy setting or $HTTPS_PROXY. The setup writes them only when the VM has a proxy address, and replaces the block on every launch.
  • On a VM that runs confined to its proxy, with transparent mode on, it sets up transparent mode, and on any other VM it takes transparent mode out.

Each placeholder ends in a random value of the VM’s own, its salt, which isn’t its password.

Tools that skip the proxy

On a confined VM, transparent mode sends a tool that ignores the proxy settings to the VM’s proxy by the names it looks up (what it covers). Nothing new runs or listens on the host, and the backends don’t change: the VM reaches its proxy over the path its proxy settings use, and the proxy judges each connection as it judges CONNECT host:port. Every piece in the VM is a program that devvm configures, dnsmasq, nftables and socat, which base installs, and one script, devvm-transparent, which each launch sends. A tool that looks up api.example.com and connects to it goes this way:

  1. Its lookup reaches dnsmasq in the VM. glibc asks systemd-resolved, which asks 127.0.0.1:53, where Lima’s DNS setting for a confined VM points, and musl on Alpine asks 127.0.0.1:53 itself. An nftables rule sends 127.0.0.1:53 to dnsmasq, which listens on the stand-in address, 198.18.0.1, alone. That rule takes every connection to 127.0.0.1:53 in the VM, so a DNS server of the user’s own there, or a forward of port 53 to it, gets nothing.
  2. dnsmasq answers the A query with 198.18.0.1, with a time to live of 0, and every other type, AAAA and HTTPS included, with an empty answer, never REFUSED, which musl waits 5 seconds on. It has no upstream server, so no query leaves the VM, and it reads /etc/hosts first, so localhost, the VM’s hostname, host.lima.internal and the links’ names keep their own addresses. Names under devvm.internal that aren’t a link’s don’t exist, and neither does a name without a dot, nor a name under the search domains that the VM’s resolver appends to one, which Lima takes from this machine’s network and dnsmasq reads from /etc/resolv.conf as it starts. So a single-label name that isn’t in /etc/hosts doesn’t resolve, rather than turning into a name of this machine’s network. dnsmasq can’t tell a name the resolver made that way from one a tool names whole, so every name under those domains gets no answer, such as git.corp.example.com under corp.example.com.
  3. The tool connects to 198.18.0.1:443. The address is on the VM’s loopback interface, so the connection stays in the VM, and an nftables rule sends it to a socat listener on 198.18.0.1:61443. Nothing binds port 443 or 80 itself, so your own servers keep them.
  4. socat opens an ordinary CONNECT transparent.devvm.proxy:443 to the VM’s proxy, with the VM’s password, which it reads from a file, never from its arguments. Each port has a listener of its own, so the port reaches the proxy in the target, and nothing the VM sends can change it.
  5. The proxy checks the password, takes one of the VM’s 1024 tunnel slots, and reads the connection’s first bytes for at most 10 seconds. A TLS record is read whole, and its ClientHello’s server name (SNI) is the host. An HTTP/1.x request line or HTTP/2’s preface makes each request’s Host the host, judged on its own. Anything else is refused and logged as a refused block of transparent.devvm.proxy, with why: no SNI, an address as the SNI, a name with anything but ASCII, a name under devvm.proxy, or bytes that name no host, such as SSH’s, Postgres’s SSLRequest or a server that speaks first.
  6. From there the connection is CONNECT host:443: the links, the policy and the floor, interception for a bound host, the tunnel and its SNI check, the log, and /blocked, in the order CONNECT has them. The ClientHello goes on to whatever serves it first, so the far end gets it byte for byte. The proxy dials the host it judged, by name, so the VM can’t name one host and reach another. Its events carry "via": "dns".

A blocked TLS host gets a TLS handshake with a certificate for its SNI name from the VM’s own CA, signed as interception signs, then the proxy’s 403 text for every request on the connection, over HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. The proxy resolves nothing and dials nothing for it. Without a CA, or once it has ended, the connection closes, and the block is logged all the same. A plain HTTP request is always forwarded as http://, whatever its request line says, so no secret goes into it, and a Host that names another port than the connection’s gets 400, as does a CONNECT inside it. A link’s name gets a refused block on both ways, because dnsmasq never gives a link’s name the stand-in address. Its name in /etc/hosts reaches it. A Host of devvm.proxy reaches /blocked alone and gets 403 for every other endpoint, the CA, the ports and the Nix cache, because socat adds the password for any client, a container without the proxy settings included.

The ports. The proxy serves the ports to redirect at http://devvm.proxy/transparent/ports: 80 and 443, then each port an allow rule names for hosts by name, **:8443 included, the lowest first, at most 32 of them. It leaves out :*, address rules’ ports, 22 and 53, and every port but 80 and 443 while a deny is broken. The proxy’s own log names the ports past 32, once each time they change. devvm-transparent fetches the list every 10 seconds and at each launch, and takes it only when it’s 2 to 34 ports, each once, with 80 and 443 and neither 22 nor 53. A new port gets the lowest free listener from 61100 to 61131, and a port that stays keeps its own. The list shows the VM the ports its rules name, never their hosts, which it can’t read otherwise. That’s a small disclosure, and it gives the VM nothing to reach: each connection is still judged by its own host and port.

The nftables table. The table inet devvm_transparent is loaded whole, in one transaction, and devvm-transparent loads it again within 10 seconds when something removes it, such as nft flush ruleset. Its NAT chains run at priority -110, before Docker’s at -100, and the first NAT chain that gives a connection a mapping is the only one that does, so they give every TCP and UDP port of the stand-in address one: a redirected port goes to its listener, DNS to dnsmasq, and every other port to port 61079, where nothing listens, so the kernel refuses it at once with a reset, or for UDP, QUIC included, with a port-unreachable. Docker’s chains, which would send a published port’s traffic to a container, so never see the stand-in address, and neither a VM process nor a container that connects to db.example.com:5432 reaches a container that publishes 5432. The refused connections are logged in the kernel’s log, five a second at most, which devvm-transparent status reads. DNS to any public server goes to dnsmasq too, from the VM and from Docker’s bridges (docker0 and br-*), so Docker’s fallback servers, 8.8.8.8 and 8.8.4.4, and resolvers that tools hard-code reach it. So does DNS to the VM’s own name servers but loopback’s, as /etc/resolv.conf and systemd-resolved’s list name them, such as the one Lima’s DHCP adds beside 127.0.0.1, which Docker gives its containers once it drops the loopback one; devvm-transparent reads them again every 10 seconds. Other loopback addresses, private, link-local and CGNAT ones are left alone, so a DNS server on a container’s or the LAN’s address still answers, and Lima’s DNS addresses that aren’t the VM’s name servers answer nothing, as the host’s confinement has it. Two filter chains run before every NAT chain, at priority -150: one drops traffic to the stand-in address from any interface but the loopback and Docker’s bridges, such as Podman’s or LXD’s bridges and Lima’s network, and both drop anything to it but TCP, UDP and ICMP, such as SCTP, which no NAT rule maps. So neither reaches Docker’s DNAT of a published port through the stand-in address. An input rule keeps the same interfaces off it again, and only connections the NAT rules translated, and DNS, reach it. The listeners’ ports, 61080, 61443 and 61100 to 61131, and the dead port, 61079, are above Linux’s range for outgoing connections, 32768 to 60999, so no connection out is given one.

The service. devvm-transparent run is the service, under systemd or OpenRC, as root: it adds 198.18.0.1/32 to lo, loads the table, starts dnsmasq and a socat listener for each port, and then restarts any of them that ends within a second, sends dnsmasq SIGHUP when /etc/hosts changes, and fetches the ports every tenth second. dnsmasq runs as the user devvm-transparent, and so does each socat connection’s process, which reads the password file through its group. When the service stops, it removes the table, the address and what it started, so names stop resolving, and a stopped or broken service never leaves a way out. It starts at each boot, before any launch, with the last ports and settings, and each launch’s setup turns it on, off, or restarts it when its settings changed, such as a new proxy port or password. Its files are root’s, in /etc/devvm/transparent, and the VM’s password, which every program in the VM has in its environment already, is in files only, never in a process’s arguments. On an open VM, and with transparent mode off, the setup stops and removes all of it, and flushes systemd-resolved’s cache. The setup decides by the confinement the VM runs with, so a VM whose tier changed into or out of open keeps what it had until its next start.

What doesn’t change. The host’s confinement is the boundary: root in the VM can change or stop all of this, and then names stop resolving, or a query to Lima’s DNS goes nowhere, as for a VM without transparent mode. The self-check’s direct connection is to an address on port 443, so transparent mode never answers it. The VM’s names never reach the host’s resolver for a blocked host, because the proxy asks the policy before it resolves anything. Design notes has the threat check.

The shared Nix cache

VMs with the nix layer share their downloads from Nix’s binary cache, so each package comes from cache.nixos.org once per machine instead of once per VM. Each VM keeps its own Nix store and daemon, and only the host writes the cache, so no VM can change what another VM gets. The design note says why it’s a cache that the host fills rather than a shared store.

In the VM. devvm starts the VM’s proxy with nix_cache set to ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/nix-cache in its config when the VM’s image has the nix layer, and the VM’s setup puts http://devvm.proxy/nix before https://cache.nixos.org in Nix’s substituters (the VM’s setup). It leaves trusted-public-keys as Nix has it, which is cache.nixos.org’s key alone. Nix’s daemon reaches devvm.proxy through its own proxy settings, so its requests are absolute-form GETs with the VM’s password, and the proxy answers them itself, as it does /blocked and /ca.pem, and never forwards them. When the cache answers with anything but a file, Nix goes on to cache.nixos.org, through the proxy as any other download.

What a VM can ask for. The proxy takes only GET and HEAD requests with no query, for three kinds of path under /nix/. These are nix-cache-info, a narinfo named <hash>.narinfo with a 32-character hash in Nix’s base 32, and a NAR named nar/<hash>.nar with a 52-character hash and no suffix or .xz, .zst or .bz2. Anything else gets 400. The proxy makes up nix-cache-info itself, with priority 30, so Nix asks the cache before cache.nixos.org, whose priority is 40. It serves the other files from the folder, or fetches them from https://cache.nixos.org when the VM’s policy allows cache.nixos.org:443 and, when rules by method and path narrow that host, a GET of the file’s path there. That’s the only host it fetches from, and its fetches go through the same address floor and company proxy as the VM’s own requests. It follows no redirect, and nothing of the VM’s request goes with it, so nothing a VM sends is ever stored.

What the host checks. Before it keeps a narinfo, the proxy checks that its StorePath is the path the VM asked for, and that cache.nixos.org-1, whose Ed25519 key devvm pins, signed its fingerprint, 1;StorePath;NarHash;NarSize;References. The signature doesn’t cover the NAR’s URL, so the proxy also checks that the URL is named by the narinfo’s own NarHash or FileHash, and no narinfo can put a file in another NAR’s place. It fetches a NAR only after it checked a narinfo that names it, never for a HEAD, and it keeps the NAR only when its SHA-256 and size are that narinfo’s FileHash and FileSize. The host can’t check a NAR’s NarHash, which is the hash of the archive before compression, because the proxy uses Go’s standard library alone, and that has no xz or zstd. Each VM’s Nix checks the signature and the NarHash again, so a narinfo with an added reference, or a corrupted NAR, fails there too. A file that fails a check, a not-found and an error all get 404, and the proxy keeps nothing of them, so Nix goes to cache.nixos.org itself.

The folder and its cap. The proxy writes each file whole into a temporary file in the folder, then renames it into place, mode 600 in folders of 700. The cache’s cap is the nix-cache.size retention setting, 10 GiB when it’s off, which devvm puts in the proxy’s config as nix_cache_max when the proxy starts. The cap counts the disk each file takes, in whole blocks, and a NAR being fetched counts at its full size from the start. When a new file would take the cache past its cap, the proxy deletes the least recently used files, down to nine tenths of the cap, and when the NARs being fetched leave no room, it refuses the fetch. One proxy fetches each NAR once, however many requests ask for it, and at most four at once. A hit marks a file used by setting its modification time. Every VM’s proxy and devvm gc take one lock on the folder before they change it, so the cap holds while many VMs fill it, and a running total in the folder saves counting it for each file. devvm gc and the daily retention run trim the cache to its cap too, and devvm gc --nix-cache empties it.

Logs. Each request is a nix-cache event in the VM’s own log, with its path and what came of it: hit, fetched, or why it wasn’t found or was refused. devvm network log shows these as cache.

Open VMs have their proxy too, so they share the cache. An open proxy allows cache.nixos.org as it allows every host.

What stays open. What one VM can learn of another through the cache, and how it can push other VMs’ files out, is under Attack vectors. Private caches, such as Cachix or one behind a netrc, are never shared, because only root in a VM can add a substituter, and Nix reaches it directly through the proxy’s allowlist.

A company’s CA

The CA certificates in ~/.config/devvm/ca (a company’s CA) reach every project VM, whatever its tier, and the VM’s proxy. Builds trust them too, as Images and caching describes, and so does the mise that resolves the shared tools’ versions on this machine, which on macOS trusts them for every connection but its Sigstore client’s, as the host’s mise below explains.

Reading them. trust.Read reads the folder’s *.pem and *.crt files at each launch, each build, each proxy start and each run of the host’s mise, and nothing outside the folder. It checks the folder and each of those files with os.Lstat and follows no link: a folder that is a link fails with ca_folder_link, and a file that is one, dangling or not, with ca_link. A link into a project folder would otherwise let that project’s VM write the CA that every VM, build and proxy trusts. A file or folder that it can’t read fails with ca_unreadable or ca_folder_unreadable, which name it and carry the error. It decodes every PEM block and refuses a block that isn’t CERTIFICATE (ca_not_certificate), a certificate that crypto/x509 can’t parse (ca_invalid) and a certificate without CA basic constraints (ca_not_ca). It also refuses a file with no certificate in it. It tells a private key apart by its PEM type, not by the file’s name, and a refusal fails the whole launch or build. What leaves the host is each certificate encoded again from its parsed bytes, once each, so the text around a block never does.

Installing them. assets/guest/ca.sh DIR runs as root and makes devvm’s CAs in /usr/local/share/ca-certificates exactly DIR’s devvm-*.crt files: the VM’s own CA and its next one, devvm-proxy.crt and devvm-proxy-next.crt, and the user’s devvm-extra-N.crt. When anything changed, it runs update-ca-certificates --fresh, so a CA that went leaves neither the bundle nor its hashed link. update-ca-certificates tells the hooks in /etc/ca-certificates/update.d only about the CAs it links, never about a file that was deleted, so ca.sh tells them itself. It runs each hook that run-parts would run, with a -/etc/ssl/certs/NAME.pem line on its input for each CA it removed, as Debian’s update-ca-certificates does for a CA it deselects. That way Java’s cacerts (ca-certificates-java’s jks-keystore hook) and Mono’s store drop a removed CA, in a project VM and in an image whose layer installed Java. A hook that rebuilds its store from the bundle ignores that input. A hook that fails stops nothing, and ca.sh says so in the run log. It also writes them all to /etc/ssl/devvm.pem, for Node. In a system without update-ca-certificates, such as a container image before its ca-certificates package, it adds them to /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt itself. It keeps the bundle as it was in /var/lib/devvm-ca, or a mark that there was none, and puts it back once they go, and a package that arrives in between makes the bundle again from the same folder. Run without DIR, ca.sh removes every one of devvm’s files. Its unit tests run it in a folder that stands for / (DEVVM_CA_ROOT).

Project VMs. The setup that devvm sends at each launch carries ca.sh and the certificates in ca/, and sync.sh runs it, so a change applies at the next launch and a running VM needs no restart. Every project VM starts with trust.Env in its environment, whatever its tier and whether there are CAs or not, so adding a CA changes nothing that its backend sets at a start. On Lima, the clone that makes the VM sets the environment too (VMSpec.Env), and the VM’s first start adds its proxy’s address to it in the one edit before its first boot. The variables are NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/etc/ssl/devvm.pem, which is empty when there are none (Node warns only about a missing file), SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE and PIP_CERT, set to the system’s bundle, and UV_SYSTEM_CERTS=1.

The proxy. netpolicy.Proxy.Prepare reads the folder too, and writes the bundle into the proxy’s config, proxy.json in the VM’s run folder, as upstream_cas, which the proxy adds to the system’s roots for its own TLS connections. Each secret lookup’s context carries those roots (proxy.WithRoots), and an agent’s OAuth refresh on the host trusts them (proxy.RootsOf, set on its client with fetch.Client.Trust), so it goes through a company proxy that inspects TLS as the VM’s own requests do. devvm’s other host requests, such as registry digests and Ubuntu’s image check, use the host’s own store, as the host’s other programs do. A VM can’t change that file or the folder, so the proxy’s roots grow only by what you put there. A proxy whose bundle differs from the folder’s starts again, as one whose CA was replaced does.

The host’s mise.
