Prose is never built with fmt: every sentence devvm shows the user is a message. A message made from an error carries that error with .Because(err), rather than only its text from err.Error(). Data output, such as a table or --json, isn’t a message, and neither is text in a script that runs somewhere else. Data goes to the UI’s Stdout(), and a log line that isn’t a message goes to its Stderr().

The locale files are in go-i18n’s TOML format, with only go-i18n’s own message fields, so go-i18n’s loader reads them as they are and its goi18n tools work on them:

[no_vm]
other = "There's no VM for {{.dir}}. Run devvm to make one."

[gc_tools]
one = "{{.count}} shared tool image is unused ({{.size}})."
other = "{{.count}} shared tool images are unused ({{.size}})."

[gc_tools_no_vm]
description = "tools lists the tool images, as \"node 24.21.0, claude 2.1.295\""
one = "{{.count}} current shared tool image no VM has ({{.size}}): {{.tools}}."
other = "{{.count}} current shared tool images no VM has ({{.size}}): {{.tools}}."
  • The ID is the table’s name, in snake_case.
  • other is the text: a Go template whose fields are snake_case ({{.vm_name}}). Only plain fields are allowed, no logic.
  • one is the text for a count of 1, when the wording changes with the count. Both texts then take {{.count}}.
  • description is an optional note for translators.
  • Nothing else: the generator refuses keys go-i18n doesn’t know, nested tables, plural forms English doesn’t use (zero, two, few, many) and leftDelim/rightDelim.
  • Voice: a message’s text follows the docs-voice skill’s Messages rules, which set its length (an error or a warning has at most two sentences, and a prompt at most two lines of context), and the mechanism goes in its doc link rather than its text.
  • One line: a value renders on one line without control, bidi or invisible characters, because msg.OneLine cleans every value as the message renders. Text from a VM that devvm shows as data goes through msg.Printable instead, which keeps its newlines and tabs. Colors says what the two drop.

Doc links

A message links a docs page through the docs map in internal/msg/docs.go, from message ID to a page in docs/content/docs and a heading on it. The page is its path without .md, and a section’s own page, its _index.md, is the section’s folder:

var docs = map[string]string{
 "vm_outdated": "using/images#outdated-vms",
 "backend_lacks": "backends#when-a-backend-lacks-something",
}

devvm prints the page’s address on the docs site on the line after the text.

After editing en.toml, run:

mise exec -- go generate ./internal/msg

It writes internal/msg/messages_gen.go, with one function per message. The parameters are the template’s fields in sorted order, in camelCase, and count int for plural messages: [no_vm] becomes msg.NoVM(dir string) msg.M, and a value that’s missing or extra is a compile error. msg.M is also an error: one made from another error carries it with .Because(err), so errors.Is and errors.As see through it, while the text stays the message’s own.

The tests fail when:

  • messages_gen.go is stale;
  • a message doesn’t render with sample values, or shows <no value>;
  • a generated function is never called outside the generated file and the tests;
  • a doc link names a message that isn’t in en.toml, or a page or heading that doesn’t exist. mise run lint runs this check too.

Questions

A prompt asks a msg.Question, never a bare message, so every question declares what answers it where devvm can’t ask: without a terminal, with --no-input, or once the input ends. A message becomes a question in one of two ways. msg.X(...).AnsweredBy("--force") names the flag or command that answers it, and its refusal is no_input, which names that answer and shows the question first when the prompt wasn’t printed. RefusedWith(msg.Y(...)) makes a question that no flag answers, and its refusal is the message given, which says what to do instead. About(...) adds the messages said before the question, which devvm shows only when it asks.

The Reporter’s Ask, Confirm, Answer and Secret take the question and, where devvm can’t ask it, return its *msg.Refusal, an error whose Msg is the refusal’s message. A command returns it as it would any failure, and a caller with something to fall back on does that instead, so no caller checks for a terminal itself. TestQuestionsDeclareAnswers checks every question in the code, as The CLI rule tests says, and a CLI test answers one with ttyin or DEVVM_PIPED_ANSWERS=1, as CLI tests says.

Names mode

With DEVVM_MESSAGES=names, a message prints as its ID and its values in sorted key order, so tests check which message devvm printed and with what, never its wording or language:

! exec devvm _msg nope
stderr 'msg_unknown name=nope$'

Every CLI test runs in names mode unless it sets env DEVVM_MESSAGES=.

Names mode belongs to internal/ui, which reads it once, with the rest of a stream’s style, in New: a msg.M itself always renders as its text, so its String and Error are the same whatever the environment says. Whatever shows a message as data, a table’s cell or a --json field, goes through the UI’s Text, or a Table’s, to get the names in names mode. New takes the function it reads the environment with, os.Getenv for devvm’s own UI, so a Go test makes a UI in names mode without setting the environment and can run in parallel; cli’s testUI does. A Go test that checks a message without a UI compares Names, msg.IDOf or msg.NamesOf.

devvm _msg NAME key=value… prints a message’s text (never its names), for end-to-end tests that look for it in a VM’s output. It’s hidden from the help.

Colors

Only internal/ui adds color, through a style for each stream that onTerminal makes, and colorOn decides each one: NO_COLOR or DEVVM_MESSAGES=names turns it off, then FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE (but 0) turns it on, then TERM=dumb turns it off, and otherwise the stream gets color only when it’s a terminal. Names mode stays plain in a terminal too, so end-to-end checks that run devvm under script read the names as they are. A UI from New, as tests make, has no terminal, so it’s plain unless the environment it reads sets FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE, which is how cli’s tests get a colored one.

The colors are SGR codes from the 16 base colors only, which the theme maps to its own shades. devvm uses no bright colors (90–97), because Solarized maps them to greys and bright black is Solarized Dark’s background, and it uses no backgrounds, 256 colors or truecolor. The codes go on labels, links, log text and a message’s values, never on the template’s own words:

  • A message’s values are bold (1), on the status line and in prompts too. msg.M.Segments renders the template with each value between two private-use runes, U+E000 and U+E001, after dropping those runes from the values, so a value can’t start or end a marking of its own. It returns the text cut into segments, each one the template’s words or a value, beside the doc link. Joined, the segments are Text, and String and names mode don’t change. Every value goes through msg.OneLine as the message renders, in Text, Segments and Names alike, so a value has no newline or other control character, whoever made it, bold or not. The log end that ErrorLogged prints is the message on one line without bold, because bold inside dim would cancel it.
  • Error’s devvm: label is bold red (1;31), and Warn’s is bold yellow (1;33).
  • A doc link is underlined blue (4;34). msg.M.Segments gives the doc link apart from the text, so ui colors the link alone.
  • Info’s ==> is bold (1).
  • The run log’s end that ErrorLogged prints, with its --- lines, the log text on the status line, and the log’s lines that -v streams (SetVerbose: LoggedCmd and LogWriter copy the log to stderr through msg.Printable, with no status line) are dim (2).
  • The done mark that a slow step leaves is green (32).

The codes are added after msg.Printable and msg.OneLine, so they’re the only ones devvm prints. Those two are devvm’s one cleaner, and msg.Safe is its one rule for which characters reach the terminal. They drop every character that msg.Safe refuses but newline and tab (which OneLine drops too), and a lone C1 byte. msg.Safe takes a graphic character in any script, such as an accented letter, a CJK character or an emoji, so a VM’s file names still read as they are. It refuses the control characters (C0, DEL and C1), the bidi controls such as U+202E, which reorder the text after them so a name could read as another, the format characters, such as the zero-width space and joiners, the word joiner, the soft hyphen and the tag characters, the variation selectors, and the fillers that show as nothing, such as U+3164 and the braille blank U+2800, which could hide or fake text in a prompt. The diff of devvm agent save writes each character that msg.Safe refuses as its code instead, and the names of the files it saves must hold none. The status line, the run log’s end, Pick, devvm network log and the port forwarder’s log use them as well. The status line cuts and counts its plain text with style.fit before painting it, so it still fits the terminal’s width and clears the right number of rows. The run log is never colored.

Tables on Stdout() are colored as stdout is. A command gets a ui.Table from u.Table() and adds a header, rows of ui.Cells and a totals row, and cli never reads the environment itself. Each cell has a ui.Role: Good is green (32), Attention yellow (33), Bad red (31), Secondary dim (2), and Plain stays in the default color, while the header and totals rows are bold. Table pads each cell on its plain text before painting it, because text/tabwriter counts the codes’ bytes as width, and a plain table is byte for byte what text/tabwriter writes with a padding of 2 (TestTableLikeTabwriter). The roles for each table’s values are next to the code that writes it:

  • devvm images: current is good, stale, unfinished, unused and not built need attention, and digests and keys are secondary.
  • devvm ls: Running and the .git protections on and clone are good, Stopped needs attention, and any other status, such as Broken, is bad, as is the tier unenforced, while a confined tier, internet, allowlist or none, is good and open stays plain.
  • devvm space: only copy and leftover in KEPT need attention.
  • devvm doctor: native is good, emulated needs attention, and unreviewed and none are bad.

Every command’s --json output is for scripts and stays plain.

mise run test unsets NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR and CLICOLOR_FORCE, and the end-to-end tests unset the last two, so your own settings never change what they check.

Translations

A translation is locales/<language>.toml (de.toml) with the same tables, one and other translated (and the language’s other plural forms, such as few), loaded by go-i18n the same way. Doc links are the same in every language: the docs site is English. devvm picks the language from the first of LC_ALL, LC_MESSAGES and LANG that is set (de_DE.UTF-8 is German); C and POSIX are English. A message missing from a translation is shown in English.

JSON output

Every command that shows or lists something takes --json, which jsonFlag in internal/cli/json.go adds. The command builds a struct of its own with snake_case json tags, next to the code that writes its table, and writes it with printJSON, which puts "version": 1 (jsonVersion) first, writes HTML characters as they are and refuses anything but an object. A list it prints is never nil, so it’s [] rather than null, and a field that doesn’t apply is omitempty. Sizes are bytes unless the field’s name gives the unit, as in memory_gib.

The root command’s PersistentPreRun calls u.DataOnly() for any command given --json, so Say, Info and LogNote print to stderr from then on, and stdout gets only the JSON. A settings command that also changes its setting with a value wraps its Args in showsOnly, which refuses the value with --json (json_shows_only) before anything else runs.

TestJSONShapes in internal/cli/json_test.go holds each command’s shape, a path: type line for each field of a sample with every field set. A field renamed, removed or given another type fails it. Shapes only gain fields, so a new field goes into the sample and the test, and any other change raises jsonVersion. A new command that shows or lists something gets --json, a row in that test, a CLI test and a section on its page with an example, which output for scripts links to.

item.title: .git protection
item.description:
This page explains what devvm locks in a project’s git folder, when it locks and checks the locks again, and what the locks can’t stop. .git protection covers what still works, turning protection on or off, VMs that were strict, and what isn’t covered.

On macOS devvm locks with the user-immutable flag (chflags uchg), which even root in the VM can’t clear. A read-only mount wouldn’t hold, because root in the VM can unmount it.

On Linux devvm makes the same paths read-only in the user and mount namespace it runs the VM’s QEMU in (on Linux hosts), so the VM, which reaches the folder only through QEMU, can’t change them.

Each check reads each repo’s .git once, the folder’s own and those nested in it, finding its git folders, submodules, what it would lock, what the locked files hand over and what points git elsewhere, and then locks, unlocks, watches and reports from what it found. The host’s locker does the locking: the flag on macOS, and on Linux nothing at the check itself, because the VM’s next start makes the paths read-only. A Linux host whose kernel refuses devvm the namespace locks nothing, and devvm watches .git there instead.

What’s locked

devvm locks these paths, of the folder’s own repo and of each nested repo it protects:

  • .git/hooks and .git/config. A repo without a hooks folder gets an empty one, locked, so the VM can’t make one.
  • The same paths for each submodule devvm finds, submodules of submodules included. Those are the git folders under .git/modules, and those in the working tree, which are sub/.git or the folder that a sub/.git file points to. devvm finds the submodules from the index, which it reads with core.fsmonitor off. It takes a folder for a git folder only when it has what git looks for in one, which is a HEAD, and objects and refs in the folder or in the folder its commondir names, as git’s own test has it. The VM can point a sub/.git file at any folder in the project, such as src, and locking that folder’s hooks and config would lock your own files, so devvm locks and creates nothing in a folder that fails the check and reports it instead.
  • .git/config.worktree, when extensions.worktreeConfig is on. devvm creates it empty if it’s missing.
  • What linked worktrees elsewhere on your machine read from here, which is .git/worktrees/<name>/commondir and config.worktree.
  • The project folder’s .git file, if the project folder is itself a linked worktree. The repo it points to is outside the VM.

When devvm locks

devvm records a new VM’s mode in its state before its backend makes the VM, so the mode is never unset: on with locks (macOS, and Linux where the kernel lets devvm use a user namespace), off when you pass --no-git-protect or on hosts without locks, and clone for a --clone VM, which mounts no .git. devvm locks once the backend has made the VM, and again on each launch that finds the VM stopped and on devvm stop, so nothing in the VM can race the locks. A VM whose creation stopped before its first locks, or that devvm adopt moved to this folder, is locked on its next launch as a new VM is, without reports. A running VM keeps the locks it had, and devvm stop or the next launch that finds the VM stopped, such as devvm restart, sets new ones. devvm git-protect on a running VM saves the mode in the VM’s state (the git section’s next).

Each time it locks, devvm records in the VM’s state what it locked and found: the identity of .git (its device and inode, and its birth time where the file system keeps one), every git folder it locked besides .git (those under .git/modules and the submodules’ in the working tree, in one list), and a hash of what the locked files hand over to the project folder. The next check compares with those, so it reports what changed since. The same places first check .git under the mode the VM ran with, so a .git that the VM replaced meanwhile is still named (git_replaced), and then set the new mode, which locks .git as it is then.

A new VM that’s interrupted before its first shell is deleted, and devvm takes its locks off. When devvm rm deletes a VM, devvm also takes its locks off. It unlocks what it would lock now and every git folder the VM’s state records locking, so a submodule whose entry the VM dropped from the index since is unlocked too.

Symlinks

devvm never locks or creates anything through a symlink, because the VM could plant one under .git so that devvm would lock a file elsewhere. devvm reports a path that is a symlink, or is under one, instead of locking it (git_not_locked). devvm also checks each lock again once it’s set. If the path moved in the meantime, devvm unlocks it where it landed and reports it (git_lock_raced).

On each launch

Every launch of an existing VM, every export of its agents’ history, and devvm stop check .git again. devvm reports each of these once:

  • A .git that was replaced since devvm locked it (git_replaced). devvm then does nothing else, so check the new .git, and look for the old one, renamed.
  • A repo that appeared in the folder after the VM was made (git_appeared), which devvm then locks, and a nested repo that appeared since the last check (git_nested_appeared).
  • A nested repo devvm protected that’s gone (git_nested_gone).
  • A submodule git folder that appeared, in the working tree or under .git/modules (git_embedded_new), which devvm then locks. devvm compares with the git folders it recorded last time, so devvm git-protect on after a VM was made without protection names none: it locks .git as it is then, as trusted.
  • Hooks in a hooks folder that wasn’t locked, because it wasn’t there to lock or belongs to a new submodule (git_hooks_unlocked).

devvm also reports these, the first two on every launch and the last two when they change:

  • A commondir (git_commondir).
  • Linked worktrees whose commondir leads elsewhere (git_worktree_stray).
  • Includes and hook links into the project folder (git_include_inside, git_hook_link_inside), which not covered describes.
  • Submodules whose git folder, in the working tree, isn’t a git folder (git_gitdir_not_git), which devvm doesn’t lock.

Nested repos

devvm protects each git repo nested in the project folder as it protects the folder’s own: it locks the same paths of each, checks each at every launch, pins each on Linux and watches each where the host can’t lock (nested repos).

The walk

devvm finds the nested repos by walking the project folder when it creates the VM, at each launch that finds the VM stopped and at devvm stop, at devvm git-protect on a stopped VM, and when devvm clone off mounts the folder again. It’s one walk that also finds the set-id files on a Linux host (hostsafety.Walk, which only starter.walk calls), and a launch into a running VM never walks. The walk stays on the project folder’s file system, follows no symlink and never enters a .git folder, so it never finds the repos of .git/modules, which are the folder’s own repo’s to protect. It takes a folder for a repo when the folder has anything named .git, a folder, a file, which a linked worktree or a repo with its git folder elsewhere has, a symlink or anything else, whether git takes it for a repo’s now or not, because the VM can make it one at any time. On macOS, whose file systems fold case, .GIT is .git to git, so the walk takes any case of the name there (platform.FoldsCase). It looks for repos at most four folders below the project folder, and not in node_modules, vendor, .venv, __pycache__ or .terraform, which package managers and build tools fill with what they fetch, so on macOS, where there are no set-id files to look for, the walk doesn’t enter those folders at all. On Linux it walks them for set-id files anyway, and counts the .git it sees there and below four folders (git_nested_skipped). It counts the folders it doesn’t enter because they’re on another file system (git_nested_devices). It keeps the first 100 repos it finds, in the walk’s order, and counts the rest, keeping the names of the first ten of those (git_nested_past_bound).

The walk also names each folder up to four folders down that git could take for a bare repo (git_nested_bare), one shaped like a git folder by git’s own test (hostsafety.IsGitDir): a HEAD, and objects and refs, files or folders, in the folder or in the folder its commondir names. A git folder that a repo’s scan locks, or that a nested repo’s .git file names, isn’t named. devvm doctor reads safe.bareRepository from git’s global and system config (hostsafety.BareExplicit), the files that GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL and GIT_CONFIG_SYSTEM name included, which it reads by name (hostgit.UserConfig) because devvm’s host git ignores every GIT_* variable, and it gives a tip unless the setting is explicit (doctor_git_bare).

A check takes the repos the walk found, the ones the VM’s state records first. A recorded repo stays protected, whether the walk found it or not, while its folder is a real folder of the project with anything at its .git, because the VM can make a .git that the walk or git’s own test passes over while git still takes it: objects and refs renamed with a commondir that leads to a git folder of its own, a .GIT, or a .git it can’t read, which devvm can’t lock and names (git_not_locked). A check without a walk, such as devvm rm and the start that pins, takes the repos the state records. A launch into a running VM checks the folder’s own repo alone and keeps the nested repos’ records as they are, because it locks nothing and the VM can change them until it stops, so it never pays for scanning them, and the check of a running VM’s pins goes by those records without scanning them. devvm scans each repo as it scans the folder’s own, eight at once, because each scan runs a few host git commands: a check of a stopped VM with 50 nested repos, the walk and the locks included, takes under a second on an M3 Max.

Two bounds

Each repo has two bounds. Its own top folder is where its .git is, where .git/modules and a relative core.hooksPath are read from, and where its submodules’ folders are. The project folder, which the VM mounts, is what the VM can write, so it’s the bound for everything else: devvm locks only a real path in the project folder, through no symlink, an include or a hooks path leads inside when it leads into the project folder, and a submodule’s git folder outside the project folder is one devvm can’t lock (git_gitdir_outside). A nested repo’s hooks path that leads into a sibling repo is inside, because the VM can write it.

A nested repo is left to another repo only when that repo’s scan locks its git folder whole (snapshot.covered): the git folder is that repo’s .git, one under its .git/modules that reads its config from itself, with no commondir that leads elsewhere, or one of its linked worktrees under .git/worktrees whose commondir leads back. Anything else below a .git, such as a .git/evil the VM made for a src/.git file to name, isn’t locked by anything, so the repo is scanned on its own, and named as one that appeared and as one devvm doesn’t protect. A submodule in the working tree is scanned as a repo of its own as well as its parent’s submodule, because the index that names it is the VM’s to write: a gitlink the VM adds, whose .git file names a nested repo’s git folder, would otherwise hide that repo’s own submodules and worktrees behind a scan from the wrong folder. Locking a path twice changes nothing, and unlocking goes by path once. A nested repo whose .git is a file is locked as the folder’s own is when it’s a linked worktree, by its .git file. When the git folder that file names is in the project folder and no repo’s scan locks it, devvm names the repo as one it doesn’t protect, and when it’s outside the project folder, it names the repo as one whose git folder it can’t lock (git_nested_gitdir_outside), as it does a submodule’s.

A scan follows each submodule git folder once, by its resolved path, and one check’s scans follow at most 1,000 of them across every repo, so gitlinks that the VM points back at a git folder already followed, or through a symlinked folder at the repo itself, or many repos full of submodules, can’t make a check run git without end. A repo whose scan stopped there is named at every check (git_scan_bounded).

What’s recorded

The VM’s state records each protected nested repo in the git section’s made.repos, by its folder relative to the project folder, with the same fields as the folder’s own repo: .git’s identity, the git folders locked besides .git, and a hash of what its locked files hand over. made.nested is set once the VM protects its nested repos, which a new VM does, and so do devvm git-protect on and the watch on a Linux host that can’t lock. A nested repo without a record is scanned for the first time, which records it as a new VM’s repo is recorded, without reporting its git folders. At a check of a VM whose made.nested is set, devvm also reports it as one that appeared, such as a repo the VM cloned while it ran, naming each key of its config that runs a program or reads another config (core.fsmonitor, core.hooksPath, core.sshCommand, core.pager, filters, aliases that start with !, includes and the like) and each hook that isn’t one of git’s samples (git_nested_appeared_runs, else git_nested_appeared), because it locks the repo as it is. A recorded repo with nothing at its .git, or whose folder isn’t a real folder of the project any more, is reported (git_nested_gone), and a recorded repo whose .git is another one is reported as the folder’s own is (git_replaced). The record of a repo devvm stops protecting, as it’s gone or another repo’s protection covers it, moves to made.left, so devvm rm and devvm git-protect off take its locks off with the rest, and name one that isn’t in the folder any more (git_locks_left), whose locks only chflags can take off.

A VM an earlier devvm made has no made.nested, so it protects only the folder’s own repo. The first check of it that finds nested repos names them once (git_nested_protectable, recorded as nested_noticed), and devvm git-protect on protects them. The nested repos that a check finds and the protection doesn’t cover are recorded in nested, with nested_more for how many more the walk counted, and named (git_nested_unprotected, git_nested_past_bound): on a host that locks, all of them when devvm creates the VM and at devvm git-protect on, and at a check of a stopped VM those it hadn’t recorded, and how many are past the bound at every check, because the VM could keep their count and change which they are. On a Linux host that can’t lock, each launch names those the last walk recorded, after git_unprotected, which a folder without a .git of its own gets too when it has nested repos, and devvm git-protect off quiets both.

A VM that devvm 0.1.0 or 0.1.1-rc.1 made strict has strict as its mode, and its repos’ configs have the diff.ignoreSubmodules = all that strict set. devvm reads that mode as on: it locks, pins and keeps the VM’s paths as it does for on, and devvm git-protect, its --json and devvm ls show on. The first check that finds the VM stopped (gitprotect.Protector.Check, then the converter’s unstrict), at a launch, devvm stop, devvm clone on or the undo of a devvm clone off, runs as an on VM’s does. Then, under the host’s lock of .git protection, it takes the value all out of the .git/config of each repo that the VM’s state recorded protecting before that check, the folder’s own and the nested ones, with git config --unset-all diff.ignoreSubmodules '^all$', and leaves any other value. It acts only on a repo whose .git has the identity the state recorded (git_id), so a .git the VM replaced, which the check names and locks nothing in, and a VM with no record, as after devvm adopt, keep their setting, which devvm names once when it’s all (git_strict_unknown). It reads the config through internal/safefile first, so a FIFO or a symlink there is never read, and after git writes it, it checks that the config is still a regular file in that .git, else it names the path (git_lock_raced). On a host that watches as well as locks, it leaves a config whose sum isn’t the one the check just recorded, and puts the new sum of each config it changed into the watch’s, so the next check doesn’t name devvm’s own change. It locks each config again even after an interrupt (context.WithoutCancel), and an interrupt records nothing, so the next check goes again. Then it records on in mode, and in next when an earlier devvm saved strict there for the VM’s next stop, and warns once (git_strict_converted), unless next is off. A config that git can’t change keeps the setting, and devvm names it (git_strict_left). devvm git-protect on and off and the unlock at devvm rm take the setting out the same way, without the warning (strictLeft).

Two VMs, one repo

A nested repo with a VM of its own is protected by two VMs, the parent folder’s and its own. On macOS both set the same flag on the same files, so when one VM’s protection comes off, at devvm rm or devvm git-protect off, devvm leaves locked every path that another VM’s protection still covers (gitprotect.Keeps: a git folder it recorded locking, of its own repo or of a nested one), and names that VM (git_kept_locked). The inventory reads every VM’s state for that (Inventory.GitKeeper). It fails closed: a state it can’t read keeps locked every path in the folder whose hash names that state’s folder (project.Hash), and when it can’t read the VMs’ folder at all, everything stays locked, each named with the state to fix (git_kept_unread). Locking a VM’s repos and recording them, and unlocking another’s, take the host’s lock of .git protection first (paths.Dirs.GitLock, before any VM’s own lock), so one VM’s unlock never runs between another’s locks and their record. Taking a strict VM’s diff.ignoreSubmodules out never unlocks a config another VM keeps locked, because that VM, running, could race the unlocked file, so the setting stays there, and devvm names the file, that VM and how to take it out by hand (git_strict_kept). The repo goes in the state’s strict_left, as does one whose config changed since the check, and each later check that finds the VM stopped tries again, until none is left. When git can’t change a config, devvm locks it again all the same. On Linux each VM’s pins are in its own QEMU’s namespace, and the watch locks nothing, so neither needs this.

On Linux hosts

Linux hosts have no immutable flag that a user can set, so devvm makes what it locks read-only where the VM sees it, in the VM’s QEMU process, which serves the project folder to the guest over 9p. Lima starts QEMU through devvm’s wrapper (devvm _qemu exec), and a start of a VM that’s on gives the wrapper what to pin in a file of its own, run/git-pins.json in the VM’s folder, written private, which DEVVM_QEMU_PINS names, because a VM with many nested repos has more pins than one environment variable holds. The wrapper reads the file through no symlink, and it pins, for the folder’s own repo and each nested repo the VM’s state records protecting, .git and each git folder it locks besides, which stay writable, and every path of what’s locked that’s there, which become read-only. They’re the paths the check before the start found and checked, each a real path in the project folder with no symlink, and the check made a missing hooks folder and config.worktree first, so each has a place to pin. devvm then starts devvm _qemu pinned in a user and mount namespace of its own, as you, with only CAP_SYS_ADMIN, and only in that namespace. It makes the namespace’s mounts private, so nothing it mounts reaches this machine’s, and pins each path in order, a folder before what’s under it. It opens each path once, by the kernel, below the project folder and through no symlink (openat2 with RESOLVE_BENEATH and RESOLVE_NO_SYMLINKS), refuses anything but a file or a folder, and refuses a file with another name, or a folder holding a regular file with one, because a bind covers one name and macOS’s flag covers the file itself (git_pin_linked, which the check before the start names first). Then it binds what it opened over itself with open_tree, mount_setattr and move_mount, which act on that file descriptor and never on a path again, because mount(2) would follow a symlink that the VM planted. A path it can’t pin, or folders it can’t watch, stop the start (qemu_pins_failed), so the VM never runs unlocked. Then it starts devvm _qemu drop as its child, which clears every capability it has, ambient, permitted, effective and inheritable, sets no-new-privileges and replaces itself with QEMU, which runs as you with no capability at all. Its bounding set stays whole, which only CAP_SETPCAP could change, and gives nothing with no new privileges. QEMU is killed if devvm _qemu pinned ends (PR_SET_PDEATHSIG), which runs as long as QEMU does, keeping the pins, so QEMU never outlives what keeps them. devvm _qemu exec waits for both and passes them the signals Lima sends, and if it’s killed, QEMU is killed with it, an unclean stop for the guest, as if its power went.

The guest reaches the project folder only through QEMU, so a write to a pinned path gets EROFS, and a rename or a removal of one, .git itself included, gets EBUSY, because it’s a mount point. A mount can’t be undone from the guest, and QEMU, which has no capability, can’t undo it either. A bind mount over a folder is a file system of its own to the guest, so a rename between the working tree and .git gets EXDEV. The namespace ends with QEMU, so nothing persists once the VM stops, and nothing changes on this machine’s side, where git works as usual.

A git command on this machine that writes .git/config writes a new file and renames it over the old one, and the new file isn’t pinned in the namespace. devvm _qemu pinned watches each pinned path’s folder with inotify, a few folders for each repo, so the 100 nested repos devvm protects at most stay far below the kernel’s limit of watches, and it pins again whatever lost its pin as soon as one changes, and every two seconds besides. Until then the guest can write the new file, rename it away and put its own in its place, which then gets the pin, open it for writing, a handle the pin doesn’t take back, or give it another name. So each pin it makes again, and each it can’t, it records in the VM’s run folder (run/git-pins.jsonl), a JSON object a line, after a first line that says it keeps the pins from then on, which it writes before QEMU starts and without which QEMU doesn’t start (qemu_pins_failed). The next check of the stopped VM, at devvm stop or at the next launch, names them before anything else, one line for each path and kind however often it happened (git_pin_again, git_pin_linked_run, git_pin_lost), then removes the file. An event devvm _qemu pinned can’t add goes to Lima’s log, with a warning, and to the file as a mark if it still takes one. A record the check can’t trust is named (git_pins_unrecorded): one it can’t read, which it keeps, a line that isn’t an event, a mark, or a file that doesn’t start with a run’s first line, as when it was removed while the VM ran and made again. The check also sums what a lock covers, as the watch does, and names what changed since the VM’s last check, so a file the guest changed in that window, or through a handle it kept, is named too. macOS’s flag has no window, because a locked config can’t be replaced on the host either.

Each launch of a running VM that’s on, and devvm stop before it stops it, read QEMU’s mounts (/proc/<pid>/mountinfo, QEMU’s pid from Lima’s qemu.pid) and name what of .git and of the git folders it locked QEMU lacks (git_pins_missing): .git and each git folder that isn’t a mount point of its own, and each read-only path that QEMU doesn’t see read-only,, such as all of them for a VM that limactl start started. A VM that’s on whose .git has nothing devvm can pin, such as one whose .git is a symlink, is named at its start (git_pins_none).

devvm checks that the host can pin by doing it: it pins a file in a namespace of its own, with its own binary, and checks that writing it fails (devvm _qemu probe). Lima’s read-only-paths feature is native where that works and none elsewhere, and a VM that’s on needs it to start, so where the kernel stops letting devvm in, the start is refused (backend_lacks) and never goes on unlocked. Where the probe fails, new VMs get off, devvm watches .git instead, and devvm doctor says why: Ubuntu’s kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns, kernel.unprivileged_userns_clone or user.max_user_namespaces at 0, or the probe’s own error. devvm offers no AppArmor profile for Ubuntu, because a profile for a binary in a folder you can write gives any program running as you what Ubuntu’s restriction holds back (Ubuntu). devvm makes the namespace itself rather than through unshare(1), so the program that asks for it is devvm.

devvm doesn’t pin .git/commondir against the VM making one, which would point git on this machine at another config: a file has to be there to be pinned, and devvm puts no file in .git that git doesn’t, so it reports a commondir at each check, as on macOS.

The watch

Where the host can’t pin, devvm locks nothing, and every VM that mounts its folder gets off as its mode. devvm watches the paths it would lock instead, and names what changed after the fact (git_changed), which Linux hosts tells the user how to check.

devvm hashes the same paths that what’s locked lists, found in the same way, and .git/commondir, there or not, the files that include.path and includeIf.*.path lead to in the project folder, and the folder that core.hooksPath names in it. For a hooks folder, it hashes each entry below it, except git’s .sample files, which git never runs, starting with the entries at its top that have a hook’s name (githooks(5)), which git runs, and then the rest. It hashes a regular file’s contents with SHA-256, opened with O_NOFOLLOW and O_NONBLOCK and checked to be a regular file once it’s open (internal/safefile). It records a symlink by where it points, and a path under a symlink, such as .git/config when .git is a symlink, by that fact. When the link resolves to a file or folder inside the project folder, it adds that file’s hash, or a hash of that folder’s hashes, and it never follows a link out of the project folder. Anything else, such as a FIFO, is recorded by its type. The work is bounded: past 1,000 entries, a hooks folder is recorded by that count, its inode and its change time, a file larger than 16 MiB by its size, inode and change time, and a watch keeps at most 2,000 hashes of the folder’s own repo and 200 of each nested repo, so a folder with many nested repos never overflows it. The VM can’t set a change time back over 9p, so a change that keeps a large file’s size is still named. Each check names, in its own warning (git_watch_blind), every path that is a symlink or under one, past a bound, or past the 2,000, because the watch can’t see every change there.

The same checks first run what a lock’s check reports, without locking (protect with watching): a .git replaced since the last check (git_replaced), after which the next check compares with the new one, a commondir (git_commondir), linked worktrees whose commondir leads elsewhere, a repo or submodule git folder that appeared, a submodule’s folder that isn’t a git folder (git_gitdir_not_git), which the watch doesn’t hash as one and where devvm creates nothing, and includes, hook links and core.hooksPath into the project folder. They don’t report hooks in folders that aren’t locked, because nothing is, and the watch names their changes. .git’s identity and the git folders and delegations found are recorded in the git section’s made, as a lock’s check records them. A VM whose made isn’t set yet reports as a new VM does.

The watch reads .git only when the VM is stopped, so it misses a change the VM made and undid before it stopped. It’s a report, not a security boundary.

The hashes go in the VM’s state, in the git section’s watched, by each path relative to the project folder, with scanned set once a check has recorded them. devvm records them when it creates the VM, and checks them again on each launch that finds the VM stopped and on devvm stop, the same places that check the locks on macOS. Each check names every path whose hash changed, appeared or went since the last one, in one warning, at most ten of them and then how many more (git_changed_more), and then records the new hashes. A launch of a running VM checks nothing. A VM whose state has no watched yet, such as one an older devvm made, or one that devvm adopt gave this folder, records its first hashes without naming anything.

Each launch also warns that the VM can change .git (git_unprotected), unless the folder has no .git or the VM is a --clone VM. The warning stops once the user has chosen the mode, which devvm records as the git section’s chosen: devvm git-protect off sets it, and so does --no-git-protect when devvm creates the VM.

What a lock can’t stop

The VM can rename .git and put a new one in its place, add .git/commondir to point git at another config, or do the same with a linked worktree’s folder in .git/worktrees. When devvm creates the VM, and on each launch, it reports a commondir that’s there, linked worktrees whose commondir leads somewhere else, and paths it couldn’t lock because they’re symlinks. devvm reads git’s own small files, a .git file, a commondir and a linked worktree’s gitdir, through a symbolic link as git does, but only when each is a regular file of at most 16 MiB, opened without blocking (internal/safefile), so a FIFO the VM leaves there can’t hang devvm. devvm doesn’t repair anything, so check what it names before you run git in the folder. When you don’t trust what runs in the VM, use --clone, which mounts no .git at all.

The VM writes .git/index, because it has to in order to commit, so it can also add a submodule with its own config, which git status on the host reads. A submodule’s core.fsmonitor therefore also runs on the host. devvm names a new submodule at the next check that finds the VM stopped, but git on the host reads it before that. No setting in the locked config keeps git on the host out of it. The VM writes .gitmodules, whose ignore line for a submodule beats diff.ignoreSubmodules, and git falls back to the index’s and HEAD’s copies of the file when the working tree has none. git add -A, -u and . enter a submodule whatever any setting says, and git diff-index, git diff-files and git describe --dirty enter one that .gitmodules doesn’t name. A setting for a submodule’s name in .git/config holds only for the name the VM chooses in .gitmodules. Only --clone keeps the VM’s code away from git on the host.

devvm’s own git commands on the host run no program that a repo’s config or .git names, a submodule’s included, whatever the VM wrote there. devvm runs each one with these settings, given as GIT_CONFIG_COUNT pairs, which git takes over any config file:

  • core.fsmonitor=false, core.hooksPath=/dev/null and core.alternateRefsCommand=true, so git runs no fsmonitor, no hook from a hooks folder and no command for an alternate object store’s refs.
  • hook.EVENT.enabled=false for every event githooks(5) lists, and hook.NAME.enabled=false for each hook the repo’s config names, so git 2.54 and newer run no hook that a config defines.
  • filter.NAME.clean, smudge and process emptied, and filter.NAME.required=false, for each filter driver the repo’s config names, so git hashes files without running a filter and doesn’t fail on a required one.
  • protocol.allow=never and protocol.ssh.allow=always, so git reaches nothing but ssh, not a path, file://, ext::, git:// or http. A repo’s config could still allow one protocol by its own key, such as protocol.ext.allow=always, which git takes over protocol.allow, so devvm also sets GIT_ALLOW_PROTOCOL=ssh, which git takes over every protocol setting.
  • maintenance.auto=false and gc.auto=0, so a fetch starts no maintenance or gc.

Its ssh is false, which reaches nothing, in place of a repo’s core.sshCommand (GIT_SSH_COMMAND=false, with GIT_SSH_VARIANT=ssh over a repo’s ssh.variant), unless the command is a --clone VM’s push or fetch, and it fetches nothing lazily (GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH=1), so a repo that says it’s a partial clone can’t make git rev-list or git status connect anywhere for an object it lacks.

It runs without any GIT_* variable of devvm’s own environment, such as GIT_DIR, GIT_WORK_TREE or GIT_CONFIG_GLOBAL, so a hook or a rebase you run devvm from can’t point it at another repo or config, and it reads your global config from its usual place. It keeps only the absolute folders of PATH, because git looks programs up, ssh among them, from the repo’s folder, and it runs with GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0. Its git status adds --no-optional-locks, so it writes no index, and --ignore-submodules=all, so it never enters a submodule, whose own config could name filters of its own.

A --clone VM’s push adds --no-verify, --no-recurse-submodules and --no-signed, so no signing program runs, and its fetch adds --no-recurse-submodules and an empty --refmap=, so it updates only the branches its own refspecs name, never those of a remote that the repo’s config names after the clone’s address. Both run git with devvm’s own GIT_SSH_COMMAND, which ignores the host, port and options git passes to ssh. It always connects to the VM’s own address and port, the host’s loopback port that the VM’s backend gives, as the VM’s user with the VM’s own key, and it reads no ssh config (-F none). It checks the host keys devvm pinned for the VM’s current start, with the VM’s own known hosts file and no global one, -o HostKeyAlias= the VM’s name and -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes, and it runs with -o BatchMode=yes, -o ForwardAgent=no and -o ClearAllForwardings=yes. In the VM it runs only git-receive-pack or git-upload-pack, whichever git asks for, on the clone’s path, and it refuses any other command. So no url.*.insteadOf, pushInsteadOf or remote URL in the repo’s config can send the push or the fetch to another host or to another path, and they forward neither your agent nor any port. A repo’s core.sshCommand doesn’t apply, because devvm sets GIT_SSH_COMMAND, and its diff.external, textconv drivers and pager never run, because none of devvm’s commands shows a diff or writes to a terminal.

Before a --clone VM is made, and again before its push, devvm checks that what git reads in the folder is the repo’s own, so the push can’t copy another repo into the VM. The folder’s .git is a folder with no commondir, or it’s the .git file of a linked worktree whose link git made both ways. That .git file names <repo>/.git/worktrees/<name>, that entry’s gitdir file names the folder’s .git back, and its commondir leads to that <repo>/.git, which has no commondir of its own. Neither the git dir nor the common dir has objects/info/alternates, or a packed-refs or reftable that’s a symlink, or anything in objects or refs that’s a symlink, such as a pack folder or a loose object’s folder that leads to another repo’s objects. Then git rev-parse --absolute-git-dir --git-common-dir must name the same two folders. A worktree’s push sends only its branch and that branch’s upstream, when the upstream is one ref, so the repo’s other branches stay on this machine. A branch.<name>.merge that’s a pattern, such as refs/heads/*, would make the upstream push every branch, so devvm then pushes only the branch.

devvm finds the hook and filter names to turn off with one git config before each command, so a VM that keeps swapping the repo’s config could show that git config one config and the command another. Every hook event is turned off by its name as well, which covers config hooks on git that has the event setting, so the gap is a filter that the swap hides, which git status could then run on a file whose stat changed. It needs a VM that writes the repo’s .git, so on macOS, where .git/config is locked, it needs a repo devvm doesn’t lock, such as a nested repo past the walk’s bounds (nested repos).

Two things a repo’s config can still do, and neither runs code. An include.path can make devvm’s git config --get user.name read your name and email from another file in git’s config format, which then go into the VM as its git identity. A config file or included file that is a FIFO makes git, and so devvm, wait until you press Ctrl+C.

item.title: Images and tools
item.description:
Every VM is a copy of an image. An image is base with your choice of layers on it, and nothing else. A VM also gets the shared tools you chose for it, such as node or Claude Code, which are mounted into it and are never part of an image. This page covers what base and the layers bring, adding layers to a VM, how the shared tools work, what a new VM gets, and how to rebuild, list and delete images. Images and caching explains how devvm builds, pins and caches them, and toolchains and coding agents list the shared tools.

flowchart TD
ubuntu["Ubuntu's cloud image,<br>or a --from image"] --> base["base, with<br>the features you chose"]
base --> docker["docker, a layer<br>on base"]
base -. "a copy" .-> vm1["VM of base,<br>with node"]
docker -. "a copy" .-> vm2["VM of docker,<br>with node and claude"]
tools[("shared tools:<br>node, claude…")] -- "mounted<br>read-only" --> vm1 & vm2

Base

base is the image that every other image is built on. It is Ubuntu 26.04’s cloud image with git, build-essential, ripgrep, jq, sqlite3 and mise added, followed by the optional features you chose, such as oh-my-bash and fzf. Docker comes as a layer of devvm’s, so you choose it when you customize a new VM, or give devvm --layers docker. With --from, base starts from a container image instead of Ubuntu’s (details).

A VM made from base gets 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk unless you give it another size, and on a small machine it gets fewer CPUs and less memory (size and ports).

base drops the server extras that Ubuntu’s cloud image comes with, which are snapd, multipath, ModemManager, udisks, firmware updates, crash reporting, tracing tools, kernel headers, and apt’s background updates and upgrades. That saves 0.9 GB of disk and 100 MB of memory per VM. The everyday tools stay, such as htop, tmux, lsof, strace, tcpdump, rsync and nano.

The first time devvm builds base on this machine, it starts from the newest release of Ubuntu’s cloud image and installs the newest packages from Ubuntu’s archive, or first from a mirror you set. devvm keeps a copy of each package it installed, so building the same base again, such as after devvm images rm base, installs exactly those packages from the copies, with no network for them. devvm rebuild base starts again from the newest image and packages. Your VMs use Ubuntu’s live archive, and base keeps no package lists, so run sudo apt update in a VM before you install a package, and apt upgrade then gets the current updates.

Layers

An image is base with layers on it, named bottom first and joined with +, so foo+bar is bar on foo on base. You can leave base itself out, which makes base+foo the same as foo. An image name never holds shared tools, which aren’t layers, so devvm build, devvm rebuild and devvm images rm refuse a shared tool’s name, such as node, and point you to devvm tools.

A layer is a script that bash runs in the image’s VM as the VM’s user, who has sudo. It is either one of devvm’s built-in layers or one of yours, at ~/.config/devvm/layers/<name>.sh. A layer’s name is made of lowercase letters, digits and dashes, starts with a letter or digit, and is neither base, a built-in layer’s name nor a shared tool’s name. devvm refuses any other name in an image, and it refuses a layer whose script is missing. devvm layer new NAME starts a layer of your own (details).

devvm build foo+bar # builds base, foo and foo+bar, unless they're built
devvm rebuild foo # builds foo again, and deletes the old foo and foo+bar

Built-in layers

devvm ships three layers, desktop, docker and nix. You choose them like any other layer, in the list devvm shows for a new VM or as in devvm --layers docker, and you build one with devvm build nix. To give every new VM one, choose it with devvm setup --layers, and to give a VM you have one, run devvm layer add (adding layers to a VM). Their names are reserved, so devvm refuses devvm layer new docker and never reads a desktop.sh, docker.sh or nix.sh of yours. The hosts that each layer needs are in its own allowlist.

desktop

The desktop layer installs an Xfce desktop with TigerVNC’s server, which devvm desktop opens in Screen Sharing, and adds about 370 MB to the image. Its packages come from the distribution’s archive as it is when the layer builds, which on a base made --from alpine means Alpine’s own packages, and they aren’t pinned. It needs no hosts of its own on the allowlist tier, and a VM without the layer has no desktop.

docker

The docker layer installs Docker’s engine, CLI, BuildKit and Compose from Docker’s apt repository, adds the VM’s user to the docker group, and starts the daemon at each boot. On a base made --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s own packages instead. A VM without the layer has no Docker. A VM with the layer can be on any network tier like any other, because its containers’ connections go through the VM’s network, which devvm confines from outside the VM (network tiers). devvm gives every container the VM’s proxy settings, and on a confined tier, a container that ignores them, or was made without them through Docker’s API, reaches the hosts the VM’s rules allow by name through transparent mode, on Docker’s default bridge and on networks that docker network create and Compose make. Such a container doesn’t trust the VM’s CA, so a blocked HTTPS host gives it a certificate error rather than the proxy’s 403, and the block is logged all the same. A container run with --network none, or on an --internal network, reaches nothing.

nix

The nix layer installs Nix with flakes and the nix command turned on, and direnv with nix-direnv, so a project’s flake.nix, shell.nix or devenv.nix can supply its toolchain. Each VM has a Nix store and daemon of its own, which no other VM and nothing on this machine shares. VMs share their downloads from Nix’s binary cache through a cache on this machine that only devvm fills. Nix projects explains that cache, and how a flake’s dev shell and the shared tools work together.

The nix layer works on a base from Ubuntu, Debian or Alpine. On a base made --from alpine, it installs Alpine’s xz package, which isn’t pinned, and runs Nix’s daemon as an OpenRC service.

Adding layers to a VM

A VM keeps the layers devvm made it with, because a layer’s script changes the VM’s disk. devvm layer add LAYER... gives a VM more layers by making it again. devvm builds an image with the new layers on top of the VM’s own, in the order you give them, and gives the VM a new disk, copied from that image. A VM of docker with desktop added is made again from docker+desktop, so the images it already uses stay as they are. devvm names the layers the VM has already and leaves them where they are, and when the VM has all of them, devvm says so and changes nothing.

devvm layer add desktop # make this folder's VM again with the desktop layer on top
devvm layer add docker nix # docker, then nix on top of it
devvm layer add desktop --force # the same without asking, as a script must

Everything on the VM’s disk that devvm doesn’t keep is lost, so in a terminal devvm names the image and asks first, with no as the default. Without a terminal, it refuses unless you give --force. When the VM has a coding agent, devvm first exports the agents’ history, as devvm rm does, unless you give --no-export (history). In a subfolder of a folder with a VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to make that folder’s VM again, and refuses without one.

devvm refuses before it changes anything when a name isn’t a layer, or is a shared tool’s name, which devvm tools add adds instead. It also refuses when the VM’s backend can’t run one of the layers, when the VM’s creation didn’t finish, and for a --clone VM, whose clone of the repo is on its disk. To give a --clone VM more layers, run devvm clone off, which offers to fetch the clone’s work first, then devvm layer add and devvm clone on (switching a VM that exists).

devvm then works in this order:

  1. It builds the new image, so a build that fails leaves the VM as it was.
  2. It exports the agents’ history and saves the VM’s home folder on this machine.
  3. It stops the VM and sets its old disk aside under another name.
  4. It makes the VM again from the new image, with the same name and settings, and starts it.
  5. It copies the home folder onto the new disk and deletes the old disk, then opens a shell in the VM.

Until the new VM has started with its home folder, a step that fails, or Ctrl+C, deletes the new disk and puts the old one back as it was. While one devvm makes a VM again, another devvm that would make the same VM again refuses, and so does devvm in its folder, so wait for the first to finish. While devvm makes the VM again, the old disk, the new one and the saved home folder take room on this machine at the same time, and devvm checks for free space before it starts.

What a VM made again keeps

devvm keeps the project folder, which is on this machine, and everything it keeps for the VM: its name, its shared tools, its size, its ports, its network tier and allowlist, its secrets’ bindings, its SSH agent choice and its .git protection. It also keeps the VM’s links, group and published ports, its desktop’s password and port, and what its devcontainer.json gave it. The commands in its devcontainer.json that run once, such as postCreateCommand, run again on the new disk. The VM gets new SSH host keys, which devvm pins as it does for any new VM, and it keeps its identity, so links to it still reach it.

devvm keeps the VM’s home folder too. It reads the folder as the VM’s user before it stops the VM, and copies it onto the new disk before devvm’s own setup runs there. What other shells in the VM write after devvm reads the folder is lost, so close them first. A file that the new image puts in your home itself, such as ~/.bashrc, stays the image’s, so put shell settings of your own in a file of yours in ~/.bashrc.d. devvm leaves out what the new VM gets from devvm itself: ~/.config/devvm, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, the agents’ logins, and the agents’ folders and files that devvm links or copies from this machine. It leaves out ~/.cache too. devvm keeps only files, folders and symlinks, without setuid bits, and nothing from a filesystem mounted inside your home. --clean-home gives the VM the new image’s home folder instead.

Everything else on the VM’s disk is lost: the packages you installed with apt, programs installed outside your home, Docker’s images, containers and volumes, the Nix store, and the processes that ran in it. When saving the home folder fails, devvm keeps the VM as it was, and --clean-home goes ahead without it.

A remake that stops halfway

If devvm itself is killed while it makes a VM again, such as when this machine loses power, the VM’s state records the remake. The next devvm, devvm layer add, devvm layer rm, devvm update, devvm clone on or devvm clone off in the folder finishes it without asking. When the new VM already has its home folder, devvm only deletes the old disk. When the old disk is still set aside otherwise, devvm puts it back and makes the VM again from the start, and when it’s gone, devvm makes the new VM with the home folder it saved. Until then, other commands on the VM refuse and name devvm, and devvm rm deletes the VM together with its old disk.

Taking layers out of a VM

devvm layer rm LAYER... takes layers out of a VM by making it again, in the same way that devvm layer add puts them in. devvm builds an image of the VM’s other layers, in the order they had, and gives the VM a new disk, copied from that image. A VM of docker+nix+desktop without nix is made again from docker+desktop, and a VM without any of its layers is made again from base. devvm names the layers that the VM doesn’t have and leaves them out, and when the VM has none of them, devvm says so and changes nothing.

devvm layer rm desktop # make this folder's VM again without the desktop layer
devvm layer rm docker nix # take out docker and nix
devvm layer rm desktop --force # the same without asking, as a script must

The VM keeps what a VM made again keeps, its home folder included, and everything else on its disk is lost, such as what the layers you took out installed and Docker’s images. So devvm asks first in a terminal, with no as the default, and refuses without one unless you give --force. It takes the same flags as devvm layer add, works in the same steps and refuses the same VMs, before it changes anything: a --clone VM, one whose creation didn’t finish, and one whose backend can’t run the layers left. It also refuses base, a shared tool’s name, which devvm tools rm takes out instead, and a name that isn’t a layer. You can still take out a layer of yours whose script you deleted, and that’s the one way to make such a VM again with its home folder and settings, because devvm layer add and devvm update need every layer’s script to build the VM’s image.

Shared tools

The toolchains and coding agents are shared tools, not image layers. A VM of any image can have them, in any mix, such as node and Claude Code on base, or go and Codex on foo. A VM’s state lists its shared tools apart from its image. Toolchains lists the toolchains, with what each brings, and supported agents lists the coding agents.

devvm builds each tool version once and mounts it read-only into every VM that has it, so any mix of tools works without building anything new, and ten VMs with node share one copy of it. The builds are in ~/.local/share/devvm/tools. Each C library gets a build of its own, so when an Alpine VM and an Ubuntu VM both have node 24, devvm images lists two builds of that version (what devvm keeps). An Alpine VM’s builds are only ever shared with VMs on the same container image, as shared tools and glibc explains. mise runs the tools:

  • They work as usual. Each toolchain’s commands, such as npm i -g (into ~/.npm-global) or go install (into ~/go/bin), work from any shell, including bash -c from agents and from editors over SSH. Global installs go into your home, as each toolchain’s section says.
  • A project’s own version files win. A toolchain’s version files, such as .nvmrc for node, pick its version, which installs into the VM the first time it’s used, and each toolchain’s section names its files. mise also reads a mise.toml in the project folder, and devvm trusts it without asking, because the folder is yours.
  • They’re read-only. A VM can’t change the shared tools, even as root. The tools can’t update themselves, and rustup component add can’t change the shared toolchain.
  • They’re mounted, or the launch stops. When one of a VM’s tools is missing or the VM can’t mount it, devvm stops the launch and names the tool, and the VM never downloads its own copy in its place (a shared tool doesn’t mount). Only the versions that a project’s own version files pick install into the VM.

devvm doesn’t pin the tools’ versions, because agents like Claude Code release several times a week. It follows the newest release of each tool, with Node 24 for node and opencode 2 for opencode. The first time a tool is needed, devvm looks up its newest release, which needs this machine to be online once. When it makes a new VM, devvm also checks for newer releases if its last check was more than a day ago, and DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK=1 turns that check off.

A new VM gets the tools chosen for it when devvm makes it, and keeps those versions. devvm tools shows them, and in a terminal lets you choose them. devvm tools add, devvm tools rm and devvm tools update change them too, as does the first step of devvm update, and changing them never changes the VM’s disk (adding and removing tools).

What a new VM gets 

flowchart TD
run["devvm in a folder<br>without a VM"] --> defaults["the defaults: the folder's toolchains,<br>devvm setup's agents and layers"]
defaults --> flags["each flag given replaces its part:<br>--tools, --agents, --layers, --network, --cpus, --memory"]
flags --> summary["the summary says what the VM gets"]
summary --> term{{"a terminal, without --no-input,<br>and something left to choose?"}}
term -- "no" --> copy
term -- "yes" --> ask{{"Customize it? [y/N]"}}
ask -- "Enter" --> copy
ask -- "y" --> pick["the list, then the tier,<br>then the CPUs, memory and disk"] --> copy
copy["its image built if it isn't,<br>and the VM is a copy of it,<br>with its shared tools mounted"]

Before devvm makes a new VM, it shows a summary of what the VM gets. The summary names each toolchain, coding agent and layer with why the VM gets it, such as for package.json, from devvm setup or from --tools, and then the VM’s size, its network tier, its ports and the folder’s devcontainer.json, when there is one:

==> This folder's new VM, devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c, gets:
 toolchain node, for package.json
 agent claude, from devvm setup
 layers: none
 size: 4 CPUs, 8 GiB of memory and a 100 GiB disk
 network tier: allowlist
 ports: all
 devcontainer.json: .devcontainer/devcontainer.json, which devvm --no-devcontainer skips
Customize it? [y/N]

In a terminal, devvm then asks whether to customize the VM, with no as the default, so confirming makes it as shown. When you customize it, devvm shows the three parts in one list under three headings, Toolchains, Coding agents and Layers, with what the summary showed already chosen (choosing in a list). The Layers heading says that a layer is extra software built into the VM’s image:

Choose what devvm-some-project-71a99b1076d92c gets. Use up and down to move, space to toggle and enter to confirm.
Toolchains
> [x] node for package.json
 [ ] python
 [ ] rust
 [ ] go
Coding agents, which you start in the VM's shell
 [x] claude from devvm setup
 [ ] codex
 [ ] opencode
 [ ] pi
Layers: extra software built into the VM's image, such as docker, nix or desktop
 [ ] desktop an Xfce desktop, which devvm desktop opens
 [ ] docker Docker's engine, CLI, BuildKit and Compose
 [ ] nix Nix, direnv and nix-direnv

Then devvm lists the four network tiers, with learn after internet for a VM that learns the hosts it needs, each with what it reaches, unless you gave --network, and you choose one, starting from the tier the summary showed: allowlist, or the tier you saved for new VMs with devvm network -g (choosing a tier). Next, unless you gave --ports, devvm lists the ports the VM can forward: every port, none, which you add later with devvm ports add, or the ports you type, which devvm checks as --ports checks them and asks for again when they aren’t a list. The list starts on what the summary showed, every port unless config.toml or devvm ports -g set another (size and ports), and the ports you choose are this VM’s alone. Last, it asks for the VM’s CPUs, memory and disk, starting from the summary’s, and confirming keeps each one. Each question is skipped when you gave its flag, --cpus, --memory or --disk. Before the disk’s question, devvm says that the disk can grow later with devvm size --disk but never shrinks, and that it takes up only the space the VM writes. A disk smaller than the image’s, 100 GiB for base, is refused as --disk refuses it, and devvm asks again, as it does for a value that isn’t a size. The size you type is this VM’s alone, and devvm saves it for no other VM.

Each part has a default:

  • Toolchains: the ones the folder’s files call for, each naming its file in the summary and the list, such as package.json.
  • Coding agents: the ones you chose with devvm setup, which the summary and the list say. The summary says from config.toml for the ones that config.toml sets. Until you choose some, there are none.
  • Layers: the ones you chose with devvm setup, bottom first, which the summary and the list say in the same way. Until you choose some, there are none. A layer that a project file calls for, such as nix for a flake.nix, names the file in its row of the list but isn’t chosen unless devvm setup chose it, so you choose it when you want it.

Three flags choose the parts on the command line. --tools takes the toolchains, as in --tools node,python, --agents takes the coding agents, as in --agents claude,codex, and --layers takes the layers bottom first, as in --layers docker,mine. Each is the exact list for its part and replaces that part’s default, and none chooses none of it, as in --agents none. A part whose flag you leave out takes its default. devvm checks each name before it does anything. For a name that belongs to another part, such as --tools claude, it names the flag that takes it, and for a name it doesn’t know, it suggests the closest one.

A part, tier or size that a flag gives is taken as given, and the summary says so. devvm still asks whether to customize the VM while anything is left to choose, because a flag answers only its own part. When you customize it, the list shows a part that a flag gave greyed out, and the cursor skips it. devvm skips the list when --tools, --agents and --layers give all three parts, skips the tier when you give --network or saved a tier, skips the ports when you give --ports, and skips the CPUs, the memory or the disk when you give --cpus, --memory or --disk. devvm doesn’t ask at all when the flags give every part, the ports, the CPUs, the memory and the disk, and the tier is given or saved. It doesn’t ask about the tier on a backend whose VMs can only be open, either.

Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm asks nothing and doesn’t fail. The VM gets what the summary shows, and the summary ends with the flags that choose others.

devvm looks at the folder’s top level for the files that call for a toolchain, in this order:

Toolchain Files
node package.json, bun.lock, bun.lockb
python pyproject.toml, requirements.txt, uv.lock, setup.py, Pipfile
rust Cargo.toml
go go.mod

If more than one toolchain matches, the VM gets them all, so package.json and pyproject.toml give node and python. A Nix project’s files call for the nix layer, whose row names them. Those files are flake.nix, shell.nix and devenv.nix, and a default.nix that makes a shell with mkShell. In a folder with none of these files, the default is no toolchains, so a VM made without a terminal or flags gets devvm setup’s layers and agents.

A folder’s devcontainer.json adds what its features map to, such as toolchains or the docker layer, to the defaults, each naming the file in the summary and the list (devcontainer.json). Its layers go on top of devvm setup’s.

The VM’s image is base with its layers, in the order you give them, bottom first, so --layers docker,mine makes the image docker+mine. When you check layers in the list, devvm setup’s stay in their order at the bottom, and the ones you add go on top in the list’s order. Its shared tools are a list of their own, the toolchains first, then the agents.

If the image isn’t built yet, devvm builds it first, then the shared tools the share lacks, and the VM is a copy of the image with its shared tools mounted. A VM keeps the image and tools it was made from, and the options for a new VM change nothing on a VM that exists, which ignores them with a warning. The warning names the command that changes the same on that VM, such as devvm tools, which changes its shared tools, for --tools, devvm layer add, which adds layers, for --layers, and devvm size for --cpus, and for --from and --no-devcontainer it names none. Only devvm takes these options, and another command given one fails as it does for any flag it doesn’t know (flags and values).

Choosing in a list

devvm’s lists work the same way everywhere: the new VM’s list, its network tiers and ports, devvm tools, base’s features in devvm setup, and the hosts in devvm network lock. Up and down, or k and j, move. In a list where you choose several, such as the toolchains, coding agents and layers, space chooses or unchooses the row under the cursor, and a chooses every row, or unchooses them all when they’re all chosen already. In a list where you choose one, such as the network tiers, moving chooses it. Enter confirms. A row that’s greyed out, such as a part a flag gave or a VM’s layers in devvm tools, can’t change, and the cursor skips it. A list longer than the terminal scrolls with the cursor, with a line above and below that says how many more rows there are, and each row is cut to the terminal’s width. At a question with a value in brackets, such as a size, Enter keeps that value.

Rebuilding

When you edit a layer’s script, devvm builds that layer again the next time it’s used, together with every layer built on it, and it reuses the layers below. A new choice of base’s features rebuilds base and everything on it in the same way.

devvm rebuild IMAGE builds an image again from its parent as the parent is now, where IMAGE is base or a stack of layers, such as docker or foo+bar. That’s how you get the newest packages that a script installs without a pin. On Lima, devvm rebuild base also starts base again from the newest release of Ubuntu’s cloud image, which devvm otherwise picks only the first time it builds base on this machine. devvm also builds the images on it again, on the new image, the next time they’re needed. When there are such images, devvm lists them first and, in a terminal, asks before it goes on. After the build, devvm deletes the old images that no VM uses.

Shared tools aren’t images, so devvm rebuild refuses a shared tool’s name, and devvm update and devvm tools update get their newer versions. Rebuilding explains how devvm tells which images to build again.

Outdated VMs

A VM keeps the image it was made from. When that image, or one it’s built on, changes after an edited script, another choice of base’s features or a rebuild, the VM is outdated. devvm then warns on each launch, names the images that changed and devvm update, and leaves the VM as it is.

devvm update brings this folder’s VM up to date in two steps. First it moves the VM to the newest shared tools, as devvm tools update does, and that needs no question, because the shared tools aren’t part of the image and nothing on the VM’s disk changes (adding and removing tools). Then, when the VM is outdated, devvm makes it again from its own image as it builds now, with the same layers, in the same way that devvm layer add makes a VM again with more layers. devvm builds the image first, then gives the VM a new disk copied from it, and keeps its home folder, the project folder and its settings (what a VM made again keeps). Everything else on its disk is lost, such as the packages you installed with apt and Docker’s images, so in a terminal devvm names the images that changed and asks first, with no as the default. When the folder’s devcontainer.json changed since devvm made the VM, or is gone, or has appeared, devvm also makes the VM again, after asking, as the file says now (updating a VM from the file).

devvm update # move the VM to the newest shared tools, and to its image's new build after asking
devvm update --force # the same without asking, as a script must
devvm update --clean-home # the same, with the new image's home folder

When only the shared tools are newer, devvm moves the VM to them and opens a shell in it without asking, because newer tools don’t need the VM made again. When you answer no, devvm keeps the VM with any newer shared tools it moved to, and opens a shell in it if there were some. Without a terminal, devvm refuses an outdated VM unless you give --force, and it refuses before it changes anything, the VM’s shared tools included.

When the VM has the newest shared tools and nothing it was made from has changed, devvm says that the VM is current and changes nothing. To make a current VM again with the newest packages that a script installs without a pin, run devvm rebuild on its image first, which makes the VM outdated, then devvm update (rebuilding). devvm update takes the same flags as devvm layer add, and it refuses the same VMs, before it changes anything: a --clone VM, one whose creation didn’t finish, and one whose backend can’t run its layers. It exports the agents’ history first unless you give --no-export, and --clean-home gives the VM the new image’s home folder instead of its own. In a subfolder of a folder with a VM, devvm asks in a terminal whether to make that folder’s VM again, and refuses without one. The steps, and what happens when one fails, are those of adding layers to a VM.

For a VM made with --from, devvm tells whether the VM is outdated from the container image’s digest that it last recorded, without looking anything up. When devvm makes the VM again, the build looks up the digest as every build does, so a tag that has moved since gives the VM the container image’s newer version too, and a pinned digest stays as it is (--from).

devvm tools update moves the VM to newer shared tools alone, and it never makes the VM again, even when the VM is outdated (adding and removing tools).

Listing images

devvm images prints two tables, each with a header, and it shows what a row lacks as -. The first table lists the images by name, with unfinished builds last:

Column
IMAGE its name, such as base or foo+bar
FROM what its base started from: the --from image, or Ubuntu’s cloud image with its release’s date, ubuntu 26.04 (20261001)
DIGEST the first 12 hex digits of that image’s SHA-256
KEY its key, which devvm images rm also takes
STATE current, stale when what it’s built from has changed since it was built, unfinished for a build that didn’t finish, or building while another devvm builds it
SIZE the disk it takes, in powers of 1024 (2.1G). On macOS an image is a clone of its parent’s disk, and the blocks they share count for both

The second table lists the shared tools that devvm has built, by the name you choose them by, such as node for node, pnpm and bun. The toolchains come first, then the agents, with each tool’s versions newest first:

Column
NAME a toolchain’s name, such as node, or an agent’s, such as claude
TOOL, VERSION the tool and its version
LIBC the C library (gnu, or musl for an Alpine base) that this build is for, because each gets a build of its own, or - when devvm can’t tell
SIZE the disk it takes
VMS how many VMs have it
STATE current for the version new VMs get, in use for another version a VM has, unused for neither, not built for the current version of a tool devvm has other versions of, and not installed when devvm has no version of it

After the tables, devvm says on stderr how many images are stale or unfinished and how much disk the unused tools take, when there are any. It ends with the disk that the images and shared tools take together, and when the shared Nix cache holds anything, the disk it takes of its cap. devvm space shows the rest of what devvm keeps (what devvm keeps).

devvm images –json
