Each CA lasts 30 days, and the next one, which the VM already trusts, takes over a week before the current one ends. The certificates that the proxy makes never outlast their CA. What a copy of a key could do, and for how long, is under the proxy’s CA keys.

Set-id files on Linux hosts

Root in a VM can set the set-user-id and set-group-id bits on files in the project folder. On macOS these bits don’t reach the host, because virtiofs drops them, but on Linux they do. A file that a Lima VM writes is yours, so a set-user-id file runs as you for anyone else on the machine who runs it. A set-user-id file that your machine’s root owns runs as root for anyone who runs it, you included, and since the VM’s writes are yours, such a file came from something else on this machine.

devvm names such files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped, by devvm stop or found stopped at a launch, but not at a launch into a running VM, because the search reads every file’s metadata and takes about a second for 200,000 files. It skips .git folders, which hold most of a big project’s files and whose files nothing runs by their path. It lists root’s files apart with setid_root_files, and you shouldn’t run them but delete them with sudo rm. It lists the rest with setid_files, and chmod u-s,g-s FILE clears their bits.

What it doesn’t protect

Each defense on this page leaves something open, such as what allowed hosts and secrets permit, open VMs, files the VM writes into the project folder, links between VMs, and escapes from the VM itself through bugs in Lima, Apple’s Virtualization framework or QEMU. Attack vectors keeps the one list of them, under Narrowed, not closed and Left to you, and each entry there links back to its mechanism.

Found a way out of a VM? See SECURITY.md.

item.title: Writing docs
item.description:
Writing docs

The site is Hugo with the Hextra theme, built from docs/. Hextra is a Hugo module pinned in docs/go.mod; update it with hugo mod get github.com/imfing/hextra@<version> in docs/.

  • Pages are Markdown files in docs/content/docs/, one per topic, in a folder per section of the sidebar. The sections run in the order a new user needs them: getting-started/, using/, safety/, backends/, compared/, cli/, internals/, then contributing/. Each folder’s _index.md is the section’s own page, which lists its pages. Update the page for any behavior you change, in the same change. The README stays high level: it says what devvm is and links to the pages for the rest.
  • What goes where: the user pages, in getting-started/, using/, safety/, backends/ and compared/, say what devvm does, what you type and what you see, and they name no repo paths, Go identifiers or message names. How it works, in internals/, explains how devvm does it, for readers who want to check a claim, and it holds the mechanisms and the message names that come from them. Contributing, in contributing/, covers changing devvm, so repo paths, Go identifiers, version bumps, releases and tests go there. A user page links once to its How it works page where there is one.
  • Front matter sets title, shown as the page’s heading, weight, the page’s place in its section, or a section’s place in the sidebar for an _index.md, and explainer, the line under the title on the page’s social card, which Social cards below describes. Start the body at ##.
  • Links to other pages point at their files ([Contributing](_index.md)), so the linters can check them.
  • Diagrams are Mermaid code blocks, fenced with mermaid, which the browser draws when the page loads. docs/layouts/_partials/scripts/mermaid.html takes the place of Hextra’s partial of the same name. It loads the Mermaid version that hugo.yaml pins in params.mermaid.base, which Hugo fetches when it builds the site, and it gives every diagram the same theme, so a diagram never sets its own colors or font. The theme uses the site’s palette: panels on the surface color with blue borders, lime arrows, and text in Departure Mono at 14px, larger than the home page’s art so labels read easily. It uses Mermaid’s classic look, because its newer neo look draws a decision’s hexagon 70px taller than its label. A diagram can set its own layout in front matter, as Staying safe’s three columns set minNodeWidth, but never its own colors or font. Mermaid draws each diagram at its own size and never scales it to fit, and a diagram wider than the page scrolls sideways. Keep labels short, and break a long one with <br>. In a label, write < as #lt; and > as #gt;. A diagram goes where it helps the reader follow the text, with at most one sentence to introduce it, and the text keeps every fact the diagram shows.
  • Style: succinct and direct. Commands are written as devvm x or in backticks, never in quotes. No please, simply or note that.
  • The home page is docs/content/_index.md, on Hextra’s hextra-home layout: its hero shortcodes, then plain Markdown. custom.css styles it through the one div that the layout wraps its content in. After the hero, the page has a quick start, what’s supported, why to use devvm with its feature cards, a short FAQ, and a closing call to action with the hero’s buttons. It keeps a marketing tone, but each of its claims matches the docs page it links to, it uses the same terms, and it says each thing once.
  • The quick start shows the three commands to run first, each after a comment short enough to fit a phone’s width, because a comment after its command would scroll out of view there.
  • Feature cards on the home page come from two shortcodes in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/, which make a {{< features >}} grid of {{< feature title="Ready in seconds" icon="high-voltage" art="copies" >}} cards, each closed with {{< /feature >}}. A card shows its title as a heading, after the pixel icon its icon names, drawn in the title’s own color at 24px, then the Markdown inside it, then its illustration, which is optional. The cards are in one centered column on smaller screens. From 1024px wide, they go into two columns, the first, third and so on on the left and the rest on the right, and each card is as tall as its content, so no card leaves a gap under it. features places them: feature renders its card through docs/layouts/_partials/feature-card.html and hands it over, and each card’s order style keeps the page’s order when the columns stack. What’s supported uses the same cards with smaller illustrations, and Quick start uses them with a terminal in each card. {{< features columns="3" >}} puts three in a row from 1024px wide, and level="3" on a card makes its title an h3, under the section’s own heading.
  • Art beside a section’s text comes from {{< beside art="blast-radius" >}}, closed with {{< /beside >}}, in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/beside.html. It renders the Markdown inside it, then the illustration it names. From 1024px wide, the text and the drawing each take half the column, with the drawing on the right, centered on the text. On narrower screens, the drawing goes below the text. Why use devvm? uses it.
  • Install commands come from {{< install >}} in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/install.html, which the home page and Installing use. The commands are written in one place, docs/layouts/_partials/install-tabs.html, which the tabs and the pages’ Markdown copies both read. It renders Hextra’s tabs with a macOS tab, which has the Homebrew command, and a Linux tab, which has the install script. The macOS tab is selected in the HTML, so it shows when JavaScript is off. A small script in docs/layouts/_partials/install-os.html selects the Linux tab as the page loads when the browser’s platform or user agent string says Linux, apart from Android. To check the Linux tab in headless Chrome, pass --user-agent= with a Linux user agent string. custom.css styles the tabs on a blue line, with the selected tab in lime.
  • Other content per operating system goes in {{< os-tabs >}}, with a {{< os-tab name="macOS" >}} and then a {{< os-tab name="Linux" >}} inside it, each holding Markdown, as Installing’s requirements tables do. It uses the same tabs, styles and script as the install commands, so the visitor’s system is selected, and the build fails unless the tabs are macOS’s, then Linux’s.
  • Colors: the site is dark only (hugo.yaml’s params.theme). Its palette is in docs/assets/css/custom.css: a black background and one lime accent, #7fff00, which sets Hextra’s primary color. The home page’s illustrations also use #0086b3, the blue that Hextra’s syntax highlighting gives commands like cd, and #ff5370 (--devvm-red), the JustBlack theme’s red, which marks only what an attack has compromised. The red’s contrast is 6.7:1 on the black and 6.0:1 on the surface color, and it’s much darker than the lime, so the two stay apart for readers who can’t tell red from green.
  • Fonts: the site uses Instrument Sans for text, Martian Mono for code, and Departure Mono, a pixel font, for the logo and the home page’s headings, badge and buttons. All three are in docs/static/fonts/, each in its own folder with its license, and docs/layouts/_partials/custom/head-end.html declares them. Instrument Sans and Martian Mono are upstream’s variable WOFF2 files, so one file holds every weight, and the partial’s comment records where each font came from, at which commit or release, and its SHA-256. To update a font, download the new version from the same place, check its SHA-256, and update the comment. Departure Mono is sharp at multiples of 11px and has one weight.
  • No third-party requests: devvm.dev and next.devvm.dev load every script, stylesheet, font and image from the site itself, so a visitor’s browser asks no other host for anything. mise run lint:docs checks this after it builds the site: TestNoThirdPartyLoads in internal/cli/docgen/site_test.go reads every page and stylesheet and fails on a link, script, image, frame or CSS url() that points at a host other than the ones in hugo.yaml’s and next.yaml’s baseURL. Hugo fetches FlexSearch, which Hextra’s search uses, and the Mermaid version that hugo.yaml pins when it builds the site, and the site serves both itself, so they pass. Links that a visitor clicks, such as GitHub’s, aren’t loads, and the check ignores them. The social cards draw it from docs/assets/fonts/departure-mono/, which has the same release’s OTF and license, because Hugo can’t draw text from a WOFF2.
  • The logo in the navbar is the branding page’s devvm-logo-on-dark.svg at its own size, which hugo.yaml’s params.navbar.logo names, with the site’s title as its alt text. Right-clicking it opens the branding page instead of the browser’s menu, through a script in docs/layouts/_partials/custom/footer.html. A left click, or Enter on the focused logo, still goes to the home page.
  • The branding page is docs/content/branding.md, at /branding/, on its own layout, docs/layouts/branding.html, which is Hextra’s home layout with the home page’s look and the script that copies a swatch’s hex. Its front matter keeps it out of the sidebar. It has the logo as box-drawing text in a code block, the logo’s SVGs and PNGs, the icons, the social card, the palette, the fonts, how to use the logo and the credits.
    • Its downloads are in docs/static/branding/, and {{< brand-asset >}} tiles inside {{< brand-assets >}} show each one on its background, with a link to each file. The build fails when a file doesn’t exist, and it reads each PNG’s size for its link. devvm-logo-on-dark.svg and devvm-logo-on-light.svg are the logo, drawn on a pixel grid as the favicon is, made from Departure Mono’s 11px glyphs. The prompt and devvm are at twice the glyphs’ size, the box is in 1-pixel lines, and the lock, a block with a keyhole under a 2-pixel arch, sits on the box’s bottom-right corner, with the box’s lines stopping short of it so that the arch stands clear. The version for light backgrounds is black, with its prompt in the dark lime, #408000 (--devvm-accent-dark), which is the lime’s hue at half its lightness, with a contrast of 4.9:1 on white, where the lime has 1.2:1. Each logo’s PNG is its SVG at four times its size on a transparent background, and devvm-icon-64.png to devvm-icon-1024.png are docs/static/favicon.svg at 4 to 64 times its size. After changing an SVG, render its PNGs again with headless Chrome’s --screenshot at the exact size, passing --default-background-color=00000000 for the logos’ transparency, and look at each one.
    • The palette comes from {{< palette >}}, which reads the colors that docs/data/palette.yaml lists, with each one’s name and use, and takes each hex from its variable in custom.css, so the page always shows the site’s colors. The build fails when a variable isn’t there. A new color goes in both files.
    • The fonts each come from {{< font-sample >}}, which shows a line of text in the font, with a link to the license the site serves for it.
  • The favicon is the same mark drawn on a 16-pixel grid in docs/static/favicon.svg: the box, a lime prompt in its middle and a small lock centered on its bottom-right corner, overhanging it by 2 pixels each way, its shackle a closed arch, with the box’s lines stopping a pixel short of the lock, on black, with a pixel of black around the whole mark. Hextra links its icons by name, and the ones in docs/static/ take the place of its own: favicon-16x16.png and favicon-32x32.png, favicon.ico, which holds those two PNGs, apple-touch-icon.png, which is the grid at 160px with 10px of black around it, and the two android-chrome-*.png icons that site.webmanifest lists. Each PNG is the SVG at a whole multiple of its size, so its pixels stay sharp. The social card in docs/static/images/social-card.png is the 1200x630 card that the branding page offers for links to devvm. It has devvm-logo-on-dark.svg at twice its size, the home page’s headline and tagline in Departure Mono, and the site’s colors. After changing the SVG or the card’s text, render the PNGs again with headless Chrome’s --screenshot at the image’s exact size, and look at each one.
  • Social cards: every page gets a 1200x630 card of its own, which Hugo draws when it builds the site, and which sites and chat apps show when someone shares the page’s link.
    • The card is docs/assets/images/og-template.png, which is social-card.png with the headline and tagline painted out in the background’s black, so it has the logo, devvm.dev and the lime bar, in the same four colors and nothing else. docs/layouts/_partials/og-image.html draws three things on it with Hugo’s images.Text, in Departure Mono: the page’s section in lime capitals at 22px, its title in white at 66px, or at 55px or 44px when a smaller size fits it in two lines, and its explainer in gray at 33px. A docs page’s section is its section’s title, such as Using devvm, a section’s own page has Docs, and the home page and the branding page have none. The text is centered between the logo and devvm.dev. Each size is a multiple of 11px and each line starts at a whole pixel, so the text is as sharp as the logo, and the card keeps only the template’s four colors. docs/layouts/_partials/og-wrap.html wraps the lines at spaces, and because the font is monospaced, a line’s width is its length.
    • The explainer is the explainer in each page’s front matter: a few plain words on what the reader gets from the page, such as Install devvm and check what it needs, without a full stop. It isn’t the page’s description, which search engines and llms.txt show, because that’s a sentence or two, and most pages have none. The home page’s card shows its cardTitle, the hero’s headline, in place of its title, because the logo already says devvm. The CLI reference’s pages get their command’s Short as their explainer when mise run cli-docs writes them. TestExplainers in internal/cli/docgen fails when a page has no explainer, or when its explainer takes more than two lines of 48 characters or its title more than two lines of 36, which are the card’s lines at 33px and 44px.
    • The tags: docs/layouts/_partials/custom/head-end.html writes og:image with its type, width, height and og:image:alt, and twitter:image:alt, whose text is devvm docs, the title and the explainer. docs/layouts/_partials/_funcs/get-page-images.html takes the place of Hugo’s own, which its Twitter card and schema templates call for a page’s images, so twitter:image and the schema’s image are the same card. hugo.yaml names no params.images, so Hextra’s Open Graph template writes no second og:image. A card’s address is the site’s, so next.devvm.dev’s pages show next.devvm.dev’s cards.
  • The illustrations on the home page are SVGs in docs/assets/home/, and {{< art "name" >}} inlines one into the page, so that it gets the page’s fonts and colors. A feature card’s art parameter inlines one the same way, through docs/layouts/_partials/art.html. Each one is drawn on Departure Mono’s 11px cell, 7 pixels wide and 14 tall, so its text and shapes are sharpest at its own size or at twice its size. The art shortcode shows it at twice its size, 728px wide. A card shows it as wide as the card, at whatever scale that takes.
    • Each card’s drawing shows what its text says, and nothing more. The big cards’ drawings are 364 by 140 pixels, or 168 for isolated.svg: zero-config.svg shows a dev server’s forwarded port, devvm code and a commit authored by you, copies.svg the base image and its copies, isolated.svg the mount and the proxy, agents.svg the agents’ mounts, the history that stays and the token, and make-it-yours.svg the stack of base, your layer and the VM, with --from. The What’s supported cards’ drawings are 224 by 70 pixels: toolchains.svg, coding-agents.svg and layers.svg, which shows the image docker+nix as a stack and the built-in layers beside it. The Quick start cards’ drawings are terminals of 254 by 181 pixels, which a card shows at most twice their size: step-cd.svg types cd ~/some-project on your machine, step-pick.svg types devvm, shows a short version of the new VM’s summary and presses enter at Customize it? [y/N], and step-agent.svg types claude in the VM’s shell. Why use devvm?’s drawing, blast-radius.svg, is 364 by 210 pixels and shows the same four attacks as its text on two machines. Without devvm, they light up on your machine, and the project, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh and another project turn red one after another. With devvm, they light up in the VM, each one’s path toward your machine ends at the VM’s border with a cross, and your machine’s folders stay as they are.
    • Every text element holds one run of characters at its own x, because Hugo’s --minify removes the spaces between tspan elements. A gap of a cell is 7 pixels added to x.
    • Animations are CSS keyframes in custom.css, which classes in the SVGs turn on. pulse dims and brightens a lime arrow every 3 seconds, and pulse-2 and pulse-3 start a part of the arrow 0.3 and 0.6 seconds later, so the pulse runs along it. pulse-slow does the same every 4 seconds. lit lights a text’s fill and lit-chip a chip’s opacity for most of a 4-second loop, and lit-2, lit-3 and lit-4 start them 0.5, 1 and 1.5 seconds later, so they light one after another. blink turns a cursor on and off every 2 seconds. mover marks a block that travels a path, mover-token along the token’s line, under the proxy and down to the API in 3 seconds, and mover-egress under the proxy, down to the allowlist and back, then out to the internet in 4 seconds. A block is drawn before the shapes it passes under. attack-1 to attack-4, path-1 to path-4 and reach-1 to reach-4 tell blast-radius.svg’s story in an 8-second loop, and every part of the drawing stays in place all along, so the story only changes colours and draws lines. Each attack’s chip turns from gray to lime at 0.4, 1.6, 2.8 and 4 seconds. In the VM, its path then draws itself down to the VM’s border, and when it gets there, the cross at the border turns lime and, on the machine without devvm, the folder it reaches turns red. Everything holds from 5.2 seconds, and from 6.6 seconds the colours go back and the paths draw back up, so the drawing rests from 7.2 seconds until the story starts again. Each step has its own keyframes, so that all of them end together. The SVG draws each part in its end colour, and --rest in custom.css gives the colour it has before its step, so a drawing without animation shows the end of the story. The Quick start terminals each loop on their own. type marks a cover over a command, which shrinks from the right one cell at a time while caret moves the cursor along, both in --chars steps across --width, and caret-blink keeps the cursor solid while it types and makes it blink after. In step-pick.svg, pick-summary shows the summary once devvm is typed, pick-ask shows the question after it, and key lights enter as it’s pressed. Their styles in custom.css are each part’s end state too, and their keyframes start from the beginning. When the visitor’s system asks for reduced motion, prefers-reduced-motion turns every animation off and hides the blocks.
    • To see an animation’s state in a screenshot, pause the animations with a stylesheet of your own and set each class’s animation-delay to minus the time you want, because headless Chrome’s --virtual-time-budget barely moves CSS animations.
  • Icons are pixel icons in docs/assets/icons/, one SVG per icon. Most come from Dinkie Icons, which is MIT licensed, and the folder keeps its license and a README that names the version they were copied from. The penguin, prompt, warning and light bulb icons are drawn for devvm in the same style. {{< icon "rocket" >}} inlines one through docs/layouts/_partials/icon.html, so it takes the text’s color, and the build fails when no icon has that name. An icon is 0.75em square, which makes each of its pixels one screen pixel in 16px text, and it sits on the text’s baseline. Screen readers skip it, unless a second argument gives it a label, as in {{< icon "warning" "Warning" >}}, for an icon that says something the text doesn’t. To add a Dinkie icon, copy its path data from the same version of the @dinkie-icons/react npm package into a new file named after the icon in kebab case, with the same svg attributes as the others. A new icon of your own uses the same 12-pixel grid and 1-pixel lines, and the README lists it.
    • Each section’s icon is chosen once, in docs/data/sections.yaml, which maps a section’s folder under docs/ to an icon’s name, as in getting-started: rocket. A new section gets a line there. The section cards and the sidebar both read it, so they always show the same icon, and the build fails when the list names a section or an icon that doesn’t exist.
    • Section cards on the docs’ first page are Hextra’s {{< cards >}} holding a {{< section-card path="getting-started" >}} for each section, with its one-line description inside, closed with {{< /section-card >}}. The shortcode takes the section’s title and link from its page under docs/, and its icon from sections.yaml, and the build fails when there’s no such page. Hextra’s card takes an icon only from Hextra’s own set, so the shortcode puts ours in the card’s title, at 24px. It’s dimmed as Hextra dims its own cards’ icons, and it turns lime on hover.
    • The sidebar’s top-level items show their section’s icon at 12px, in the link’s color, so it’s gray, and lime for the section you’re in. Hextra’s sidebar has no icons, so docs/layouts/_partials/custom/head-end.html writes a CSS rule for each section when the site builds, keyed to the section page’s address, with the icon from docs/assets/icons/ as a mask. Nothing is generated into the repo, so there’s no step to rerun.
    • The OS tabs of install and os-tabs show the Apple icon before macOS and the penguin before Linux, which docs/layouts/_partials/os-tab-name.html adds to each tab’s name.
    • ✓ and ✗ go before a table cell’s word: {{< yes >}} yes puts a lime check before it, and {{< no >}} doesn't a gray cross. They go only in cells that are a plain yes or no, or what stands for one, such as the install script’s offers it, never in cells that are sentences, and the word stays, because screen readers skip the icon. Icons in tables are 12px, because a table’s text is smaller than 16px.
    • Buttons take an icon before their text: docs/layouts/_shortcodes/hextra/hero-button.html is Hextra’s hero-button with an icon parameter, as in {{< hextra/hero-button text="Install" link="docs/getting-started/install/" icon="download" >}}, drawn at 24px like the headings’ icons. The 404 page’s two buttons have their icons in its layout, a rocket for Getting started and the open book for the docs, as the home page’s Read the docs has it.
    • The navbar’s GitHub link uses Dinkie’s GitHub icon, which docs/data/icons.yaml adds to Hextra’s own icons as dinkie-github, and hugo.yaml’s menu names. Hextra’s icon partial reads only that data, so an icon for the navbar goes there as its SVG, not in docs/assets/icons/.
  • Heading icons: a heading gets an icon before its text with an icon attribute, as in ## Quick start {icon="rocket"}, which the home page’s section headings use. docs/layouts/_markup/render-heading.html takes the place of Hextra’s heading render hook and adds the icon after Hugo makes the heading’s anchor, so the anchor comes from the text alone, such as quick-start. On the home page, custom.css draws these icons in lime at 24px, so each icon pixel is two screen pixels, as each of Departure Mono’s pixels is at 22px.
  • Callouts are GitHub’s alerts: a blockquote whose first line is [!NOTE], [!TIP] or [!WARNING], which GitHub shows the same way. docs/layouts/_markup/render-blockquote-alert.html takes the place of Hextra’s alerts and draws each one on the surface color with a line down its left side, and a title with its icon: information-circled in blue for a note, the light bulb in the soft lime for a tip, and warning in lime for a warning. Any other type fails the build. Hextra’s own callout shortcode isn’t used. Use a callout only for a real warning, such as what the VM’s boundary rests on, or a tip that saves the reader trouble, such as keeping a VM on a strict tier, and move the sentence into it instead of repeating it.
  • For agents and other tools that read the site, hugo.yaml turns on three things that Hextra has. The site’s root has llms.txt, which lists every section and its pages. Each page has a Markdown copy beside its HTML, such as /docs/using/clone.md beside /docs/using/clone/, and a section’s copy is index.md in its folder, such as /docs/using/index.md. Each docs page has a Copy page menu beside its title, which copies the page’s Markdown or opens it. hugo.yaml lists every output for the home page, the sections and the pages, so the home page and the sections keep their RSS feeds, and the search index is built apart from these outputs.
    • llms.txt comes from docs/layouts/llms.txt, which takes the place of Hextra’s. It has the site’s title and description, then each section under its title, with the section’s own page first and its pages after it. Each one is a link to its Markdown copy, as the llms.txt convention prefers, which docs/layouts/_partials/llms-link.txt writes, and a line of plain text, which docs/layouts/_partials/llms-summary.txt writes. A page without a copy gets a link to its HTML page instead. The line is the page’s description from its front matter when it has one, and otherwise its first paragraph, cut at 200 characters. A description is also the page’s description for search engines and link previews, so give a page one when its first paragraph doesn’t say what the page covers, as Coding agents has. llms.txt also lists the CLI reference, with each command’s one-line summary.
    • The Markdown copies come from docs/layouts/page.markdown.md and section.markdown.md, which take the place of Hextra’s and both use docs/layouts/_partials/markdown-copy.md. A copy is the page’s title as a heading, then its Markdown with its shortcodes rendered. In a copy, a link to a section’s _index.md points at index.md, the section copy’s name, so the links work between the copies, and a link written in code stays as it is.
    • Each shortcode that docs pages use has a Markdown version beside its HTML one in docs/layouts/_shortcodes/, named after it with .markdown.md, which renders it in the copies. install writes each system’s name in bold, then its commands, which come from docs/layouts/_partials/install-tabs.html, the same partial its tabs use. os-tabs writes its tabs the same way, through docs/layouts/_partials/os-sections.md. section-card makes a list item that links the section’s copy, and Hextra’s cards keeps only what’s inside it. yes and no become ✓ and ✗. A shortcode without a Markdown version puts its HTML into the copy.
    • The home page and the branding page are mostly shortcodes, and neither layout shows the menu. hugo.yaml gives the home page no Markdown copy, and its front matter sets contextMenu: false. The branding page’s front matter sets outputs: [html], contextMenu: false and llms: false, so it has no copy, no menu and no line in llms.txt. Any other page can set llms: false to stay out of llms.txt, or contextMenu: false to have no menu.
    • After you add a page or a shortcode, build the site and read the page’s line in llms.txt and its Markdown copy. The line should say what the page covers, and the copy should have no shortcode left in it, such as {{< os-tabs >}}, and no HTML from one. A shortcode that docs pages use gets its Markdown version. To try the menu, serve the site with mise run docs and open a docs page. custom.css gives the menu the site’s border and secondary text, lime on hover, and its list the surface color.
  • The 404 page is docs/layouts/404.html, which takes the place of Hextra’s and uses the site’s navbar and footer. It shows a VM’s terminal answering cd ./this-page with “no such page”, drawn like the home page’s art in docs/assets/home/not-found.svg with the blink cursor, then Hextra’s search box and links to Getting started and the docs. Build the site and open /404.html to see it.

mise run lint:docs, which mise run lint includes, checks docs/ with:

Linter Checks Config
markdownlint-cli2 Markdown .markdownlint-cli2.yaml
Vale the style rules .vale.ini, .vale/styles/devvm/
lychee (--offline) links to pages and files

It also builds the site with Hugo’s --panicOnWarning, into a temporary folder it removes, so any warning fails it. That includes a deprecation, such as a template that reads site.Data where Hugo wants hugo.Data, so a Hugo upgrade that deprecates something the templates use fails here before the feature is removed. It runs TestExplainers too, so a page without an explainer fails it.

The CLI reference

The CLI reference in docs/content/docs/cli/ is generated from devvm’s commands with Cobra’s docs generator, and checked in. Don’t edit it: change the command’s Use, Short, Long, Example or flags, or its docs page in internal/msg/docs.go, then run:

mise run cli-docs

It runs internal/cli/docgen, which replaces every page in that folder: _index.md, listing the commands, and a page per command named after its path (devvm_build.md), with title and explainer front matter, the explainer being the command’s Short, and links to the other pages as files. Each page has the command’s examples, and a Docs section before See also that links to the command’s docs page on the site. Hidden commands (_msg, _qemu) and Cobra’s help command are left out. The pages carry no dates, so the same commands give the same files. They carry no weight either, so Hugo sorts the section by title, and a new command adds its own page and changes only _index.md and the root’s devvm.md; TestPagesHaveNoWeight checks this. The .gitattributes file marks the pages as generated, so GitHub collapses them in a diff.

A command’s help

Every command’s help, which its reference page also shows, has the same shape. Short is an action in sentence case without a full stop, such as List the project VMs. Long is one to three short sentences on what the command does, and the rules and edge cases go on its docs page. Example comes from examples in internal/cli/help.go, which takes each command line with a short comment and lines the comments up, the most common invocation first. A flag’s description is short, and its long explanation goes on the page.

Each command describes itself where it’s made, so its docs page and group are in its own file, not in tables elsewhere. Its Annotations come from an about in internal/cli/help.go: docs, the user page that covers it as page#anchor; group, its section of the root’s help; and noJSON, why a command without --json has none. addDocs gives the root Cobra’s usage template with a Docs section at the end, which shows the address of the command’s page, and the root’s help also ends with the issue tracker, msg.IssuesURL. The CLI reference links each command’s page too, and TestDocLinks in internal/msg reads those links from the reference and checks that each page and heading exists and is a user page. helpGroups in the same file lists the root’s sections, in order, and addGroups adds each group that has a command and sets its commands’ GroupID, so a group whose commands don’t exist yet stays out of the help. A subcommand can name a group too, such as layer add in Change your VM, when it belongs in another group than its parent. addGroups then adds that group to the parent, so the parent’s own help groups its subcommands the same way, and the usage template lists the subcommand by both names in the root’s group, after the group’s own commands. Cobra lists a group’s commands in alphabetical order, and help goes in Cobra’s own Additional Commands.

The tests fail when the checked-in pages are stale: TestReferenceIsCurrent in internal/cli/docgen generates the reference into a temporary folder and compares it with docs/content/docs/cli/. mise run docs regenerates it before serving the site.

Building the site

mise run docs serves the site at http://localhost:1313/ and reloads on every change. mise exec -- hugo -s docs --minify builds it into docs/public/, as the Docs workflow does for devvm.dev, and mise exec -- hugo -s docs --minify --config hugo.yaml,next.yaml builds the site as next.devvm.dev has it, with its banner and its noindex (the docs sites).

item.title: Backends
item.description:
This page explains how a backend gives devvm what it needs to run a VM, what devvm does when a backend lacks something, and how devvm names VMs. devvm runs its VMs on Lima, and another backend would plug in the same way, through the features below (how a backend plugs in).

What a backend does

A backend has four roles, and every backend has all of them:

  • The host: it says what it needs that this machine lacks, which devvm doctor reports, how long a VM’s name can be, where its VMs live, and which folders hold their disks, so devvm can check the free space before a step that writes them.
  • Images: it builds images and the shared tools’ images, keeps the images, and names the files of its own that it puts into base, which base’s key hashes.
  • Machines: it makes, starts, stops, renames and deletes VMs, runs commands and shells in them, and says how ssh and devvm’s port forwarder reach them. It also says how a VM runs now: which start it’s on, whether that start is confined to the VM’s proxy, and the file the VM’s proxy and forwarder follow, which ends them when the process that runs the VM ends.
  • Housekeeping: it says how much disk its VMs and caches take for devvm space, lists the VMs with devvm’s label that this devvm has no state for, and lists and deletes devvm’s share of its own caches for devvm gc --caches. A backend that can’t tell one of these returns nothing, so devvm shows no size or deletes nothing.

A backend may also keep files of its own for a VM besides the VM, which devvm gc --orphans deletes once the VM is gone. Lima keeps none.

Features

Each thing devvm needs from a backend is a feature, such as building images, mounting the project folder or confining a VM to its proxy. devvm doctor lists them as “features” too, but they aren’t the base image features you choose with devvm setup. Each backend declares how it has each feature:

  • native: the backend does it itself.
  • emulated: devvm builds it from other parts of the backend.
  • none: the backend can’t do it.

A backend lists every feature, the ones it lacks too, and devvm refuses to use a backend that leaves one out, so a new feature makes each backend say how it has it. Some features are built on others: read-only-paths and mount-cache on project-mount, ports-all on ports, agent-toggle on agent-forwarding, and link on ssh. A backend has such a feature no better than the one it’s built on, so the feature is emulated wherever its base is emulated, and none wherever its base is none.

devvm uses an emulation only once its review has passed, and until then it refuses the emulation. A review takes a design note, a threat check with the security-audit skill, and end-to-end checks that prove the guarantee.

devvm doctor lists Lima’s features, and devvm doctor --json those of every backend devvm has. Both show an emulation whose review hasn’t passed as unreviewed.

The feature table

Feature What it is Lima
build-image build images from the layer and feature scripts native
build-confinement builds reach the internet but not the host’s loopback, or nothing native: Seatbelt on macOS. On Linux, QEMU’s restrict=on confines a build with no network, but a build with the internet reaches the host’s loopback (details)
from base from a container image (--from) native: devvm converts the image to a disk
clone a project VM from an image native: an APFS copy-on-write copy on macOS, and a qcow2 overlay on Linux (details)
project-mount the project folder, read-write native: virtiofs on macOS, and 9p on Linux
read-only-paths paths in the project folder that the guest can’t change while the VM runs, which .git protection asks for on Linux native on Linux where the kernel lets devvm use a user namespace: QEMU runs in one of its own, with the paths bound read-only over themselves (details). None on macOS, where .git protection locks the host’s files itself, and none where devvm’s check of the kernel fails
mount-cache choosing how the guest caches the project folder’s mount, which devvm mount-cache sets native on Linux, where it’s 9p’s cache option, none for new VMs (details). None on macOS, where virtiofs has no such option
agent-folders agents’ host folders, read-only native: read-only mounts, enforced by the host
tools-share the shared tools, read-only native: a read-only mount, enforced by the host
egress-proxy network traffic only through devvm’s proxy native: Seatbelt on macOS, and on Linux QEMU’s restrict=on with a guestfwd to the proxy (details)
ssh ssh for editors native: Lima’s ssh forward and config
ports the listed ports forwarded to the host’s loopback emulated (reviewed): devvm’s forwarder over Lima’s ssh, for the listed ports alone, with Lima’s own forwards off (details)
ports-all every port forwarded, servers on the VM’s loopback included emulated (reviewed): the same forwarder, for whatever listens in the VM from port 1024 up, and never a port the host has (details)
agent-forwarding ssh-agent forwarding, chosen when the VM is made native
agent-toggle turning a VM’s ssh-agent forwarding on or off later native
cpus a VM’s CPUs native
memory a VM’s memory native
disk a VM’s disk size native: it grows but never shrinks
docker-layer the docker layer: Docker’s engine running in the VM native
nix-layer the nix layer: Nix’s daemon and its store in the VM, with builds in Nix’s sandbox native (details)
link links between VMs: a program in one VM reaches a port another VM publishes, by name native: a link session of devvm’s own over Lima’s ssh, with remote forwards to 127.77.0.0/16 alone (details)

egress-proxy is what every network tier but open needs. The open tier needs no feature of its own: every backend must let a VM on its own network (NetDirect) reach a port on the host’s loopback and set the guest’s proxy settings from the confinement (Confinement.GuestProxy, ProxyURL), which the conformance suite checks (checkProxyURL), because every VM’s proxy carries its requests. So a backend without egress-proxy still has open VMs, and devvm refuses every other tier on it in one line (net_tier_backend).

What each backend emulates

On Lima, devvm emulates forwarding ports, both the listed ones and every one, through its forwarder, and the emulation is reviewed (port forwarding). Everything else on Lima is Lima’s own.

The forwarder is devvm’s own on every backend, never a backend’s. A backend that has ports turns its own forwards off, and devvm’s forwarder reaches a running VM’s sshd the way the backend’s SSH says, which is a user, a key and a port. devvm refuses that target unless it’s on this machine’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, with the same check it uses for links and the ssh config (vmssh.FromTarget). devvm reads which ports the VM forwards from its state, chooses which of them are free, pins the VM’s host keys for its current start and starts the forwarder, which follows the backend’s lifeline for the VM.

Missing and unreviewed features

devvm checks each feature an image or a VM needs this way:

flowchart TD
need["a feature the image<br>or the VM needs"] --> how{{"how the backend has it"}}
how -- "native" --> ok["allowed"]
how -- "emulated, reviewed" --> ok
how -- "emulated, unreviewed,<br>or none" --> np{{"egress-proxy, for<br>a new open VM?"}}
np -- "no" --> refused["refused: devvm stops<br>and names the VM,<br>the feature and the backend"]
np -- "yes" --> warned["the VM is made open,<br>as asked"]

Before devvm builds an image, makes or starts a VM, or changes a VM’s settings, it checks that the backend has every feature the image or the VM needs. The backend itself is behind the same check: every time devvm asks it to build an image or the shared tools, make a VM or start one, devvm checks the features that request needs before the backend sees it, so a request that skipped the first check is refused too. When the backend lacks one, devvm stops and names the VM, the feature and the backend (backend_lacks). It does the same for a feature the backend only emulates when that emulation’s review hasn’t passed (backend_unreviewed). devvm never falls back to something weaker, so a VM on a confined tier never starts with an open network.

To get the feature, use a backend that has it. A VM keeps its backend, so that means making a new VM.

A new VM’s tier is the one exception, because allowlist is the default, and When a backend lacks something says what devvm does instead.

What a start changes

A backend makes a VM as devvm asks, and then changes it only when it starts. Each time devvm starts a stopped VM, it tells the backend what the VM’s state asks for, which is its size, the agent folders in devvm’s agent store and whether it forwards your SSH agent, together with how the VM is confined. The backend compares that with the VM it has and changes only what differs, so a start that changes nothing leaves the VM’s config as it was. Nothing changes a stopped VM’s config between starts, so devvm size and devvm ssh-agent save what you ask for in the VM’s state, and the VM gets it when it next starts.

A running VM is left as it is, and devvm says what changes when it next starts. Its ports aren’t the backend’s, so devvm ports changes them at once, and a running VM’s forwarder starts again with the new ones (port forwarding). A disk can’t shrink, so a start that asks for a smaller disk than the VM has fails before the backend changes anything (disk_shrink).

Which ports a VM forwards stays in the VM’s state alone, and the backend never hears of them. The backend keeps only what it needs for the start it made, such as Lima’s record of the hostagent it started confined (confinement).

VM names

A project VM’s name is devvm-<folder>-<hash>. The folder part is up to 20 characters of the folder’s name, in lowercase, with characters other than letters and digits turned into dashes, and the hash part is 14 hex digits of a hash of the folder’s path. devvm takes a name as a project VM’s only when it has that form, so a name in a state file or a backend’s list whose folder part has any other character, or starts or ends with a dash, isn’t a project VM’s.

A backend may need shorter names, and then devvm cuts the folder’s part to fit. When fewer than 4 characters of it would fit, devvm refuses (vm_name_no_room). On Lima the room for a name depends on the Lima home’s path, because Lima keeps each VM’s ssh socket under it, so there the fix is a shorter Lima home (lima_home_too_long, limits).

Only a new VM gets a name, which fits the limit of the backend that makes it. devvm finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder’s path, in the VM’s folder in devvm’s data folder (vms/<hash>/, named by the hash that ends the VM’s name), so an existing VM keeps the name and the backend its state records, whichever backend new VMs get, and keeps them when its folder moves (a moved folder).

Which backends a launch asks

A launch asks a backend about its VMs only when some VM’s state names that backend. It asks them to write the ssh config and to check the SSH agent’s folders. So a backend that no VM uses never runs during a launch, even when it isn’t running or isn’t installed (a VM’s backend).

item.title: Settings and files
item.description:
devvm writes nothing into your project folders. It keeps the settings you edit in ~/.config/devvm and everything it writes itself in ~/.local/share/devvm, and it reads a few environment variables. Your settings lists the files you edit, devvm’s data folder lists the ones devvm writes, and Overview explains how devvm keeps them.

Your settings

~/.config/devvm ($XDG_CONFIG_HOME/devvm) holds what you edit, and it’s the only folder of devvm’s that you should change by hand. devvm never rewrites a file of yours there. It reads config.toml and your own layers and CAs, it creates a new layer’s files when you run devvm layer new, it changes single lines of policy when you add or remove a rule for every VM, and it writes version when the folder has none and when it changes its folders to a newer layout.

File What it holds Written by
config.toml the defaults that new VMs get and the retention settings, which win over what devvm’s commands save, the company proxy and an Ubuntu mirror (config.toml) you
policy your network rules for every VM devvm network allow -g, deny -g, rm -g, or you
layers/ your own layers and their allowlists devvm layer new, then you
agents/ your agents’ settings in devvm’s agent store, one folder for each agent devvm agent import, devvm agent save, or you
ca/ your company’s CA certificates, which VMs and builds trust you
version the folder’s layout version, which says how devvm keeps its files here devvm, when it’s missing or older

Edit the files in ~/.config/devvm, and never edit the ones in ~/.local/share/devvm. devvm writes those itself and rewrites them whole, so a change you make there can be lost, or can stop devvm from reading the file. To set a default by hand, put it in config.toml instead.

Upgrading devvm keeps this folder as it is. Back it up, such as in a dotfiles repo, to keep your settings and layers.

config.toml

~/.config/devvm/config.toml sets the defaults that new VMs get, the retention settings, the company proxy, an Ubuntu mirror, the release check, transparent mode and the API keys that VMs get as they are, in a file you write by hand. devvm reads it and never writes it. Every key is optional, and devvm has no config.toml until you write one. This example sets every key:

# The network tier new VMs get: open, internet, allowlist or none.
network = "allowlist"

# The ports new VMs forward: all, none, or ports and ranges.
ports = "5173,8000-8010"

# The features base gets, in the order they run, or [] for none.
features = ["cli-tools", "fzf", "omb"]

# The coding agents new VMs get, or [] for none.
agents = ["claude", "codex"]

# The layers new VMs get, bottom first, or [] for none.
layers = ["docker"]

# A mirror of Ubuntu's archive that base's first build tries first.
ubuntu-mirror = "http://mirror.example.com/ubuntu-ports"

# Whether a launch checks once a day for a newer devvm release.
release-check = true

# Whether confined VMs send tools that ignore the proxy settings to their proxy.
transparent-proxy = true

# New VMs' CPUs, and their memory and disk in GiB.
[size]
cpus = 4
memory = 8
disk = 100

# What devvm deletes on its own, with the keys devvm retention takes.
[retention]
logs.runs = 20
history.age = "90d"
history.count = 10
tools.unused-age = "30d"
orphans.age = "30d"
nix-cache.size = "20G"

# The company proxy, when the shell you run devvm in sets none.
[proxy]
https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com"

# Providers whose API keys an agent's VMs get as they are.
[pass-keys]
opencode = ["ollama"]
pi = ["ollama"]

Each key takes what its command takes. network is a tier, open, internet, allowlist or none, as devvm network -g sets it (choosing a tier), and never learn, because each VM learns the hosts it needs on its own. ports is all, none or a list, as devvm ports -g takes it (size and ports). features lists the features that base gets, agents the coding agents that new VMs get, and layers the layers that new VMs get, bottom first. cpus is a whole number, and memory and disk are a number of GiB, such as 8, 8.5 or "8G", as devvm size -g takes them. The [retention] keys are the retention settings, with a duration such as "90d" or a size such as "20G" in quotes, and a count as a number.

The [proxy] table is the company proxy that every VM’s proxy, builds and devvm’s own downloads go through when the shell you run devvm in sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, whatever the VM’s tier. No VM gets the company proxy’s settings itself. That shell’s settings win over the whole table. https and http take what HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY take, an http:// URL or host:port, and no-proxy takes what NO_PROXY takes. A URL never holds a password, and devvm refuses one that does, so put only the user in it and save the password with devvm secret set proxy. No command saves the proxy, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

The [pass-keys] table names, for an agent, the providers whose API keys its VMs get as they are, which devvm otherwise keeps on this machine because the VM’s proxy can’t put them in, such as a local model server’s. It takes opencode and pi, each with a list of the agent’s provider IDs as its auth.json names them, in lower case, such as ["ollama"] (opencode logins, pi logins). devvm refuses another agent, a name that isn’t a provider’s ID and a repeat (config.toml names the line). A provider whose key the VM’s proxy puts in (API keys the proxy puts in) never needs the table, because the proxy puts its key in without it. When the table lists one all the same, the VM gets that key’s placeholder from its next launch on, not the key, and devvm notes at each launch that you can take the provider out. A VM that got such a key as it was before then may still hold copies of it, which keep working, so make a new key when you don’t trust that VM (API keys the proxy puts in). Every VM with the agent gets the change at its next launch. No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

An Ubuntu mirror

ubuntu-mirror is a mirror of Ubuntu’s archive, such as one your company or university runs, which the first build of base gets its packages from before it tries Ubuntu’s own. It must mirror the archive for this machine’s architecture: archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu on an Intel or AMD machine, or ports.ubuntu.com/ubuntu-ports on an Apple silicon Mac or another arm64 machine. Give it as an http:// or https:// address without a user, a query or spaces, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). A package that the mirror doesn’t have, or a mirror that doesn’t answer, falls back to Ubuntu’s archive for that file.

A mirror can’t give base a package that Ubuntu didn’t publish. apt checks every list and package against Ubuntu’s archive key whichever server sends it, and refuses one that doesn’t match, and devvm checks them against that key again on this machine before it keeps any package. A mirror that’s behind, or one that’s lying, can still serve lists older than Ubuntu’s, because Ubuntu’s signed lists don’t expire. devvm refuses lists more than a day older than the Ubuntu cloud image base starts from, and it names the mirror and keeps none of the build’s packages (old package lists). devvm compares the lists with the cloud image’s date, not with today’s, so a mirror that fell behind after that date can still give base packages older than Ubuntu’s, and you should only set a mirror you trust to keep up. Only the first build of each base uses the mirror, because a later build of the same base installs the packages devvm kept from that first build (base). VMs don’t use it, and neither do layers or a --from base. No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

The release check

When you run devvm in a terminal, it checks at most once a day for a newer devvm release, and when one is out it says so in one line before it opens the VM, naming the release, the version you have and devvm upgrade. devvm never installs anything on its own, so you upgrade with devvm upgrade when you choose to. release-check = false turns the check off, and so does setting DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 in the environment, as CI can. release-check must be true or false, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

The check reads only where GitHub’s latest devvm release is, over HTTPS, and sends nothing about you or your machine. The latest release is never a prerelease, so the check never announces one (trying a prerelease). The exception is a devvm that Homebrew’s devvm-rc formula installed, which follows prereleases: its check reads GitHub’s list of devvm’s newest releases instead, and it announces a newer prerelease or release, whichever is newest. It runs beside the launch, so it never makes devvm wait, and when you’re offline it says nothing and tries again the next day. The line comes from what the last check found, so a release that came out since then shows up at the launch after the next check. devvm keeps what the check found in ~/.local/share/devvm/cache/release.json, and devvm doctor shows it. devvm says nothing without a terminal, with --no-input, for a devvm built from its source, or for a copy that neither the install script nor Homebrew installed, which devvm upgrade can’t upgrade.

Transparent mode

On every tier but open, devvm sends a tool that ignores the proxy settings to the VM’s proxy by the names it looks up, which is transparent mode. It’s on unless you turn it off. transparent-proxy = false turns it off for every VM that has no setting of its own, and devvm network transparent on or off gives one VM its own, which comes first. A change applies at each VM’s next launch. transparent-proxy must be true or false, and devvm refuses anything else (config.toml names the line). No command saves it, so it’s only ever in config.toml.

Where a default comes from

For each default, devvm uses the first of these that sets it:

  1. A flag for one VM, such as --ports or --cpus.
  2. config.toml.
  3. What devvm’s commands saved: devvm setup, devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention save in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json.
  4. devvm’s own default.

A command that would save a default that config.toml sets refuses, names the file and the key, and changes nothing, because the value in config.toml would still win. To change that default, edit it in config.toml, or delete it there to let devvm’s commands set it again. In a terminal, devvm setup doesn’t ask about what config.toml sets, and it says so.

devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention show where each value came from, after a #. They show config.toml’s path for a value from config.toml, devvm: settings.json for one that a command saved, and devvm: default for devvm’s own:

$ devvm ports -g
5173,8000-8010 # /Users/you/.config/devvm/config.toml
$ devvm network -g
allowlist # devvm: default

With --json, the same commands add source, or sources for each value of devvm size -g and devvm retention, which is config.toml, settings.json or built-in.

When devvm can’t read it

devvm reads all of config.toml each time it needs a default, and it checks every key and value. A key it doesn’t know, such as a typo, a value that a key can’t take, and a file that isn’t TOML each stop the command, and devvm names the file and the line. Fix the line, and run the command again. config.toml has no key for the backend, because every new VM runs on Lima, so a backend key stops the command as an unknown key.

devvm setup

devvm setup chooses what new VMs get. In a terminal, it asks five questions, each starting from the current choice, and saves each answer in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json, as the command for that setting saves it. It skips a question that config.toml answers, saying so, and it refuses a flag that would change what config.toml sets.

  1. The features that base gets.
  2. The CPUs and memory that new VMs get, as devvm size -g saves them.
  3. The network tier that new VMs get, as devvm network -g saves it: open, internet, allowlist, which is the default, or none. Each new VM’s summary shows that tier, and when you customize the VM in a terminal, devvm asks for its tier, with Enter keeping the one the summary showed (what a new VM gets). --network TIER chooses for one VM and wins over the saved choice.
  4. The coding agents that new VMs get.
  5. The layers that new VMs get.
devvm setup # asks all five questions
devvm setup --features fzf,omb # base's features, without asking
devvm setup --features none # base gets no features
devvm setup --agents claude,codex # new VMs' coding agents, without asking
devvm setup --layers docker # new VMs' layers, without asking

devvm setup has three flags of its own, and each one chooses without asking anything. --features LIST chooses base’s features, as a comma-separated list or none for none, and devvm refuses an empty --features ''. --agents LIST chooses new VMs’ coding agents in the same way, and --layers LIST chooses new VMs’ layers. With any of the flags, what the flags leave out stays as it is. Without a terminal and without flags, devvm setup asks nothing and keeps base’s features, saving every feature when none was chosen yet. To change new VMs’ size without asking, use devvm size -g (choosing new VMs’ size), and to change their network tier, use devvm network -g (choosing a tier).

Coding agents for new VMs

The coding agents you choose in devvm setup are the ones a new VM gets unless you choose others for it. The summary devvm shows before it makes the VM names each of them as coming from devvm setup, and when you customize the VM, they’re checked in the list (what a new VM gets). --agents chooses others for one VM. The choice is for new VMs only, so a VM that exists keeps its agents, and devvm tools changes them.

devvm asks for them on its first run in a terminal, together with the size and base’s features, until you’ve chosen them. Until then, and when you choose none, new VMs get no agents by default. devvm setup --agents claude,codex and devvm setup --agents none choose them without asking, and devvm refuses a name that isn’t an agent’s, suggesting the closest.

Layers for new VMs

The layers you choose in devvm setup are the ones every new VM gets unless you choose others for it. They can be devvm’s built-in layers, desktop, docker and nix, and your own, which is how you give every new VM an extra of your own (extras of your own). The summary devvm shows before it makes a new VM names each of them as coming from devvm setup. When you customize the VM in a terminal, they’re already chosen under Layers in the list, and you can leave any of them out of that VM (what a new VM gets).

devvm setup --layers docker,desktop # every new VM gets docker, with desktop on top
devvm setup --layers none # new VMs get no layers
devvm --layers nix # this VM gets nix alone, not setup's layers
devvm --layers none # this VM gets no layers

devvm setup --layers takes the layers bottom first, in the order the image’s name joins them, so --layers docker,desktop gives new VMs the image docker+desktop. It refuses a name that isn’t a layer’s, suggesting the closest, and changes nothing. Until you choose some, new VMs get no layers by default, and devvm doesn’t ask for them on its first run. In a terminal, devvm setup asks for them last, after the coding agents. To set them by hand, use the layers key in config.toml, which devvm setup --layers then refuses to change.

--layers on devvm is the exact list of one VM’s layers, so it replaces setup’s layers, and --layers none makes a VM without any. A devcontainer.json’s layers go on top of setup’s (devcontainer.json).

The choice is for new VMs only. A VM that exists keeps the layers it was made with, and devvm setup says so when it saves the choice. To give that VM more layers, run devvm layer add in its folder (adding layers to a VM), and to take some out, devvm layer rm (taking layers out of a VM).

When a layer of yours that you chose in devvm setup has no script in ~/.config/devvm/layers, such as after you delete it, a new VM is made without it, and devvm warns, naming the layer. Run devvm setup --layers to choose the layers again. When the VM’s backend can’t run a layer you chose, such as docker on a backend without Docker’s engine, devvm makes no VM and names the layer. Then choose other layers for that VM with --layers, or change new VMs’ layers with devvm setup --layers.

Retention

devvm keeps what it makes until you delete it, and the retention settings tell it to delete some of it on its own. Every setting is off until you set it, so first run devvm space to see what each one would free: its RETAIN column shows each setting that’s on, beside the row it applies to, with what it would delete now (devvm space).

devvm retention shows every setting and its value, and off for each one that isn’t set. devvm retention KEY=VALUE... sets them, and devvm retention KEY=off turns one off, for example devvm retention history.age=90d tools.unused-age=30d. devvm refuses a key or value it doesn’t know, and a key with no value such as history.age=, and then it writes nothing. devvm saves the settings in ~/.local/share/devvm/settings.json. The [retention] table of config.toml sets them too, and a setting there wins over the saved one, so devvm retention refuses to change it. Each line that devvm retention shows ends with where its value came from, after a #. When devvm can’t read a file that sets them, it names the file, and the line for config.toml, and applies none of them.

Key What devvm deletes
logs.runs the run logs beyond the newest this many, which is 20 when it’s off
history.age the exports of agents’ history written this long ago or more, such as 90d
history.count the exports of agents’ history beyond the newest this many
tools.unused-age the current shared tools that no VM has had for this long, counted from when devvm first found that no VM has them. While a VM is being made or is getting new shared tools, retention deletes none of them in that run, because that VM may not list the tools it picked yet, and it still applies the other settings
orphans.age what devvm keeps for VMs that their backend no longer has, once their state hasn’t changed for this long, as devvm gc --orphans does
nix-cache.size the shared Nix cache’s least recently used files, while it takes more than this, such as 20G; it’s 10 GiB when it’s off

Ages are durations, a whole number of minutes, hours, days or weeks, such as 30m, 12h, 30d or 2w. Sizes are a whole number of K, M, G or T, each 1024 of the one before, such as 500M or 20G, as devvm space shows them. The shared Nix cache also keeps to its size while VMs fill it, because a VM’s proxy deletes the cache’s least recently used files before a new file would take it past that size. A size you set applies to each VM from its next start. devvm applies the settings at the start of a command, at most once a day, except for orphans.age, which needs to ask each backend about its VMs, so only devvm gc --retention applies it. devvm gc --retention applies all of them at once. When it deletes something, devvm says what in one line. Retention never deletes a VM, an image, a shared tool that any VM’s state lists, or anything in the backends’ own caches, which only devvm gc --caches frees. In cache/, the folder in devvm’s data folder that holds what devvm makes again when it needs it, retention deletes only the shared Nix cache’s files. When two devvms start at once, only one of them applies the settings.

devvm retention –json

devvm retention --json prints the settings as one JSON object, as output for scripts describes. settings has every key with its value as you wrote it, and off for each one that isn’t set. sources has every key with where its value came from: config.toml, settings.json for one that devvm retention saved, or built-in for one that’s off. With --json the command only shows, so devvm refuses a KEY=VALUE with it.

{
 "version": 1,
 "settings": {
 "history.age": "90d",
 "history.count": "off",
 "logs.runs": "off",
 "nix-cache.size": "off",
 "orphans.age": "off",
 "tools.unused-age": "30d"
 },
 "sources": {
 "history.age": "config.toml",
 "history.count": "built-in",
 "logs.runs": "built-in",
 "nix-cache.size": "built-in",
 "orphans.age": "built-in",
 "tools.unused-age": "settings.json"
 }
}

A company’s CA

Some company networks inspect TLS through a proxy, such as Zscaler or Netskope, that shows its own certificates, signed by the company’s certificate authority (CA). This machine trusts that CA, but VMs and the VMs that devvm builds images in don’t, so their TLS connections fail. To make them trust it, put the CA’s certificate in ~/.config/devvm/ca:

mkdir -p ~/.config/devvm/ca
cp company-root.pem ~/.config/devvm/ca/

devvm reads every *.pem and *.crt file in that folder each time you open a VM, each time it builds an image and each time it resolves the shared tools’ versions, and it leaves other files alone. A file can hold one certificate or several, in PEM, the text form that starts with -----BEGIN CERTIFICATE-----. devvm accepts only CA certificates. When a file holds anything else, such as a private key, a certificate devvm can’t read or a certificate that isn’t a CA’s, devvm refuses the whole folder and names the file. It sends only the certificates it read out of a file, never the rest of the file. devvm doesn’t follow links there, so copy each certificate into the folder rather than linking to it. When a *.pem or *.crt file is a link, or the folder itself is one, devvm refuses the whole folder and names the link, because a link into a project folder would let that project’s VM replace the CA that every VM, build and proxy trusts. devvm also refuses the folder, naming the file, when it can’t read a file there or the folder itself.

Every project VM trusts these CAs in its system’s store from its next launch, and so does every VM that devvm builds an image or shared tools in. devvm takes them out of a build VM before the image is finished, so images never keep them, and adding or removing a CA rebuilds nothing. A layer script of yours that copies the system’s CA bundle somewhere else does keep that copy. On every network tier, the VM’s proxy also trusts them for the connections it makes itself, and so does the refresh of a coding agent’s login that the proxy makes on this machine when the login is due, so a company proxy that inspects TLS doesn’t make the refresh fail. devvm also resolves the shared tools’ versions on this machine, with a mise of its own that it downloads once, and that download trusts these CAs as well as this machine’s own store, and on Linux so does that mise. On macOS, mise trusts them for most of its connections, but the part of it that checks where each tool’s release was built trusts only the CAs that macOS trusts, which Keychain Access shows. So on macOS, a company’s CA that mise needs has to be there too, where a Mac that your company manages usually has it already. When mise doesn’t trust a server’s certificate, devvm says so and names this folder. devvm’s other connections from this machine, such as checking an image’s registry or Ubuntu’s image, trust this machine’s own store, as your other programs here do. When you take a certificate out of the folder, VMs stop trusting it at their next launch, and stores that copy the system’s CAs, such as Java’s cacerts, drop it too.

Most tools read the system’s store, among them apt, apk, curl, git and Python’s ssl module. For those that don’t, every VM’s environment points them at it:

Variable Value For
NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS /etc/ssl/devvm.pem, which holds only devvm’s CAs and is empty when there are none Node, npm and Bun
SSL_CERT_FILE /etc/ssl/certs/ca-certificates.crt, the system’s bundle Go programs, and Rust programs that read the system’s roots
REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, PIP_CERT the system’s bundle Python’s requests and pip, which use their own CA list otherwise
UV_SYSTEM_CERTS 1 uv

A CA in the folder can read every TLS connection a VM makes, as it can this machine’s, so put only CAs there that you trust as much as this machine does. How it works › Network tiers explains how the CAs reach VMs, and Images and caching how builds use them.

devvm’s state

~/.local/share/devvm ($XDG_DATA_HOME/devvm) holds what devvm makes and keeps for you, and devvm writes everything in it, so don’t edit it by hand. It holds the defaults that devvm setup, devvm size -g, devvm ports -g, devvm network -g and devvm retention save in settings.json, below config.toml’s, and a folder for each VM in vms/, with the VM’s state, its own allowlist and its network logs. It also holds the images and the shared tools, the run logs, the agents’ history that devvm history export and devvm rm save, the ssh config for your VMs, and devvm’s own Lima home (lima/), where the Lima backend’s VMs and images live. devvm’s data folder lists each file and folder in it, with how each one is cleaned up.

On Linux hosts this folder also holds your secrets, in files under secrets/ that only you can read, so keep that in mind when you back it up. On macOS they’re in the Keychain.

devvm’s Lima home is its own, whatever LIMA_HOME says, so Lima settings meant for other VMs never reach devvm’s. Set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME to move it, for example to a sandbox or to a shorter path.

Only you can read devvm’s files, in either folder, because each time devvm runs, it makes both folders yours alone (devvm’s data folder). When devvm can’t read one of its files, it names the file and the line (a file devvm can’t read).

Project folders devvm refuses

A VM mounts its project folder read-write, so devvm refuses to make a VM for a folder that would give the VM more than the project. It refuses a folder that is or holds your home folder, ~/.config/devvm, ~/.local/share/devvm or devvm’s Lima home. It also refuses a folder inside one of devvm’s own folders, because a VM there could rewrite the scripts that every image build runs, or the files that devvm runs on this machine.

When devvm refuses a folder, make the VM in a project folder inside it, or keep the project somewhere else. A --clone VM mounts nothing from the folder, so devvm doesn’t refuse its folder.

Warning

If you mean to give the VM the whole folder, pass --unsafe-folder when you make the VM, and devvm warns you that the VM gets read-write access to it (only the project folder).

Colors

In a terminal, devvm colors the labels and links around its messages, while the messages’ own text stays in your terminal’s usual color. The values a message fills in, such as a VM’s name, a path, a port or a count, are bold, so they stand out from the words around them. An error’s devvm: label is red and a warning’s is yellow, a doc link is blue and underlined, and the ==> before what devvm did is bold. When a step fails, the end of the run log that devvm prints is dim, and so is the log’s latest line on the status line and each line that -v shows. The mark a slow step leaves when it’s done is green.

The tables that devvm ls, devvm images, devvm space and devvm doctor print are colored too. Each table’s header row and the totals row are bold, and a state is green when it’s good, such as current, Running or native, yellow when it needs your attention, such as stale, unused, Stopped or emulated, and red when something is wrong, such as an unenforced tier or an unreviewed emulation. Digests, image keys and a feature a backend doesn’t have, which devvm doctor lists as none, are dim, and names, paths, sizes and counts stay in your terminal’s usual color. The columns line up the same with colors or without.

devvm uses only your terminal’s 16 base colors, so your theme picks shades that read well on its background, light or dark. It never sets a background color.

devvm decides for standard output and standard error apart, and colors one only when it’s a terminal, so output you pipe or redirect to a file stays plain, tables included. What a command prints with --json is plain even in a terminal, and the run log is never colored. These environment variables change when devvm colors, and the first one that applies decides:

  • NO_COLOR, set to anything but an empty value, turns colors off.
  • FORCE_COLOR or CLICOLOR_FORCE, set to anything but 0, turns them on even when the output isn’t a terminal.
  • TERM=dumb turns them off.

Environment

NO_COLOR, FORCE_COLOR, CLICOLOR_FORCE turn devvm’s colors off, or on when the output isn’t a terminal (details)
DEVVM_LIMA_HOME move devvm’s own Lima home (details)
DEVVM_FROM the container image that the base of new VMs and builds starts from when there’s no --from (details)
DEVVM_NO_TOOL_CHECK=1 don’t check for newer shared tools once a day (details)
DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 don’t check for a newer devvm release once a day (details)
DEVVM_SECRET_SERVICE the Keychain service devvm saves and reads secrets in, instead of devvm (details)
CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN the Claude Code token that VMs get, over the saved Claude Code login, whichever it is (details)

item.title: Lima
item.description:
This page explains how devvm runs its VMs on Lima: the Lima home it keeps them in, how it builds images and clones VMs from them, what it sets in each VM’s config, how it confines VMs and builds, and how it forwards their ports. Lima covers what you need to run it, devvm limactl and Lima’s limits.

A Lima home of its own

Lima merges _config/default.yaml and _config/override.yaml from its home into every VM it creates or starts. A network you set there for your own VMs would give a devvm VM a second network card with a route around its proxy, and an extra mount set there would go unnoticed. So devvm keeps its VMs in a Lima home of their own, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima, whatever LIMA_HOME says (devvm’s Lima home says what that means for you).

devvm refuses to start a VM while that home holds either file (lima_global_config), and it refuses a VM that has a network devvm didn’t give it (vm_has_networks).

devvm runs limactl from its own data folder. When a config is invalid, Lima writes lima.REJECTED.yaml into the folder it runs in, and a project folder belongs to the VM to write.

Clones and overlays

An image is a stopped VM in devvm’s Lima home, named devvm-img-<key>. devvm makes base’s from Ubuntu’s cloud image with base.yaml, base’s size as --cpus, --memory and --disk, and --mount-none, and it gives limactl create the template on its standard input (-), from the binary, so no copy of base.yaml is on disk. With --from, it makes base’s from the converted disk instead, and boots its kernel and initrd directly (details). A layer’s image is a clone of its parent’s, also made with --mount-none, so a build mounts nothing from the host. A project VM is a clone of its image’s VM, which devvm makes while the image is stopped.

  • macOS: the clone’s disk is an APFS copy-on-write copy. It shares the image’s blocks until the VM writes them, so du overcounts it.
  • Linux: Lima’s disks are qcow2 files, and a clone would be a full copy. So a project VM’s disk is a qcow2 overlay of its image’s, readable only by you, which shares the image’s blocks and holds only the VM’s changes. An image’s disk is read-only once it’s built, and devvm can’t delete an image while VMs’ disks are overlays of it (image_in_use). devvm reads each VM disk’s backing file with qemu-img info -U, which shares the disk with the QEMU of a running VM, because that QEMU’s write lock refuses qemu-img info otherwise.

What devvm sets on a VM

devvm sets these in each VM’s Lima config:

  • Mounts: the project folder (read-write), agents’ folders (read-only), and the shared tools at /mnt/devvm-tools (read-only). Each folder but the tools is mounted at its host path. devvm mounts nothing else, and it leaves out the home folder that Lima’s templates mount. On macOS, where Lima runs VMs with vz, the project folder’s mount names the folder by the device and inode that devvm recorded when it made the VM, as location: /.vol/<device>/<inode> with mountPoint set to the folder’s path. macOS’s /.vol opens a folder by its device and inode, so Virtualization.framework shares the folder devvm made the VM for, wherever that folder is when the VM starts, and never follows a link put at its path (an existing VM). Virtualization.framework then serves the share by the path the folder had at the start, so a folder moved back while the VM runs answers “Operation not permitted” in the VM until its next start. QEMU’s 9p on Linux has nothing like /.vol, so there the mount is by the folder’s path, with the cache mode the VM’s state records as its 9p: cache: option: none for a new VM, and nothing for a VM whose mode nobody chose, which keeps Lima’s mmap (why). The read-only mounts keep Lima’s fscache, and a build VM’s writable output folder gets none. The start that changes a VM’s cache mode mounts its folder again once the VM runs, because the guest mounted it with the old options before cloud-init wrote the new ones into its /etc/fstab, and it then checks the mount: a folder left unmounted fails the start (why). A start that rewrites the mounts, for a folder that moved, another cache mode or other agents’ folders, keeps each mount’s settings that devvm doesn’t set, such as its other 9p and sshfs options, where they differ from Lima’s defaults, and leaves the defaults out for Lima to fill in.
  • ssh: agent forwarding on or off, and the host port. devvm chooses the port when it makes the VM and records it, so no other VM’s forwarded ports take it. The port changes only when another program on the host has it, on any address, while the VM is stopped, or when the VM lists it to forward.
  • Ports: none, because Lima’s own forwards are off and devvm’s forwarder forwards the VM’s ports instead (below).
  • Size: CPUs, memory and disk.
  • Guest environment: Lima’s env:, which Lima writes to /etc/environment at every boot. On every tier it holds the VM’s proxy’s address and its settings, and Lima doesn’t pass the host’s proxy settings in.
