Once a VM’s state is gone, devvm gc treats its shared tools like any others. devvm space counts the whole folder of each VM that devvm gc --orphans would forget as leftover state, and each socket a link session left counts there too. A VM that gc leaves alone for one of the reasons above isn’t leftover state, so its folder counts as state and its logs as network logs.

VMs devvm has no state for

A VM can also be the other way around: the backend has it, with devvm’s label, but devvm has no state for it. Usually it belongs to another devvm, such as one run with another XDG_DATA_HOME for a test or a sandbox. devvm space names each one, with the data folder its label names, and devvm never deletes it, because the other devvm may still use it. To delete one yourself, run devvm limactl delete NAME.

VMs whose folder is gone

A VM whose project folder you deleted or moved still takes its disk, and it isn’t leftover state, because its backend still has it and it may hold that project’s work. devvm space names each VM whose backend has it and whose folder is gone, with that folder, and counts it among the VMs. Neither devvm gc nor retention ever deletes one. devvm rm VM deletes it after asking, exporting its agents’ history first (a VM whose folder is gone).

devvm space also names each VM whose folder is on a disk that isn’t connected, with that folder, and counts it among the VMs too. Connect the disk to use the VM again. devvm rm VM deletes one only after you confirm in a terminal, and --force never answers that question (a folder on a disk that isn’t connected).

What devvm doctor finds in vms/

vms/ should hold only VMs’ folders, each named by a hash of 14 hexadecimal digits and holding the VM’s vm.json. devvm doctor warns about anything else it finds there, says what to do, and changes nothing:

  • An entry that isn’t a VM’s folder, such as a file or a folder with another name, which devvm never uses. Move it out of vms/ or delete it.
  • A VM’s folder without vm.json, which a devvm that stopped while making or deleting a VM leaves, for example one holding only the VM’s lock. No VM uses the folder, so delete it.
  • A folder doctor can’t read, vms/ itself or a VM’s folder, so it can’t check what’s in it. Check that you own it and can read it, for example with ls -ld.

These warnings never make doctor fail, and devvm doctor --json lists them in warnings.

Your settings

~/.config/devvm holds what you edit: config.toml, your network rules, your agents’ settings, your own layers, and your company’s CA certificates. devvm also writes the folder’s layout version into version there when the file is missing or older. Your settings lists each file. devvm never deletes any of them.

Lima

The Lima backend’s VMs and images are in devvm’s Lima home, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima. Each image is a stopped VM named devvm-img-<key>, and each project VM is a clone of one. On macOS a clone’s disk shares its image’s blocks until the VM writes them, so du counts those blocks twice. On Linux hosts a VM’s disk is an overlay of its image’s. devvm rm deletes a VM, devvm gc deletes stale and unfinished images, and devvm images rm deletes any image you name.

Lima keeps a download cache of its own, ~/Library/Caches/lima on macOS and ~/.cache/lima on Linux, or $XDG_CACHE_HOME/lima when XDG_CACHE_HOME is set. When devvm builds base, Lima downloads Ubuntu’s cloud image into that cache, which is 600 to 900 MB for each release, and on macOS it also keeps a copy converted to a raw disk, which takes about 2.4 GB more. The cache is Lima’s and it isn’t in devvm’s Lima home, so your own Lima VMs’ downloads share it. devvm deletes something in it only when you run devvm gc --caches. Lima keeps each download in a folder named by the SHA-256 of its address, and gc frees only the folders of Ubuntu’s cloud images at the address devvm downloads base from, for its Ubuntu release, that no image record of devvm’s names and that haven’t changed in the last hour. A cloud image that one of your own Lima VMs downloaded from that same address can be among them, and Lima downloads it again the next time it needs it. No VM needs its entry once it’s made, because Lima copies the disk out of the cache. limactl prune deletes the whole cache, your own downloads included, so devvm never runs it.

Outside devvm’s folders

devvm also changes a few things outside its own folders:

  • The Keychain: on macOS, the secrets you save are Keychain items under the service devvm. devvm secret rm deletes one.
  • ~/.ssh/config: when you let it, devvm adds the line Include ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config so that ssh reaches VMs by name (SSH and editors).
  • Time Machine: on macOS, devvm keeps each VM’s run/ca/ out of Time Machine’s backups, because a copy of a key elsewhere could impersonate any site to that VM.
  • devvm itself: the install script puts each version in ~/.local/lib/devvm/<version> and links ~/.local/bin/devvm to it. A newer install removes older versions that nothing runs (upgrading). Homebrew keeps devvm in its own folders.

Uninstalling removes all of it.

item.title: The command line
item.description:
This page covers what works the same way in every command: the help, flags and their values, the questions devvm asks and what answers them beforehand, --json for scripts, and shell completion. Everyday commands lists the commands, and the CLI reference has every command with all its flags.

Help

devvm help COMMAND, devvm COMMAND --help and devvm COMMAND -h print a command’s help. It starts with a few sentences on what the command does, then its usage line and its examples, the most common first, each with a comment. Then come its commands, if it has any, and its flags, and the help ends with the address of the docs page that covers the command. devvm --help lists the commands in the groups that Everyday commands has, which are Your VM, Change your VM, Images, Disk space and This machine, with help under Additional Commands, and it ends with devvm’s issue tracker after its docs page.

devvm itself takes no word after it but a command’s name, so every word there is a command, and a layer may have any name a command has. When the word after devvm isn’t a command, devvm refuses it as a usage error. If the word names a toolchain, an agent or a layer, your own layers included, devvm points you to the flag that chooses it for a new VM, such as devvm --tools node for devvm node, and a word that joins several with + or a comma gets one line with each flag, such as devvm --tools node --agents claude for devvm node+claude. Any other word gets the closest command, such as devvm stop for devvm stpo. devvm stpo --help and devvm help stpo are refused the same way.

Flags and values

Each flag belongs to the commands that list it in their help, and only -h or --help, -v or --verbose and --no-input work with every command. -v shows the output of the commands devvm runs as they run (details), and --no-input makes devvm ask nothing (questions devvm asks). A flag can come before or after the command’s arguments, and options that take a value also work with an equals sign, such as --cpus=N.

The options for a new VM, such as --tools and --cpus, are taken only by devvm. Another command given one of them, such as devvm ls --cpus 4, fails as it does for any flag it doesn’t know (what a new VM gets).

When a flag or a setting can mean none or off, you write that as a word: devvm setup --features none, devvm --agents none, devvm ports none, devvm retention history.age=off and devvm ssh-agent add KEY_FILE --lifetime forever. devvm refuses an empty value, such as --features '', and an empty argument, so a blank never stands for none or for a default.

Every duration is a whole number followed by a unit, which is m for minutes, h for hours, d for days or w for weeks, as in 30m, 12h, 30d or 2w. That covers devvm gc --older-than, the retention settings’ ages and devvm ssh-agent add --lifetime, and only --lifetime also takes forever, for a key that devvm’s agent keeps until it ends.

Questions devvm asks

devvm asks a question only in a terminal, and each question has a flag or a command that answers it beforehand, so a script never needs to answer one. Without a terminal, with --no-input, or when the input ends before an answer, devvm can’t ask, and every question is handled the same way in all three cases. A question that only adds something, such as an agent’s folders or the Include line, gets its usual answer or a warning that says what to do, and a command that deletes something refuses unless you give it --force.

Question Answered by
the CPUs and memory new VMs get, on the first run --cpus and --memory, or devvm size -g, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, new VMs get the size they would anyway
the coding agents new VMs get, on the first run and in devvm setup devvm setup --agents LIST or devvm setup --agents none
base’s features, on the first run before the new VM’s summary, or on the first build devvm setup --features LIST or devvm setup --features none
whether to customize a new VM, after its summary --tools, --agents, --layers, --network, --ports, --cpus, --memory and --disk, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, the VM gets what the summary shows
a new VM’s toolchains, coding agents and layers, when you customize it --tools, --agents and --layers
a new VM’s network tier, chosen from a list when you customize it --network TIER, or devvm network -g with a tier for every new VM, or nothing: where devvm can’t show the list, the VM gets the tier the summary shows
the ports a new VM forwards, chosen from a list when you customize it: every port, none, or the ports you type --ports, or devvm ports -g with the ports every new VM forwards, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, the VM forwards the ports the summary shows
a new VM’s CPUs, memory and disk, when you customize it --cpus, --memory and --disk, or nothing: where devvm can’t ask, the VM gets the size the summary shows
the layers new VMs get, in devvm setup devvm setup --layers LIST or devvm setup --layers none
a VM’s toolchains and agents, in devvm tools devvm tools add and devvm tools rm, or --json to show them
new VMs’ network tier, in devvm setup devvm network -g
whether to load an SSH key into your agent devvm ssh-agent add KEY_FILE beforehand
whether to restart a running VM to apply a change from devvm size, devvm network, devvm ssh-agent or devvm git-protect, or, as devvm opens it, the changes that wait for its next start, such as an agent’s new folders devvm restart afterwards, or nothing: without a terminal or with --no-input, the change waits for the VM’s next start
whether to add the Include line to ~/.ssh/config --ssh-config on devvm, devvm host and devvm code
a Claude Code token or a GitHub token devvm secret set NAME --stdin
an agent’s API key, in devvm agent login --api-key --stdin
whether to delete, in devvm rm, devvm gc, devvm gc --caches, devvm images rm and devvm secret rm --force
whether to replace the images built on one, in devvm rebuild --force
whether to replace what devvm’s agent store has, in devvm agent import --force
whether to install a release, in devvm upgrade --force
whether to use the VM made for an earlier folder here, in devvm adopt, or to move a VM to this folder, in devvm adopt VM --force
whether to move the VM made for this folder at the path it had before, in any command on this folder’s VM devvm adopt --force

--force only skips a confirmation, and it never deletes more than the command does without it. A command that would delete something asks first in a terminal, and where devvm can’t ask, it refuses unless you give --force.

A few questions protect work that only you can judge, so no flag answers them, and devvm asks them only in a terminal. They are devvm rm deleting the VM of a folder this one is inside or the VM made for an earlier folder at this path, a --clone VM’s commits that this repo hasn’t fetched and its uncommitted changes, a command giving the VM of a folder this one is inside more access, and devvm agent save saving a VM’s settings for every VM. Where devvm can’t ask, each of them refuses and says what to run instead.

With --no-input, devvm asks nothing even in a terminal, and it never reads an answer from a pipe or a file either. A question that has no usual answer fails instead, after devvm shows the question, and the error names the flag or command that answers it. A question fails the same way when the input ends before an answer, as it does when you press Ctrl+D at the prompt.

Output for scripts

Every command that shows or lists something takes --json, which prints what the command shows as one JSON object instead of a table or lines, so a script can read it. The object’s first field is "version": 1, and the page for each command lists its other fields with an example. A shape only ever gains fields. devvm adds new fields to version 1, and any other change to a shape, such as a field renamed, removed or given another type, comes with a new version.

With --json, standard output gets only the JSON. devvm’s messages, such as warnings and notes, still go to standard error, as they do without it, and the JSON is never colored. A list with nothing in it is [], never null. Sizes are in bytes, unless a field’s name gives the unit, such as memory_gib. A field that doesn’t apply, such as a VM’s from when its base is Ubuntu’s cloud image, is left out.

A command that shows a setting when you run it bare and changes the setting when you give it a value, such as devvm network or devvm size, only shows with --json. devvm refuses a value given with --json, such as devvm network open with --json, and changes nothing.

Command Its JSON
devvm ls --json the project VMs
devvm images --json the images and the shared tool images
devvm tools --json this folder’s VM’s shared tools
devvm size --json, devvm ports --json this folder’s VM’s size and ports, or with -g, new VMs'
devvm network --json this folder’s VM’s network tier and allowlist, or with -g, new VMs’ choice
devvm network log --json this folder’s VM’s network log, or with --blocked its blocks
devvm secret --json the secrets, whether each is saved and the VMs using it
devvm ssh-agent --json this folder’s VM’s SSH agent forwarding and devvm’s own agent’s keys
devvm link --json this folder’s VM’s links
devvm link publish --json the ports this folder’s VM publishes to links
devvm git-protect --json this folder’s VM’s .git protection
devvm history --json the saved exports of agents’ history
devvm space --json what devvm keeps on this machine
devvm retention --json the retention settings
devvm doctor --json what devvm needs on this machine and what’s missing, and it prints nothing else
devvm upgrade --json the newest release and how this devvm was installed, and it installs nothing

Shell completion

devvm completion SHELL prints the shell completion script for bash, zsh or fish. The script completes commands, flags and the image names that devvm build and devvm rebuild take, including layers joined with + after the ones you’ve already typed. It also completes shared tools for devvm tools add and devvm tools rm, the lists that --tools, --agents and --layers take, after the names you’ve already typed and their commas, and all and none for --ports and devvm ports. Load it from your shell’s startup file:

Shell Line In
bash source <(devvm completion bash) ~/.bashrc, with the bash-completion package installed
zsh source <(devvm completion zsh) ~/.zshrc, after compinit
fish devvm completion fish | source ~/.config/fish/config.fish

item.title: Upgrading and uninstalling
item.description:
This page covers upgrading devvm, switching between Homebrew and the install script, and removing devvm with everything it keeps. Each depends on how you installed devvm, and your images, VMs and settings stay through an upgrade or a switch, because they don’t live with devvm. Installing and updating explains what the install script and devvm upgrade check.

Upgrading

To upgrade devvm, run devvm upgrade, which installs the newest release the way you installed devvm:

devvm upgrade # install the newest release, asking first
devvm upgrade --check # say whether a newer release is out, and install nothing
devvm upgrade --force # install it without asking, as a script must
devvm upgrade --to 0.1.0 # install that release, even one older than the devvm you have
devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.1 # install a prerelease, which only --to installs

It says which release it will install in place of the devvm you have, and asks first, so without a terminal or with --no-input it needs --force.

You don’t have to remember to check. When you run devvm in a terminal, it checks at most once a day for a newer release without making you wait, and when one is out it says so in one line that names devvm upgrade. It never upgrades on its own, and release-check = false in config.toml or DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 turns the check off (the release check).

You can also upgrade devvm without devvm upgrade, with the command for the way you installed it:

brew upgrade devvm

If you installed devvm-rc, Homebrew’s formula for prereleases, run brew upgrade devvm-rc instead (trying a prerelease). If you installed devvm with the install script, run the script again, as on Linux.

curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash

Running the install script again installs the newest release.

Your images and VMs stay, because they live in ~/.local/share/devvm, and your settings and layers stay in ~/.config/devvm, apart from devvm itself.

Images whose inputs changed are built again the next time you use them. Existing VMs keep working, and devvm tools update moves a VM to the new shared tools. devvm gc deletes the copies of devvm’s files that older versions wrote out, except those that a VM’s proxy was started with.

How devvm upgrade upgrades

devvm upgrade tells how devvm was installed from where the devvm you ran is, and it never runs anything to find out:

  • With the install script, devvm is ~/.local/lib/devvm/<version>/devvm, and ~/.local/bin/devvm links to it, or the same folders under DEVVM_PREFIX. devvm upgrade downloads the new release and checks it, as What devvm upgrade checks describes. It unpacks the release into a folder of its own beside the devvm you have, runs the new devvm to see that it works, and then switches ~/.local/bin/devvm to it. When anything fails before the new devvm runs through ~/.local/bin/devvm, the link goes back, so the devvm you had stays the one that runs. The version you upgraded from stays in ~/.local/lib/devvm, and so does any older version that a running VM still uses, until a later upgrade finds nothing using it.
  • With Homebrew, devvm is in Homebrew’s Cellar, and devvm upgrade runs brew upgrade devvm after asking, or brew upgrade devvm-rc when you installed the formula for prereleases. Homebrew may upgrade Lima at the same time, because the formula needs it. Homebrew installs the release its formula names, which can come out a little after the release itself, so until then brew upgrade devvm finds nothing to upgrade.
  • Any other way, such as go install, a build from devvm’s source, or a copy of devvm somewhere else, devvm upgrade can’t upgrade. It says how that devvm was installed and how to upgrade it, such as with go install github.com/devvmhq/devvm/cmd/devvm@latest, and fails.

A devvm built without devvm’s release key can’t check a release’s signature, so devvm upgrade refuses to install a release with it and says to run the install script again.

What devvm upgrade checks

devvm upgrade downloads over HTTPS only, and checks each file before it uses the next:

  1. It downloads the release’s SHA256SUMS and its signature, SHA256SUMS.minisig, and checks that devvm’s release key signed it for that release’s version. The key is built into the devvm you have, so a replaced release can’t bring its own.
  2. It downloads the archive for this machine and checks it against its checksum in SHA256SUMS.
  3. It unpacks the archive, which must hold only devvm’s files in one folder.
  4. It runs the new devvm with --version, which must say the release’s version.

When a check fails, devvm upgrade installs nothing, and the devvm you have stays the one that runs. It checks the signature itself, so it doesn’t need minisign on this machine, as the install script does. It never runs a script that it downloaded, only the new devvm’s --version.

An older release

When the newest release is older than the devvm you have, devvm upgrade refuses to install it, even with --force. A server that offers an old release in place of the newest could bring back problems that a newer release fixed, so devvm upgrade never goes back a version unless you name it. devvm upgrade --to VERSION installs the release you name, newer or older, and it asks first, saying when the release is older than the devvm you have. When the devvm you have is a prerelease of a release that isn’t out yet, the newest release is older too, and devvm upgrade says so and installs nothing, without failing (trying a prerelease).

Homebrew installs only its formula’s release, so with Homebrew devvm upgrade doesn’t take --to.

Trying a prerelease

A prerelease is a version of devvm that you can try before its release is out, such as a release candidate, 0.2.0-rc.1, or a beta, 0.2.0-beta.1. devvm upgrade and the install script never pick a prerelease as the newest release, and the daily release check never announces one, so you get a prerelease only when you name it or when you install devvm-rc, Homebrew’s formula for prereleases.

The docs at devvm.dev are for the newest release. The docs for the next release, which a prerelease comes before, are at next.devvm.dev, and they change as that release is written, so they can describe more than a prerelease has.

Versions go in this order: a prerelease comes before its release, a beta before a release candidate, and the numbers in order, so 0.2.0-beta.3 comes before 0.2.0-rc.1, then 0.2.0-rc.2, then 0.2.0.

With Homebrew

Homebrew’s devvm formula always names the newest release, and the devvm-rc formula names the newest prerelease, or the newest release when that’s newer. Both install the same devvm command, so Homebrew installs only one of them at a time. To switch from devvm to devvm-rc, uninstall devvm first, then trust and install devvm-rc:

brew uninstall devvm
brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc
brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm-rc

To install devvm-rc when Homebrew hasn’t installed devvm before, run only the last two lines. Your images, VMs and settings stay, because they don’t live with devvm.

brew upgrade devvm-rc moves to the next prerelease once it’s out, and to the release once that’s out, so devvm-rc never leaves you on an old prerelease. devvm upgrade runs it for you, after asking, and the daily release check announces each newer prerelease and release. Homebrew installs only its formula’s version, so devvm upgrade doesn’t take --to here either.

To go back to releases only, uninstall devvm-rc and install devvm again, after trusting it if you never installed it before:

brew uninstall devvm-rc
brew trust --formula devvmhq/tap/devvm
brew install devvmhq/tap/devvm

devvm installs the newest release, even when that’s older than the prerelease you had.

With the install script

To install a prerelease with the install script, run the copy of the script that comes with the prerelease, which installs that prerelease, or give its version to the newest release’s script with --version:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/download/v0.2.0-rc.1/install.sh | bash
curl -fsSL https://github.com/devvmhq/devvm/releases/latest/download/install.sh | bash -s -- --version 0.2.0-rc.1

When the install script installed the devvm you have, devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.1 installs the prerelease too. Both check a prerelease’s signature and checksum as they check a release’s.

While you run a prerelease that the install script installed, devvm upgrade offers the release it comes before once that release is out, and the daily check says so. It never offers a newer prerelease, such as 0.2.0-rc.2, so install one with devvm upgrade --to 0.2.0-rc.2.

To go back to the newest release before the prerelease’s own release is out, name the newest release’s version, such as devvm upgrade --to 0.1.0. devvm upgrade asks first, because that release is older than the prerelease you have.

devvm upgrade –json

devvm upgrade --json prints what devvm upgrade --check says as one JSON object, for scripts, as output for scripts describes, and installs nothing:

  • current is the version of the devvm you ran.
  • latest is the newest release’s version, which is never a prerelease’s, except with Homebrew’s devvm-rc, where it’s the newest prerelease’s or release’s, whichever is newer.
  • newer says whether that’s newer than current.
  • install is how devvm was installed, install.sh, homebrew or other.
  • path is where the devvm you ran is, its links followed.
{
 "version": 1,
 "current": "0.1.0",
 "latest": "0.2.0",
 "newer": true,
 "install": "install.sh",
 "path": "/Users/you/.local/lib/devvm/0.1.0/devvm"
}

One devvm

Install devvm one way, with Homebrew or with the install script, but not both. With two copies, the one that comes first on your PATH is the one that runs, and brew upgrade devvm may update the one you don’t run. So when Homebrew installed devvm, the install script stops before it downloads anything and says to run brew upgrade devvm instead, or brew uninstall devvm first if you want to use the script, and it names devvm-rc in both commands when that’s the formula you installed. It stops whether or not it runs in a terminal, and its --force installs a second copy anyway.

To switch from one way to the other, remove devvm with the command for the way you installed it, as step 5 of Uninstalling shows, and then install it the other way. Your images, VMs and settings stay, because they don’t live with devvm.

After it installs devvm, the script warns when another devvm comes before ~/.local/bin on your PATH. The warning names that copy’s path and says to remove it, or to put ~/.local/bin before its folder in PATH. devvm doctor warns the same way when the devvm first on your PATH isn’t the one you ran, naming both, and the warning doesn’t make it fail.

Uninstalling

  1. Delete your VMs: devvm ls, then devvm rm in each folder. For a --clone VM, this also removes the devvm git remote from the repo.

  2. Delete the images: devvm gc, then devvm images rm with every name devvm images lists. Images built --from a container image need the same --from: devvm images rm --from node:24 base.

  3. Free Lima’s cache. In a terminal, devvm gc --caches frees devvm’s share of it, after asking. If you don’t use Lima yourself, you can also empty its cache: Lima keeps Ubuntu’s cloud images in ~/Library/Caches/lima on macOS and ~/.cache/lima on Linux, and limactl prune deletes that whole cache.

  4. Delete your saved secrets: devvm secret rm NAME for each one devvm secret lists. On macOS they’re in the Keychain under the service devvm, and on Linux in ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/.

  5. Remove devvm itself, with the command for the way you installed it:

    brew uninstall devvm

    If you installed devvm-rc, run brew uninstall devvm-rc instead. If you installed devvm with the install script, remove it as on Linux.

    rm -rf ~/.local/lib/devvm ~/.local/bin/devvm

  6. Remove its state: rm -rf ~/.local/share/devvm ~/.config/devvm. That includes your layers, in ~/.config/devvm/layers, so copy them somewhere first to keep them. It also includes your exports, the agents’ history that devvm rm saved, and devvm’s agent store, the agents’ settings in ~/.config/devvm/agents and their logins in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins. On macOS, the Time Machine exclusions that devvm set on its CA folders and logins folders go with the folders.

  7. If you let devvm add it, remove the Include ~/.local/share/devvm/ssh_config line from ~/.ssh/config.

item.title: Troubleshooting
item.description:
Each section below starts with what you see, then says what to do, with a link to the details.

A command fails

devvm prints its own steps, and it sends the output of the commands it runs to a log instead of the terminal. When a step fails, devvm prints the end of the log.

To see the commands’ output as they run, add -v or --verbose to any command, as in devvm -v build base or devvm -v. devvm then shows each line on standard error as the log gets it, without the status line, and it still writes the log. The lines are the log’s own, so a VM’s proxy key is hidden in them as it is in the log, and devvm drops the control characters a command prints, so its output can’t move the cursor or change your terminal. When a step fails with -v, devvm names the log instead of printing its end again.

Each run that runs a command has one log, ~/.local/share/devvm/logs/runs/<date>-<time>-<pid>.log, which only you can read, and devvm keeps the newest 20. In the log, each command appears as a + line with its arguments, followed by its output, and a numbered step adds a # [2/5] <step> line first. A command that devvm runs in a VM adds at most 4 MiB of output to the log, because a VM could otherwise fill this machine’s disk with it, and a devvm: truncated line marks where devvm left out the rest. A VM’s proxy key and the build proxy’s password are written as devvm:<key>@. Any other password in a URL, in a command’s arguments or its output, is written as user:<password>@, and so is the password in a proxy’s address without a scheme, such as user:password@proxy.corp:8080, when the address has a port. So a company proxy’s password from your shell’s HTTPS_PROXY, which Lima can print as it starts a VM, stays out of the log, even when a command writes it in pieces. This covers the output of the commands devvm runs in a VM too, such as a VM’s setup or a devcontainer.json’s commands.

Lima keeps a log of its own for each VM, ha.stderr.log in the VM’s folder in devvm’s Lima home, and it writes a proxy password into that log as it starts the VM. Once Lima has started the VM, devvm replaces each password there with as many *, so the log keeps its length and Lima goes on writing to it. If devvm can’t change the file, it warns you and names it, and you can delete the file, which Lima makes again at the VM’s next start.

In a terminal and without -v, a status line shows the step, how long it has run, and the log’s latest line. A step that takes more than a few seconds leaves a line with its time.

A command is refused before it runs

devvm checks a command’s arguments and flags before it does anything else, so a mistyped one never reaches your VM. When one is wrong, such as a missing argument, one too many, a value the command doesn’t take or a flag it doesn’t have, devvm says what the command expected, then names that command’s own help on the last line:

$ devvm ports 5173 8080
devvm: The command devvm ports takes [all|none|LIST], not 5173 8080.
devvm: https://devvm.dev/docs/using/troubleshooting/#a-command-is-refused-before-it-runs
Run devvm ports --help to see how to use it.

Nothing has changed at that point, so you can fix the command and run it again.

Exit codes

devvm exits with one of four codes, so a script can tell what happened:

Code Meaning
0 The command succeeded.
1 The command failed, and devvm’s error says why.
2 devvm refused the command line, such as a bad argument or flag or an unknown command, before anything ran.
130 The command was interrupted by Ctrl+C or a closed terminal (you pressed Ctrl+C).

Two programs can take devvm’s place and exit with their own codes. Once devvm opens a shell in your VM, the shell replaces devvm, so the code is the shell’s, and devvm limactl exits with limactl’s code.

A build fails

When an image’s build fails in its script, or as the build VM starts or stops, devvm keeps the build VM, stopped and without a record, so you can look inside. devvm’s error names the VM and says how to open a shell in it. On Lima, that’s devvm limactl:

devvm limactl shell --start devvm-img-<key>

--start starts the VM first, outside the build’s confinement.

The next build of that image deletes the VM and starts over, and devvm gc also deletes it. A build whose create or clone fails deletes the image, once devvm has shown the end of the log, because there’s nothing in the image to look at.

A first build of base also fails when the packages its VM gives back aren’t exactly the packages apt downloaded, each named by its own checksum with apt’s entry for it. devvm then keeps none of them, so nothing it didn’t check reaches its package cache (base’s packages).

Either way, the images under it, which are already built, stay. devvm deletes and builds again any image it finds without its record, such as a failed build’s or one devvm couldn’t clean up after a crash or a power cut.

Not enough free space

Before each build and each new VM, devvm checks the free space on the disk that will hold it, and it refuses when there’s less than the step needs. With Lima on macOS, that’s 8 GiB for base, 2 GiB for another image or a VM, and from 4 GiB for one shared tool to 8 GiB for all ten, and free space gives the numbers for Linux hosts. The message says which folder’s disk it checked, how much is free and how much the step needs. Nothing has been built or made yet, so you can make room and run the same command again:

  • devvm gc deletes stale and unfinished images and unused shared tool images (cleaning up).
  • devvm images lists the images and shared tool images with the space each takes, and devvm images rm deletes those you don’t need (deleting images).
  • devvm ls lists your VMs, and devvm rm deletes one. devvm never deletes a VM to make room, because a VM may hold work you haven’t saved.

When devvm says it couldn’t read the free space, the error after the message says why, such as a folder it can’t reach.

You pressed Ctrl+C

Ctrl+C, or closing the terminal, stops the command that’s running, cleans up what the run left unfinished, and exits with code 130. A second Ctrl+C doesn’t stop the cleanup. At a question, Ctrl+C ends the run at once, and devvm doesn’t take an answer you type after it, so nothing goes ahead.

devvm deletes an interrupted new VM, with its state, until its first shell opens, because nothing of yours is in it yet. An interrupted build deletes the image it was building.

base can’t build on Lima

On Lima, base starts from a dated release of Ubuntu’s cloud image. The first time devvm builds base, it finds the newest release on cloud-images.ubuntu.com and pins it on this machine, so that build needs to reach Ubuntu’s list of releases and the release’s checksums. When it can’t, devvm says so and pins nothing, so check that you’re online and run the command again. When the newest release doesn’t boot, devvm says so and builds base from the release before it. Once an image is pinned, building base again needs Lima’s cached copy of it or the release itself, which Ubuntu removes after a few months, and devvm rebuild base pins the newest again (Ubuntu’s cloud image).

Building the same base again also needs the copies of its packages that devvm kept from its first build. When one of them is gone or changed, devvm names it and builds nothing, and devvm rebuild base makes a new base with the newest packages (base’s packages).

No package source answers

The first build of base on this machine gets its packages from Ubuntu’s archive, or first from the mirror you set. When neither answers, devvm stops at once and says so, without trying again, and it keeps the build VM stopped as for any failed build. Check that you’re online, and that the mirror’s address is right, then run the command again. Building the same base again later needs neither, because devvm installs the packages it kept from the first build.

Base gets old package lists

The first build of base checks that the package lists it got are as new as the Ubuntu cloud image it starts from, because Ubuntu’s signed lists don’t expire, and a server that stopped updating still serves them. When the lists for one part of the archive, such as resolute-updates, are more than a day older than the cloud image, devvm refuses them, keeps none of the build’s packages and names that part, its date and the image. When you set a mirror, devvm names it, so set ubuntu-mirror to one that’s up to date, or remove it to use Ubuntu’s archive. Without a mirror, the old lists came from Ubuntu’s archive itself, so check that no proxy or cache between you and the archive serves an old copy, then run the command again.

A file devvm can’t read

When devvm can’t read one of its settings or state files, it names the file, and the line when the problem is on one. Fix the line or delete the file. Your settings lists what each file you edit holds, and devvm’s data folder what each file devvm writes holds.

A VM’s own state file, vm.json in its folder in vms/, is the one to fix rather than delete, because it’s what devvm knows of that VM. While devvm can’t read it, every command on that VM fails, and the commands that read every VM leave that VM out and carry on with the rest. devvm ls warns and lists the VM with its name and status alone, when its backend has it, and devvm gc --orphans never forgets it. devvm doesn’t know which shared tools such a VM uses or which folders it mounts, so devvm space, devvm images and devvm gc fail and name the file. devvm also refuses to add a key to its own SSH agent, or to load one into it as a VM starts, because it can’t tell whether that VM mounts the key’s folder.

devvm says a newer release is out

When you run devvm in a terminal and a newer release is out, devvm says so in one line before it opens the VM, and it opens the VM as usual. Run devvm upgrade to install the release, or carry on with the devvm you have, because devvm never upgrades on its own. The line comes from devvm’s daily check, and devvm doctor shows the newest release that check found and the day it found it. When you’d rather not see the line, set release-check = false in config.toml, or DEVVM_NO_RELEASE_CHECK=1 in the environment (the release check).

When devvm never says it, even though a newer release is out, the check may not have run yet, because it runs once a day and the line comes from what it found the time before. It also doesn’t run while you’re offline, without a terminal, with --no-input, for a devvm built from its source, or for a copy that neither the install script nor Homebrew installed. devvm upgrade --check asks GitHub at once.

A newer devvm changed devvm’s folders

devvm’s data folder, ~/.local/share/devvm, and its settings folder, ~/.config/devvm, each record their layout version in a file named version, which says how devvm keeps its files there, and devvm checks both before each command. When either one has a newer version than this devvm’s, a newer devvm has changed the folders, so this one refuses to run rather than misread them, and it names the file and both versions. Run the newer devvm, or upgrade this one to it, for example after going back to an older version by mistake. devvm --version, help and completion still run. An older version is never refused, because devvm changes the folders to its own layout before the command runs, and a folder without a version file gets this devvm’s (the layout version).

devvm names set-id files

On a Linux host, root in a VM can set the set-user-id and set-group-id bits on files in the project folder, and those bits reach this machine, so such a file runs as its owner for anyone who runs it. devvm names these files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped, by devvm stop or found stopped at a launch, but not at a launch into a running VM, because looking through a big folder takes a while. It names the ones that root owns apart from the rest, because those run as root, and it doesn’t look in .git folders.

  • For a file that root owns, don’t run it, and delete it with sudo rm FILE.
  • For any other file, chmod u-s,g-s FILE clears its bits.

Either way, don’t run programs from the project folder outside the VM (files the VM writes).

HOME isn’t an absolute path

devvm finds its folders from HOME, so it stops when HOME is empty or isn’t an absolute path. Set HOME to your home folder, such as /Users/you on macOS or /home/you on Linux, and run devvm again.

A VM shows as unenforced

devvm ls and devvm network show a VM’s tier as unenforced when the VM is on a confined tier but devvm didn’t start it confined. That happens when it was started outside devvm, such as with devvm limactl start, or when it has been running since before devvm network moved it from open to a confined tier, such as with devvm network allowlist. The VM then reaches the network without its proxy.

On the VM’s next launch, devvm offers in a terminal to restart it confined, and if you decline, it warns and goes on. Without a terminal, or with --no-input, devvm stops the VM instead, and the next devvm starts it confined (the self-check).

If you press Ctrl+C while devvm starts a confined VM, devvm stops the VM and its proxy before it exits, so the VM never runs on without the proxy, and the next devvm starts both again confined.

The proxy doesn’t start

A confined VM runs only with its proxy, so when the proxy doesn’t start, devvm stops the VM, and the next devvm starts both again. When devvm says the proxy didn’t start, read the log it names for why. When it says another program took the proxy’s port, devvm picks another port the next time it starts the VM, so run devvm restart. When the proxy doesn’t stop for new settings, run devvm stop, then devvm (the proxy). An open VM runs on when its proxy doesn’t answer it, and devvm warns you, because its tools that use the proxy fail, so run devvm restart, which starts both again.

A request is blocked

On the allowlist tier, a VM reaches only the hosts on its allowlist, and on the none tier only its agents’ and secrets’ hosts. To see what the proxy blocked, run devvm network log --blocked on this machine, or devvm-why in the VM. devvm network log --blocked also shows the devvm network allow command that allows each host, and the rule applies at once, to the next connection (logs).

A tool that skips the proxy fails

On a confined tier, devvm’s transparent mode sends a tool that ignores the proxy settings to the proxy by the names it looks up, over HTTPS and HTTP, on ports 443 and 80 and the ports your allow rules name. Such a tool still fails in these cases, and devvm network log shows nothing for it, because the connection never reached the proxy:

  • A connection refused on another port, such as ECONNREFUSED or Connection refused for db.example.com:5432. devvm-why lists the port under the connections the VM refused lately. Give the tool the proxy’s address in $HTTPS_PROXY or its own setting, or, for HTTPS or HTTP on that port, allow the host with that port, such as devvm network allow db.example.com:8443, which redirects the port within 10 seconds.
  • A protocol that names no host, such as a database’s or SSH, which the proxy refuses and logs as a refused block of transparent.devvm.proxy. SSH in the VM goes through the proxy already, and a database client needs a proxy setting of its own.
  • A DNS error, such as no such host, Temporary failure in name resolution, ENOTFOUND or EAI_AGAIN, which means transparent mode is off for the VM (devvm network transparent), or the VM comes from an image that predates it, which each launch says, and devvm update makes it again from a newer image. Most tools get the error at once. On a Linux host, a few, such as workerd under wrangler dev, wait about 40 seconds for each lookup first, so a tool that seems to hang at its start may be waiting for one.

Some tools read the proxy variables only when a setting of their own turns them on, or never. Turn on the tool’s own proxy setting, so that it uses the environment, or give it the address in $HTTPS_PROXY. Hugo’s resources.GetRemote, for example, uses the proxy only when security.http.proxyFromEnvironment is true in the site’s config (inside the VM).

A server’s port is taken in a confined VM

In a confined VM, transparent mode’s programs listen on the stand-in address 198.18.0.1, on port 53 and on ports 61080 and 61443 and 61100 to 61131, so a server of yours that binds one of those ports on every address, such as 0.0.0.0:61443, fails with EADDRINUSE. Ports 80 and 443 stay free for your own servers. A DNS server of yours on 127.0.0.1:53 binds, but gets no lookups, from the VM or through a forward of port 53, because transparent mode sends them to its own names. Move the server to another port, or turn transparent mode off for the VM with devvm network transparent off, which applies at its next launch (tools that ignore the proxy).

Behind a company proxy

When this machine reaches the internet only through a company proxy and nothing in a VM or a build gets through, check where devvm finds the proxy. devvm reads HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY and NO_PROXY from the shell you run it in, as env | grep -i _proxy shows, and when that shell sets neither HTTPS_PROXY nor HTTP_PROXY, it reads the [proxy] table of ~/.config/devvm/config.toml instead (behind a company proxy). A shell without the settings, such as an editor’s terminal that didn’t load your profile, starts the VM’s proxy without a company proxy, unless config.toml names one. So set the proxy in config.toml, and it works from every shell:

[proxy]
https = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
http = "http://alice@proxy.example.com:8080"
no-proxy = "localhost,.example.com"

config.toml never holds the company proxy’s password. Put only the user in the URL, as above, and save the password with devvm secret set proxy, which asks for it. Then run devvm again in the folder, which starts the VM’s proxy again with the new settings.

When a VM’s proxy went through a company proxy the last time it started and devvm finds none this time, devvm warns you, names config.toml and starts the proxy without one, so the VM’s requests go directly. Set the proxy in that shell or in config.toml, then run devvm restart in the folder.

When devvm says that HTTPS_PROXY, HTTP_PROXY or one of config.toml’s [proxy] keys names an https:// or socks5:// proxy, ask your IT team for the proxy’s http:// address, and set that. A company proxy that inspects TLS also needs its CA, as the next section describes.

Builds behind a company proxy go through a proxy of devvm’s, which allows any host. It sends a name that this machine can’t look up on to the company proxy, which resolves it.

TLS errors behind a company proxy

When apt, npm install, pip install, git clone over HTTPS or an image’s build fails with an error such as certificate verify failed, self-signed certificate in certificate chain or unable to get local issuer certificate, the network you’re on may inspect TLS. Ask your IT team for the CA’s certificate, or export it from this machine’s store, such as Keychain Access on macOS. Put it in ~/.config/devvm/ca and open the VM again (a company’s CA).

When resolving the shared tools’ versions fails because this machine doesn’t trust a server’s certificate, mise’s lines in the run log end with invalid peer certificate: UnknownIssuer. On Linux, put the CA in ~/.config/devvm/ca, or add it to this machine’s own store, as update-ca-certificates does on Debian and Ubuntu, and run devvm again. A bundle that SSL_CERT_FILE names in devvm’s environment works too, because that mise reads it in place of the system’s. On macOS, open the CA’s certificate in Keychain Access and set it to be trusted, because the part of that mise that checks where each tool’s release was built trusts only what macOS trusts.

devvm doctor says so when HTTPS_PROXY or config.toml’s proxy.https is set and the folder has no CA certificates. Many proxies don’t inspect TLS, so that line isn’t a problem in itself. When devvm refuses a file in the folder, it names the file, and you take out anything that isn’t a CA certificate, such as a private key or a server’s certificate.

A listed port isn’t forwarded

When a program on this machine already has a port that the VM lists, devvm warns that the VM doesn’t forward it, and the VM runs on without it. Stop that program, then run devvm restart, or change the VM’s ports with devvm ports, and devvm forwards the port once it’s free (ports).

A VM won’t boot

A Lima VM that doesn’t answer over ssh within a minute of starting is stopped. Read its console log before you start it again, because every start overwrites the log. The log is serialv.log, or another serial*.log, in the VM’s folder in devvm’s Lima home, which is ~/.local/share/devvm/lima/<vm>/ unless you set DEVVM_LIMA_HOME (Lima’s limits).

A VM whose creation didn’t finish

When devvm stops after it made a VM but before the VM was ready, such as when you press Ctrl+C at the wrong moment, devvm never starts that VM. The VM never opened a shell, so nothing of yours is in it. In a terminal, devvm asks whether to delete the VM and make it again, with no as the default. Without a terminal, with --no-input or when you answer no, devvm keeps the VM and says so, and you run devvm rm to delete it, then devvm to make it again.

While another devvm is still making the folder’s VM, such as one waiting for your answers in another terminal, devvm and devvm rm in that folder refuse at once and say so. Finish or stop the other devvm, then run the command again: once the VM is made, devvm opens it.

The folder is gone

When you delete or move a project folder, its VM stays and keeps its disk, and devvm ls writes (gone) after its folder. To keep the VM, move the folder back to its path. To delete it, run devvm rm VM with the name that devvm ls lists, in any folder. devvm asks first, and when the VM is stopped and has an agent, it needs --no-export, because starting the VM to export the history would make the folder again (a VM whose folder is gone).

The folder is on a disk that isn’t connected

When a project folder is on an external disk, a USB stick or a network share that isn’t connected, devvm ls writes (not connected) after its folder, and devvm space names the VM. Connect the disk and the VM works as before. If you mean to delete the VM, run devvm rm VM in a terminal and answer yes, because devvm refuses without one, even with --force, as the disk may still hold the project’s work (a folder on a disk that isn’t connected).

The folder was made again

When you delete a project folder and make a new one at the same path, such as by cloning another repo there, devvm refuses the old folder’s VM. Run devvm rm to delete the old VM, or devvm adopt to give it to the new folder (a folder made again).

An outdated VM, or newer shared tools

devvm warns on each launch when an image the VM was made from has changed, and when there are newer shared tools than the VM’s, and it leaves the VM as it is. Both warnings name devvm update, which moves the VM to the newest shared tools first, without asking. Then, only when the VM’s image has changed, it makes the VM again from the new image, keeping its home folder, the project folder and its settings, after asking (outdated VMs). devvm tools update moves the VM to the newest shared tools alone (adding and removing tools).

A download doesn’t check out

devvm checks Ubuntu’s cloud image and its own mise against checksums before it uses them, and it refuses a download that doesn’t match. Ubuntu’s checksums must also carry a valid signature from Ubuntu’s cloud image key, which devvm checks itself, with nothing to install. When devvm refuses one, try again later, and if it keeps failing, the server or the network between may be serving something else. In the same way, when devvm rebuild base finds Ubuntu’s list of releases ending before the release that base starts from, it says so and keeps that release (Ubuntu’s cloud image).

A new tool release isn’t there yet

A shared tool’s newest release is sometimes not published for every platform yet, such as for a few days after a Node release. devvm then uses the newest older version that is, and says so, and the next daily check tries the newest again. When a release has no download for a VM’s platform yet, try again the next day (versions).

A shared tool doesn’t mount

When a VM can’t mount one of its shared tools, devvm stops the launch with an error that names the VM and the tools, and the VM keeps running. That happens when the tool’s image is missing from the folder that devvm keeps the shared tools in, such as after you deleted it by hand, or when the VM can’t mount the image. devvm doesn’t let the VM download the tool in its place, because that copy would be the VM’s own, a download you didn’t ask for, and one that the VM’s tier may block.

Run devvm tools update in the project folder. It builds the tools that are missing and then opens the shell. When the VM has the newest versions, devvm builds those, and otherwise it builds the newest versions and moves the VM to them. If the launch still stops, the run log says why the VM couldn’t mount the image (a command fails).

A tool that doesn’t mount never keeps the VM from booting. The VM mounts the tools it can and boots as usual, and only devvm’s launch stops (the share).

Reporting a bug

When none of this fixes it, open an issue on devvm’s issue tracker and choose its form for bugs, features, toolchains, built-in layers or docs. The bug report asks for what devvm --version, devvm doctor and limactl --version print, your OS and its version, the command you ran with what it printed, and the run log (a command fails). devvm hides a VM’s proxy key and passwords in the log, but it can still hold folder names, host names and a command’s output, so read it before you paste it. A security problem goes to private vulnerability reporting instead, never to a public issue.

item.title: Known limits
item.description:
These are the things devvm can’t do, everywhere, on Linux hosts and on Intel Macs.

Everywhere

  • devvm runs on macOS and Linux only, not on Windows (requirements).
  • Shared tools are read-only, so a tool can’t update itself or add components, for example with rustup component add (details).
  • A layer goes in and comes out by making the VM again. A layer’s script changes the VM’s disk, so devvm layer add gives a VM more layers by making it again, and everything on its disk but its home folder is lost (details). devvm layer rm takes layers out in the same way (details). Shared tools go in with devvm tools add and come out with devvm tools rm, and the VM’s disk stays as it is (details).
  • --from takes only Debian-, Ubuntu- and Alpine-based images, and Alpine, Debian 12 (node:24) and Ubuntu before 26.04 on arm64 build with unpinned packages (details).
  • Agent folders that you make or delete on this machine reach a running VM only after a restart, which devvm offers (details).
  • Ports are forwarded over TCP only, and forwarding every port means every port from 1024 up. You can tunnel UDP over a forwarded TCP port with socat (details).
  • Links between VMs carry TCP over IPv4 alone, and a container in a VM reaches them only with --network host (details).
  • Tools that ignore the proxy settings reach a confined VM’s proxy only over HTTPS and HTTP to a host by name, on ports 443 and 80 and up to 32 more that your allow rules name. Other ports, protocols that name no host in their first bytes, such as a database’s, addresses in URLs, HTTP/3 alone and IPv6 alone need the tool’s own proxy settings, and a client that doesn’t trust the VM’s CA sees a certificate error for a blocked HTTPS host (details).
  • Changing a running VM’s ports closes the connections that are open through its forwards (details).
  • With Lima, project paths can’t contain commas, folder names in VM names are cut short, and disks grow but never shrink (details).
  • File watchers in a Lima VM don’t see the edits you make on this machine, only those made in the VM, so set a dev server that should reload on your edits to poll the project folder (details).

Linux hosts

  • .git protection is read-only in the VM’s view, not a lock on the host’s files, so after a git command on this machine replaces .git/config while the VM runs, the VM can change or replace the new file until devvm locks it again. devvm names each such file when the VM stops (details). A VM whose .git/config or hook has another name doesn’t start, and the VM can’t rename a file between the working tree and .git (details).
  • Where the kernel doesn’t let devvm use a user namespace, such as on Ubuntu 23.10 and newer, there’s no .git protection. devvm warns about it at each launch, and it names the .git hooks and config that changed, but only after the fact, so use --clone there (details).
  • VMs mount the project folder with 9p instead of virtiofs, so file watchers in a VM also miss the VM’s own changes in the folder’s subfolders, and need polling there (details).
  • New VMs cache the project folder with the none mode, because Linux’s 9p client loses data with Lima’s mmap. A VM made before devvm chose none keeps mmap, with a warning at each launch, until you run devvm mount-cache none (details).
  • A program can’t map a file in the project folder for shared writing, and gets Invalid argument, such as LMDB, which Parcel’s .parcel-cache and Gatsby’s cache use, numpy’s memmap in r+ or w+ mode, Java’s read-write mappings and the mold linker. Keep their files on the VM’s own disk, or use a --clone VM (details).
  • SQLite’s WAL mode fails in the project folder unless the connection sets PRAGMA locking_mode=EXCLUSIVE first, while SQLite’s default journal works. Use a --clone VM for a project that needs WAL mode, as its repo is on the VM’s own disk, or keep the database outside the folder (details).
  • Set-id bits that root in a VM sets on files in the project folder reach the host, and devvm names such files when it makes a VM and once a VM is stopped (what to do).
  • devvm keeps your secrets in files under ~/.local/share/devvm/secrets/, which only you can read, instead of the Keychain (details).
  • devvm has no Time Machine to keep VMs’ CAs out of, so keep ~/.local/share/devvm/vms out of your backups (details).

Intel Macs

devvm has a release for Intel Macs, which the install script and Homebrew install, but nobody has tested it on one yet. The tested systems are Apple silicon Macs and Linux on arm64 and x86_64, so on an Intel Mac, VMs, --from and the network tiers’ confinement may fail in ways that devvm’s tests haven’t caught.

item.title: devvm
item.description:
Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first

Synopsis

Open a shell in this folder’s VM, at the same path, and create the VM first when the folder has none. devvm shows what a new VM gets, and in a terminal you can customize its toolchains, coding agents, layers, tier, ports and size, which –tools, –agents, –layers, –network, –ports, –cpus, –memory and –disk choose without asking. The VM mounts only this folder read-write, and with –clone it gets its own clone of the repo instead.

devvm [flags]

Examples 

 devvm # open this folder's VM, choosing what a new one gets
 devvm --agents claude # create the VM with Claude Code and the toolchains the folder needs
 devvm --tools node --agents none --layers docker # create the VM with node and the docker layer alone
 devvm --clone # create the VM with its own clone of this repo
 devvm ls # list every VM

Options 

 --agents LIST the LIST of coding agents a new VM gets, such as claude,codex, or none (default: devvm setup's)
 --clone create the VM with its own clone of this repo, or of each repo in this folder, instead of mounting the folder
 --cpus N the N CPUs the VM gets (default: devvm size -g, else the image's)
 --disk GiB the VM's disk in GiB, at least the image's (default: devvm size -g, else the image's)
 --from IMAGE the container IMAGE base starts from, such as node:24, instead of Ubuntu's cloud image (default: $DEVVM_FROM)
 -h, --help help for devvm
 --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside
 --layers LIST the LIST of layers a new VM's image gets, bottom first, such as docker,mine, or none (default: devvm setup's)
 --memory GiB the VM's memory in GiB, such as 16 or 16G (default: devvm size -g, else the image's)
 --network TIER the network TIER a new VM gets: open, internet, allowlist or none, or learn for internet while it learns the hosts it needs (default: devvm network -g's, else allowlist)
 --no-devcontainer create the VM without reading the folder's devcontainer.json
 --no-git-protect create the VM without .git protection
 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own
 --ports PORTS the PORTS the VM forwards: all, none or a list like 5173,8000-8010 (default: devvm ports -g, else all)
 --repos LIST the repos a --clone VM of a folder of repos gets: all, none or a LIST of their paths, such as frontend,backend (default: a picker in a terminal)
 --ssh-agent create the VM with your SSH agent forwarded, so anything in it can use your keys while you're connected
 --ssh-config add devvm's Include line to ~/.ssh/config without asking
 --tools LIST the LIST of toolchains a new VM gets, such as node,python, or none (default: those the folder's files call for)
 --unsafe-folder mount a folder devvm refuses, such as your home folder
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line
 --version print devvm's version

The docs page for devvm explains it in full.

item.title: devvm adopt
item.description:
Give this folder the VM made for an earlier folder or path

Synopsis

Give this folder the VM made for an earlier folder at this path, or for this folder before you moved or renamed it, with its files, secrets and allowlist. With VM, its name as devvm ls lists it, devvm moves that VM here from a folder that’s gone, such as one you copied to another disk. devvm asks first in a terminal without –no-input.

devvm adopt [VM] [flags]

Examples 

 devvm adopt # give this folder the VM, after asking
 devvm adopt --force # give it without asking, as a script must
 devvm adopt devvm-web-71a99b1076d92c # move that VM here from a folder that's gone, after asking

Options 

 -f, --force don't ask to confirm, which devvm needs without a terminal or with --no-input
 -h, --help help for adopt

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm adopt explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm: Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first

item.title: devvm agent
item.description:
Fill devvm’s store of the agents’ settings and logins that every VM gets

Synopsis

devvm keeps the coding agents’ settings in ~/.config/devvm/agents and their logins in ~/.local/share/devvm/logins, and every VM with an agent gets them from there, never from the agents’ own files in your home folder. devvm agent login saves a login made in this folder’s VM, devvm agent import copies those files into the store once, and devvm agent save copies a VM’s settings into it.

devvm agent [flags]

Examples 

 devvm agent login codex # log Codex in, in this folder's VM, for every VM
 devvm agent import # copy every agent's settings and logins from this machine
 devvm agent import codex # copy only Codex's
 devvm agent save # copy the settings of this folder's VM's agents, after showing what changed

Options 

 -h, --help help for agent

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm agent explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm: Open a shell in this folder’s VM, creating it first
  • devvm agent import: Copy the agents’ settings and logins from this machine into devvm’s store
  • devvm agent login: Log an agent in, in this folder’s VM, and save the login in devvm’s store
  • devvm agent save: Copy the agents’ settings from this folder’s VM into devvm’s store

item.title: devvm agent import
item.description:
Copy the agents’ settings and logins from this machine into devvm’s store

Synopsis

Copy the settings and logins of AGENT, claude, codex, opencode or pi, or of every agent, from your home folder into devvm’s store, never their history. It follows no link out of an agent’s folder, and it asks before replacing what the store has.

devvm agent import [AGENT...] [flags]

Examples 

 devvm agent import # copy every agent's settings and logins, asking before replacing the store's
 devvm agent import claude codex # copy only Claude Code's and Codex's
 devvm agent import --force # replace the store's without asking, as a script must

Options 

 -f, --force don't ask to confirm, which devvm needs without a terminal or with --no-input
 -h, --help help for import

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm agent import explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm agent: Fill devvm’s store of the agents’ settings and logins that every VM gets

item.title: devvm agent login
item.description:
Log an agent in, in this folder’s VM, and save the login in devvm’s store

Synopsis

Log AGENT in inside this folder’s VM, and keep the login in devvm’s store for every VM with the agent, which gets only placeholders. claude logs in to your Claude subscription in a browser on any machine, whose code you paste back, or gets a long-lived Claude Code token with –setup-token. codex and opencode log in to ChatGPT in a browser on this machine, or with a code with –device-code, or save an API key with –api-key, which is pi’s only login.

devvm agent login AGENT [flags]

Examples 

 devvm agent login claude # log Claude Code in to your Claude subscription
 devvm agent login claude --setup-token # get a Claude Code token with claude setup-token instead
 devvm agent login codex # log Codex in to ChatGPT in a browser on this machine
 devvm agent login codex --device-code # log in with a code, in a browser on any machine
 devvm agent login opencode --api-key --provider anthropic # save opencode's Anthropic API key, asking for it
 devvm agent login pi --api-key --provider openai # save pi's OpenAI API key, asking for it

Options 

 --api-key save an API key instead, asking for it
 --device-code log in with a code to type into a browser on any machine, so nothing is forwarded
 -h, --help help for login
 --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside
 --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own
 --provider PROVIDER with opencode's or pi's --api-key, the PROVIDER it's for: anthropic, deepseek, google, groq, mistral, openai, openrouter or xai
 --setup-token with claude, get a long-lived Claude Code token with claude setup-token instead
 --stdin read the secret from a line of input, without asking

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line

Docs

The docs page for devvm agent login explains it in full.

See also

  • devvm agent: Fill devvm’s store of the agents’ settings and logins that every VM gets

item.title: devvm agent save
item.description:
Copy the agents’ settings from this folder’s VM into devvm’s store

Synopsis

Copy the settings of AGENT, claude, codex, opencode or pi, or of every agent this folder’s VM has, from the VM into devvm’s store, so every VM with the agent gets them, never its logins or history. It shows what changed and asks first, so it runs only in a terminal without –no-input, and devvm starts a stopped VM for it.

devvm agent save [AGENT...] [flags]

Examples 

 devvm agent save # show what changed in every agent's settings, then save them
 devvm agent save claude # save only Claude Code's

Options 

 -h, --help help for save
 --here use this folder's own VM, never that of a folder it's inside
 --parent use the VM of the nearest folder this one is inside, even across a git repo of its own

Options inherited from parent commands 

 --no-input never ask, and fail where devvm would ask, naming the flag that answers it
 -v, --verbose show the output of the commands devvm runs instead of a status line
